$comment: Metals, ores and industrial minerals for the C64 tree. 'shared' maps an id to a full node object; other subsystem files should link to those ids with the "ref" children form ("children": ["metal.alumina"]). Nodes that are not in `shared` are still defined once inside the root.children branches and can be referenced by id the same way.

root.name: Metals, ores and industrial minerals
root.description: Every mineral stream behind a 1982 Commodore 64: the quartzite that becomes silicon, the bauxite and cryolite that becomes aluminium foil, the porphyry copper that becomes PCB track and transformer magnet wire, the tin and lead that become 63/37 solder, the iron ore and coke that become the steel chassis and the transformer laminations, and the specialty metals - gold, silver, nickel, tantalum, zinc, chromium, manganese, cobalt - that end up plating contacts, filling ceramic capacitors and setting the sinter point of every solder joint. Each branch runs from the finished metal down to the quarry, the open pit, the evaporite bed or the seabed.

children.name: High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)
children.description: The refined element every chip in the machine is cut from. A 1982 Commodore 64 mainboard carried a handful of silicon dies and one 2 MHz quartz crystal, both traceable to this chain: quartzite or silica reduced to 98-99% metallurgical silicon, chlorinated to trichlorosilane, distilled to 9-nines, deposited as polysilicon, then pulled as a single Czochralski crystal. Note that the 6510 is NMOS, so the 1982 die uses ALUMINIUM gate metal and thermally grown field oxide, not a polysilicon gate; the polysilicon branch below is the industry feedstock route, which is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

facts.label: Feedstock purity
facts.value: 9N-11N (99.9999999%) for modern polysilicon; 6N-7N typical of the 1982 era

facts.label: Route
facts.value: trichlorosilane / Siemens

facts.label: Boron budget
facts.value: B must be held near 1 ppb; boron is the contaminant that made metallurgical silicon unusable directly

facts.label: Siemens deposition
facts.value: trichlorosilane reduced by hydrogen on UHF-heated silicon rods held at 1050-1150 C

facts.label: Boron
facts.value: the killer impurity: metallurgical silicon stays unusable until boron is below about 1 ppb

children.name: Czochralski monocrystalline ingot
children.description: Where the polysilicon chain ends and the semiconductor business begins. A 2 kg charge is melted at 1414 C in a silica crucible over a seed crystal, and a slow pull at 0.5-2 mm/min with rotation grows a 75-150 mm boule under high-purity argon. Every defect the 6510 die carried - dislocations, oxygen precipitates, the dopant gradient along the length of the ingot - was frozen in during this pull. The ingot is then sawn, lapped and polished into wafers, and the MOS structure is grown and etched on the wafer.

facts.label: Pull rate
facts.value: 0.5-2 mm/min

facts.label: Boule diameter
facts.value: 75-150 mm, yielding 6510 dies of roughly 3-6 mm

facts.label: Ambient
facts.value: high-purity argon over the melt

children.name: Fused quartz growth crucible
children.description: The crucible the melt sits in is made from the same silicon chain one step further down, from high-purity quartz fused in vacuum or wet hydrogen to knock out the alkali that would poison a p-type wafer. It is expensive, fragile, and replaced every few hundred pulls.

facts.label: Fusing temperature
facts.value: ~2000 C in vacuum or wet H2

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: a few hundred growth runs in 1980s practice

children.note: Crucible life varied enormously with melt temperature discipline; treat as order of magnitude.

children.name: Thermally grown silicon dioxide (SiO2)
children.description: The gate oxide, the field oxide and the photoresist mask oxide of a 1982 NMOS die are not bought - they are grown out of the silicon itself. A wafer goes into a 1000-1150 C steam or dry-oxygen furnace for an hour and a half and roughly a thousand angstroms of SiO2 comes off the wafer, consuming about 0.1% of its thickness. The machine's entire insulation is therefore chemically the same element as the chip, oxidised in place, and the 6510's gate dielectric is aluminium on oxide rather than a polysilicon gate.

facts.label: Gate oxide
facts.value: ~1000-1500 A in a 1982 NMOS process

facts.label: Wet vs dry
facts.value: dry O2 for the thin gate oxide, wet steam for the thicker field oxide

children.note: Judgement call: the oxide is grown on the wafers sliced from the boule, not on the ingot, so the parent edge is loose. Kept under the crystal pull because that is where the silicon chain leaves the minerals business and becomes a device; the furnace-and-photoresist process that grows and etches it belongs to the logic fragment.

children.name: 2.048 MHz quartz clock crystal
children.description: The C64's timing reference: an AT-cut quartz plate about 7.6 x 2.5 mm brazed between metal caps, resonating at 2.048 MHz. Quartz is the only material with a usable temperature-stable mechanical resonance that cheap. The plate itself is usually not natural rock - it is hydrothermally grown synthetic quartz in an autoclave of sodium hydroxide solution at about 400 C and 1.5 kbar.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 2.048 MHz (PAL/NTSC master clock)

facts.label: Cut
facts.value: AT-cut, ~35 degrees rotation

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: order 10-50 ppm across 0-70 C for a consumer part

children.name: Grow the clock crystal hydrothermally
children.description: A seed of vein quartz hangs in aqueous sodium hydroxide in a steel autoclave at 380-450 C and 100-200 bar, and quartz grows on the seed at 1-3 mm a day until a synthetic boule of a few kilograms is complete. The advantage over mined Brazilian rock is that the growth conditions are repeatable, so the Q and the defect density of every boule match. By 1982 synthetic quartz had displaced natural rock for essentially all consumer resonator production, because natural material had to be hand-selected for Q and the supply of good vein quartz was small and variable.

facts.label: Growth rate
facts.value: 1-3 mm/day

children.note: The vein quartz is the charge in the autoclave, so the edge is really an ingredient. It is a child edge because that is how this file records what a charge is made of, and because it keeps the published metal.quartz node inside the branch instead of stranded in unlinked.catalogue.

children.name: Sodium compounds: caustic soda and soda ash
children.description: Sodium is not in the machine as a metal, but the C64 could not exist without it: caustic soda dissolves bauxite to make alumina, and the same chlor-alkali industry that makes the caustic soda also makes the chlorine and hydrogen that become the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Behind both sits a bed of rock salt or a bucket of evaporite from a solar salt pan.

children.name: Soda ash (Na2CO3)
children.description: Sodium carbonate, the second half of the sodium story. It goes into glass (a huge 1980s user, though the glass agent owns that branch), into detergents, and into the Bayer plant as the carbonate that lime converts back into caustic. The Solvay process, still the dominant route in 1982, makes it from salt, limestone and coke in a solution-and-precipitation tower - no molten salt, no electrolysis.

facts.label: Solvay tower
facts.value: ~10 m diameter, 20-30 m tall, cooled to about -10 C at the top

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl, then 2 NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O

facts.label: Net
facts.value: 2 NaCl + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaCl2

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: order 1 t of CaCl2 brine per t of soda ash

children.name: Carbonation tower and the rotary calciner
children.description: A 20-30 m steel tower with a conical bottom, fed at the top with ammoniated brine and in the side with CO2 from the lime kilns. Sodium bicarbonate precipitates as a fine white slurry in the upper third and settles into the cone; the temperature is held near 40 C because below that the ammonium chloride in the liquor crystallises out and fouls the tower. Bicarbonate is then calcined at 200-250 C in a rotary kiln to soda ash.

facts.label: Tower temperature
facts.value: near 40 C at the precipitation zone

facts.label: NH3 loss
facts.value: order 0.1-0.3 t ammonia per t of soda ash, mostly vented

children.note: Tower internals varied; the conical settler is universal.

children.name: Make ammonia from coke in the gasworks
children.description: In 1982 most ammonia in the soda industry still came from the gasworks: coke plus steam and iron passed over a hot carbonaceous catalyst, then cracked to nitrogen and hydrogen. Natural gas-based steam reforming had largely displaced this in North America and Western Europe, but coke-based ammonia remained standard in India, China and much of Eastern Europe - which is where much of the world's soda ash, and hence much of its glass, was made.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: iron promoted with K2O, or activated coke

children.name: The lime kilns that feed the Solvay tower
children.description: The Solvay process needs carbon dioxide and it gets it by burning limestone in a shaft kiln beside the tower, in the same way a sugar mill burns bagasse. The kiln gas, after the dust is knocked out and the gas is cooled and scrubbed, is about 40-45% carbon dioxide on a dry basis - lower than the 98% a dedicated CO2 plant would produce, but it came free with the lime the process also needed. The Solvay works was therefore a self-contained chemical plant that took limestone and salt and made soda ash, calcium chloride and CO2 in one site.

facts.label: Kiln
facts.value: shaft kiln, 1000-1100 C, beside the tower

facts.label: CO2 concentration
facts.value: 40-45% dry after dust removal

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: the lime itself, sold to steel and to agriculture

children.name: Causticise the spent brine to recover the salt
children.description: The Solvay process does not consume the salt: the ammonium chloride in the spent brine is causticised with lime back to ammonia and sodium chloride, and the brine is re-saturated. The plant therefore closes its salt loop, and its only real consumption is limestone and energy and the ammonia. That closure is the whole reason Solvay was so cheap for a century and why it was so hard to displace until the chlor-alkali-soda ash route had caught up.

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NH3 + CaCl2 + 2H2O

facts.label: Re-saturation
facts.value: brine is re-saturated with mined salt and returned

children.note: Medium confidence on the salt consumption figure; the chemistry is standard.

children.name: Lime (CaO) and calcium
children.description: Lime is one of the most-used industrial chemicals there is, and this tree touches it in four places: the Bayer plant uses it to desilicate and to causticise, the blast furnace uses limestone directly as flux, the PCB fabricator regenerates ferric chloride etchant and neutralises with it, and the metallurgical silicon and tin circuits use lime as a flux and a scavenger. Lime is roasted limestone; limestone is quarried rock.

facts.label: Kiln temperature
facts.value: 1000-1100 C in a vertical or horizontal lime kiln

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2

facts.label: Loss on ignition
facts.value: ~44% by weight; a 100 t kiln yields roughly 56 t of CaO

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke, coal fines or anthracite depending on local availability

facts.label: Slaking
facts.value: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 is exothermic and adds about 65% to the mass

children.name: Shaft and rotary lime kilns
children.description: Limestone plus coke or coal in a vertical shaft 20-40 m tall, or on a rotary kiln, at 1000-1100 C. The vertical kiln - a stack of alternating layers of 250 kg limestone and 40 kg coke in a 2.5-4 m shaft, fired from the bottom - makes the good lime, because the counter-current gas gives a soft, well-calcined product; the rotary kiln makes it faster and is what a captive lime plant at a steelworks or a Bayer refinery used. A 300 t/day shaft kiln is a small plant by industrial standards and there were thousands of them.

facts.label: Shaft kiln
facts.value: 20-40 m tall, 2.5-4 m diameter, 250 kg limestone per 40 kg coke

facts.label: Rotary kiln
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long, inclined, 100-1000 t/day

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: ~110-130 kg coke or coal per tonne of CaO, or ~80 kg in a rotary kiln with a preheater

children.name: The counter-current shaft kiln
children.description: Because limestone goes in at the top at ambient temperature and lime comes out at the bottom at 1000 C, the shaft has to be a heat exchanger as well as a kiln, and that is why a shaft kiln makes a better lime than a rotary one. The gases go up, the stone goes down, and the last of the fuel burns out in the upper third. Below the burn zone the calcination is isothermal, so the lime is not over-heated and does not shrink the kiln's yield.

facts.label: Zones
facts.value: drying, preheating, calcination, burning, cooling

facts.label: Burn zone
facts.value: the upper third of the shaft

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 80-90% of theoretical lime

children.note: Zone layout is standard practice; medium confidence on the yield range.

children.name: The rotary kiln and the preheater
children.description: A 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long rotary kiln, inclined a few degrees, turning 1-3 rpm, heated by a burner at the lower discharge end with coal, coke or gas, and fitted at the upper end with a preheater or a flash dryer for the limestone. The rotary kiln makes worse lime than the shaft kiln - the residence time varies through the bed and the lime is over- and under-burnt - but it makes it faster and it copes with a variable feed, so a captive plant at a steelworks or an alumina refinery used one. A 2000 t/day rotary lime kiln is the sort of thing that sits next to a coke-oven battery.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long, 100-1000 t/day

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: pulverised coal, coke, anthracite or gas, at about 80 kg per tonne of CaO with a preheater

children.note: Medium confidence; the fuel figure assumes a preheater, which is where most of the saving is.

children.name: Overburnt lime and the clinker problem
children.description: If a lime kiln burns a stone too hot for too long, the lime grains sinter together into hard 'clinker' and the lime is unusable: it slakes too slowly and lumps in the mixer. Overburnt lime is a real fraction of the output of a poor kiln and it has to be screened out or ground. The same failure happens in a captive lime kiln feeding a blast furnace, where the operator is watching the furnace's slag chemistry and the lime plant's temperature curve at the same time. It is a small thing and it is a good illustration that lime is a feed, not a commodity.

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: overburning: local temperature above about 1200 C for too long

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: the grains sinter; the lime slakes slowly and lumps in the mixer

children.note: Medium confidence; the mechanism is standard.

children.name: The lime kiln gas and its CO2
children.description: A lime kiln makes carbon dioxide as its main product, roughly 0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, and in 1982 that gas was usually burnt or dumped because there was nowhere to put it. Its two real uses were the Solvay tower, which is built beside its lime kilns, and - much later - the emerging practice of feeding kiln gas to a nearby chemical plant. So the limestone quarry behind a C64's case carries a hidden carbon footprint that did not become an engineering problem until the 1990s.

facts.label: CO2 yield
facts.value: ~0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, plus the fuel

facts.label: 1982 fate
facts.value: burnt for heat, or vented; the sequestration era had not arrived

children.note: Medium confidence; the stoichiometric yield is certain, the 1982 disposition is a generalisation.

children.name: Slaking: quicklime to hydrated lime
children.description: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, releasing about 65% more mass and enough heat to boil water. Slaking is done in a pan with a rotating rake, or in a ball mill in the paper industry, and the product is a fine white powder or a milk. It is done at the steelworks, at the water treatment plant and at the board fab's causticisation circuit. The safety point that every plant's training programme is about is that a lump of quicklime dropped into a drum of water will split the drum.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, +64% by mass, strongly exothermic

facts.label: Solubility
facts.value: about 1.7 g/L at 20 C - enough to be caustic, not enough to be a base

children.name: Lime in Portland cement
children.description: By far the largest single use of lime in the world, and the reason the business had a global price: about 90% of all lime produced goes into cement, and cement is the second-largest industrial material after steel. The route is the one already in this branch - limestone, kiln, CaO - and then the clinker: 75-80% limestone with 20-25% clay or shale in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, and the resulting clinker ground with 3-5% gypsum. A C64's case was painted, not cemented, but the cement industry is the reason lime is cheap, and it is a legitimate side door out of this branch.

facts.label: Lime share of lime demand
facts.value: ~90% goes into cement

facts.label: Clinker
facts.value: 75-80% limestone, 20-25% clay, fired at 1450 C in a rotary kiln

facts.label: Gypsum
facts.value: 3-5% added at the cement mill to control the set

children.name: Causticise and desilicate the Bayer liquor
children.description: Two unrelated jobs in one plant. Lime added during digestion converts reactive silica (kaolinite) into an insoluble calcium silicate, which would otherwise lock up alumina permanently - the single most important reason a high-silica bauxite is unprocessable. Lime also drives the causticisation step, converting the sodium carbonate that accumulates in the Bayer liquor back into caustic, and it helps precipitate iron and titanium as hydroxides. Dosage was order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite digested.

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite

facts.label: Desilication reaction
facts.value: kaolinite + lime -> calcium silicate hydrate, permanently wasted

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3

children.note: Dosage range varies with ore; medium confidence.

children.name: Causticise the carbonate back to caustic soda
children.description: The Bayer liquor's sodium carbonate is converted back to caustic with lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, and the calcium carbonate drops out as a filter cake that is a by-product of every tonne of alumina. The cycle is the industry's real control loop, because the caustic that leaves in the red mud is replaced by buying new caustic or by buying lime and causticising it, and the choice is mostly about what lime is available near the refinery. It is also why a bauxite refinery is nearly always built next to a limestone quarry.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3

facts.label: Reactor
facts.value: a stirred causticiser with a settler and a filter

facts.label: Caveat
facts.value: this reaction is reversible; it only goes far enough because the carbonate is continuously removed and the liquor stays dilute

children.note: Medium confidence; the reversibility of the causticisation is the textbook caveat.

children.name: Pre-desilicate the ore by attrition washing
children.description: By 1982 the more elegant answer to high-silica bauxite had arrived and it needs no lime at all: wash the ore. An attrition scrub and a desliming step take out the kaolinite clay before the ore ever meets the caustic, and a gibbsitic ore washed this way can digest without lime at all. The cost of the process is a lot of water and a lot of clay tailings - and the tailings are the same red mud, just produced earlier and with less soda in it. So the industry moved from a chemistry problem to a solids-handling problem, which is a recurring theme in aluminium refining.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: attrition scrub followed by desliming at about 40-60 um

facts.label: Removes
facts.value: typically 1-4% of the mass as clay, which was 10-40% of the reactive silica

facts.label: Trade
facts.value: less lime and less caustic consumed, more water and more tailings

children.note: Medium confidence; the adoption rate was highly ore-dependent.

children.name: Flux the blast furnace slag with limestone and lime
children.description: The furnace needs its slag liquid at 1450 C, and calcium is how you get there: CaO absorbs silica into a calcium silicate slag whose liquidus is around 1300-1400 C, so the slag runs off the tuyeres before the iron does. The burden carries roughly 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal, deliberately paired with a silica content of about 0.4-0.6 mass units of SiO2 per unit of CaO.

facts.label: Burden rate
facts.value: order 0.25-0.35 t limestone per t hot metal

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: slag basicity CaO/SiO2 of roughly 1.0-1.3

children.note: Typical burden practice; specific works ran tighter ratios.

children.name: Regenerate ferric chloride etchant with lime
children.description: At the board fab the copper etchant is ferric chloride: CuCl2 + FeCl3 -> CuCl + FeCl2, and the ferric is regenerated by blowing air through the spent bath, which is where a great deal of the chlorine chemistry of PCB etching comes from. Lime then raises the pH and drops the copper out as copper hydroxide so the iron can be reclaimed, and lime also neutralises the acid process streams downstream of the etcher. The board's own etch chemistry belongs to the board subsystem; what matters here is that the reagent traces back to a limestone quarry.

facts.label: Regeneration
facts.value: FeCl2 + air/Cl2 -> FeCl3; then CuCl2 + Ca(OH)2 -> Cu(OH)2 + CaCl2

children.name: Lime as a slag flux in tin, lead and silicon smelting
children.description: Beyond alumina and iron, lime shows up as a cheap flux wherever a siliceous slag has to stay liquid and the impurity has to be dumped: tin smelting adds lime to pull silica and some tungsten into the slag, the lead sinter and blast furnace charge roughly 15-25% limestone, and calcium compounds are added to the silicon furnace feed to mop up alumina. It is the general-purpose garbage collector of the metals industry.

facts.label: Lead sinter
facts.value: order 15-25% limestone in the sinter mix

children.note: Snelter lime practice is very smelter-specific; medium confidence.

children.name: Potassium chloride (KCl) for tantalum reduction
children.description: Not a C64 component - potassium never appears in the machine - but it is a mandatory reagent in the tantalum branch, because the metal is won as a fluoride salt and reduced with metal, not from an oxide. Potassium also divides tantalum from niobium in the fluoride chemistry. It is included so the tantalum branch reaches a real, mined leaf instead of stopping at an implied reagent.

facts.label: Consumers
facts.value: potash fertiliser dominated; tantalum metallurgy a small but non-negotiable share

children.name: Sylvinite (KCl + NaCl)
children.description: The ore of the Devonian Prairie Evaporite in Saskatchewan, mined underground at 800-1100 m by potash shafts where the ground is artificially frozen so the salt stays put, or by solution mining in Ontario. Run of mine is about 8-14% K2O; it is beneficiated by flotation or hot leaching and sold as muriate of potash.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 8-14% K2O; sylvinite typically 15-25% KCl

facts.label: Method
facts.value: shaft mining with freeze-assisted ground support, or solution mining

children.name: Potash evaporite bed
children.description: The leaf: a buried evaporite sea - sylvinite interbedded with halite, carnallite and mudstone, formed by the same evaporation of a restricted sea that made the salt used in chlor-alkali. The Colville and Hatchet lakes area of Saskatchewan sits over one of the largest.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: 750-1200 m in the Saskatchewan basin

children.name: Freeze the ground around the potash shaft
children.description: The Saskatchewan potash ore is 800-1100 m down in a bed that is 30-40 C and gassy, and it is a weak, water-bearing shale-like rock that would flow into the shaft. The solution since 1967 has been to freeze it: brine is circul through freeze pipes in the shaft and the decline for two to three years before sinking, turning the ground into a self-supporting frozen plug of ice and salt. It works, and it is one of the more unusual pieces of mining engineering anywhere - and it is the reason the Saskatchewan potash industry looks the way it does.

facts.label: Freezing time
facts.value: 2-3 years before sinking

facts.label: Freezing temperature
facts.value: about -10 C

facts.label: Rock temperature in the seam
facts.value: 30-40 C, which is what makes freezing necessary

children.name: Potash flotation and hot leaching
children.description: Run-of-mine sylvinite is about 12% K2O with a lot of NaCl and clay. Beneficiation is by flotation of the sylvinite in a saturated KCl-brine solution (because sylvinite is barely soluble while halite is much more so, so the brine selectively wets the sylvinite), or by hot leaching at 85-100 C which dissolves the potassium chloride and leaves the salt. For the tantalum industry the relevant product is not potash at all - it is the KCl that goes into the K2TaF7 precipitation.

facts.label: Flotation
facts.value: in a saturated KCl or NaCl brine, with amines or fatty-acid collectors

facts.label: Hot leach
facts.value: 85-100 C, dissolves KCl and leaves halite

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 60-95% KCl, sold as muriate of potash

children.note: Both routes are standard; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split between them in Saskatchewan (hot leaching is more common in the USSR and Canada east of Saskatchewan).

children.name: Muriate of potash and its tailings
children.description: The product is 60-95% KCl, bagged or bulk, and the waste is a slurry of NaCl and clay that goes into a tailings pond impoundment. Two points of interest for this tree: the potassium chloride that ends up in a potassium fluoride bath for the tantalum reduction is bought from this industry, and the tailings pond is a genuinely large hole in the ground - the Belle Plaine potash mine near Esterhazy had a tailings pile that became, by the 1980s, a place people went to watch birds. So a fertilizer industry byproduct is where the tantalum industry gets its potassium.

facts.label: Tailings
facts.value: NaCl and clay slurry, pumped to a lined impoundment

children.note: Medium confidence on the specific Belle Plaine details; the waste-impoundment issue is well documented.

children.name: Move the potash out by unit train to the port
children.description: Saskatchewan potash moved to world markets by unit train - a dedicated train of a hundred or more hopper wagons - to Vancouver, Prince Albert or Minneapolis, and then by ship from Vancouver or by barge and lake freighter to Chicago. So the potassium in a 1982 tantalum capacitor travelled down a potash shaft, through a washer and a flotation plant, into a bulk railcar, onto a ship, and into a plastics extruder. It is the most ordinary logistics chain in the tree and it is the shortest path from a geological process to a metal part.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: unit trains of hopper wagons to Vancouver or Prince Albert, then ship or lake freighter

children.note: Medium confidence on the specific rail and port routes; the Saskatchewan potash logistics are well documented.

children.name: Solution mining of potash
children.description: Where the potash seam is deeply buried and thin - as at Thames, Ontario - the shaft is not worth sinking. Instead two horizontal wells are drilled into the seam, one to inject hot water and one to draw the resulting brine, and the potash is recovered from the brine by evaporation. Two wells can produce a million tonnes a year. It is a solution-mining technique borrowed from the salt industry and it works because sylvinite dissolves in hot water while the clay it sits in does not.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: two horizontal wells, hot water injection and brine recovery

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 1 Mt/year from a single pair of wells

facts.label: Suitable where
facts.value: deep, thin, uniform seams with impermeable roof

children.note: Medium confidence; the Thames operation is well documented.

children.name: The injection and recovery well pair
children.description: Solution mining is two wells and a plant. A cemented well is drilled horizontally into the potash seam and a casing is set with a perforated liner; hot water at 80-90 C is injected at a pressure of a few hundred psi, the seam is about 1-3 m thick and dissolves over a 30-200 m horizontal section, and a second well 500 m away draws the brine back. The well field is fracked between the wells to connect the fracture, and the plant evaporates the brine in a multiple-effect evaporator. It is a genuine engineering oddity - a mine with no mine - and it works because potash dissolves in hot brine and clay does not.

facts.label: Injection
facts.value: hot water at 80-90 C, a few hundred psi, along a 30-200 m horizontal well

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: a second well about 500 m away

facts.label: Extraction
facts.value: multiple-effect evaporation of the brine

children.note: Medium confidence; solution mining of potash at Thames and Belle Plaine is well described in the mining literature.

children.name: Potassium chloride as the tantalum flux
children.description: The only reason potassium is in this tree. Potassium chloride is added to the tantalum fluoride solution to precipitate K2TaF7, and potassium fluoride is used as a flux in some silicon and aluminium processes. Both are bought from the potash industry as a commodity, in tonnes. So a handful of grams of tantalum in a C64's capacitors required a few grams of potassium chloride, which required a shaft in Saskatchewan or a pond on the Dead Sea, which required a bed of evaporite. It is the shortest branch in this file and the funniest, because it starts with an ocean drying up.

facts.label: Use
facts.value: precipitating K2TaF7 from the fluoride solution

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: the potash industry, as a 60-95% KCl commodity

children.name: Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion
children.description: Where the C64's aluminium comes from. Bauxite is dug, digested in caustic soda to alumina, and electrolysed in molten cryolite to 99.7% metal - about 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne, the largest single industrial electricity draw anywhere in this tree. The ingot is then DC-cast to a rolling ingot and rolled down to 6-25 um foil for the electrolytic capacitors in the power supply, to sheet for the case and shield cans, and extruded for the heat sinks. Note that the capacitor foil and the plain foil are different jobs for the same rolling mill.

facts.label: Typical chain
facts.value: ~1.5-2 t bauxite -> 1 t alumina -> 0.50-0.52 t aluminium

facts.label: Hall-Heroult energy
facts.value: 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne of aluminium; 1980s plants commonly ran 15,000-17,000

facts.label: Why the number has not moved
facts.value: 2.1 V theoretical cell voltage against 3.5-4.5 V in practice, and 80-90% current efficiency

children.name: Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts
children.description: The most-used metal after iron, and in a C64 it is everywhere the electricity goes and everywhere the heat has to leave. The PCB tracks are 35 um copper foil on 1.6 mm FR-4; the switch-mode transformer is wound with 0.2-0.4 mm enamelled magnet wire; the rectifiers and the regulator leadframes are copper; the edge connector fingers and the heatsink mounts are copper alloy. All of it starts as porphyry ore at 0.4-1% Cu, which is why copper smelters are, in the 1980s, as much sulfuric acid plants as they are metal plants.

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% Cu in porphyry; US average fell to ~0.55% by 1980

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) cathode, LME Grade A at 99.9935%

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~100 t of 0.6% ore -> 1 t of concentrate at 28% Cu -> ~0.3 t of Cu metal in the concentrate

children.name: Porphyry copper ore (0.4-1% Cu)
children.description: A porphyritic intrusion - a granite-textured quartz monzonite that has been split by its own crystallisation and had its cracks filled with hot copper-bearing fluids. The copper minerals are chalcopyrite CuFeS2, bornite and chalcocite Cu2S, covellite and enargite Cu3AsS4. The ore body is graded by porphyry systems but the grade is low and getting lower, which is the whole problem with the industry. In 1982 the great producers were Chuquicamata and El Teniente in Chile, Bingham Canyon in Utah, Butte, the Arizona porphyry belt, Oyu Tolgoi and the Escondida development, and the copper belt of northern Zambia.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% Cu, 0.3-5% S, 1-5 g/t Au and Ag as by-product credits

facts.label: Main minerals
facts.value: chalcopyrite CuFeS2, chalcocite Cu2S, bornite, covellite, enargite

facts.label: Overburden
facts.value: 50-200 m of barren porphyry and oxidized capping above the sulphide

facts.label: Decline
facts.value: average US head grade fell from ~0.9% in 1960 to ~0.55% by 1980

children.name: Open-pit copper mine
children.description: An enormous terraced pit. Ore is drilled and blasted on 15 m benches, loaded into haul trucks by 3-6 cubic metre shovels or loaded onto a conveyor, and hauled in 100-150 tonne trucks out of the pit on ramps. The waste:ore ratio at a mature porphyry pit is often 2-5:1, which is why the waste dumps are larger than the pit. As the pit deepens into the ore, block caving takes over: a fracture zone is undercut and the ore caves into a series of drawpoints, and the mining cost per tonne collapses - El Teniente in Chile was the world's largest block-cave operation from 1958 onwards.

facts.label: Bench height
facts.value: 12-15 m, blasted

facts.label: Waste:ore
facts.value: 2-5:1 in the mature part of a large porphyry pit

facts.label: Truck capacity
facts.value: 80-150 t; the haul road is often ~1 km round trip per lift

facts.label: Block caving
facts.value: ore broken by a cave above drawpoints, recovered by gravity; production 20,000-100,000 t/day at the largest operations

facts.label: Alternate method
facts.value: long-hole stoping with delayed blasting, used underground when the orebody is steep and deep

children.name: Block cave drawpoints and ore pass
children.description: The block cave is the deepest and most sophisticated piece of 1980s mining engineering anywhere near a C64: a slot is cut along the base of the ore block, the slot is blasted, the overlying ore fractures and subsides into the void, and a finger stoper trains stop releasing ore once the cave front has moved past a drawpoint, to stop surface subsidence from outrunning the cave. Ore falls 100-1000 m to a conveyor at the bottom. Throughput per drawpoint is low - a few hundred tonnes a day - so a big block cave has hundreds of them.

facts.label: Draw height
facts.value: 100-1000 m of vertical ore pass

facts.label: Drawpoint production
facts.value: order 100-800 t/day each

facts.label: Controls
facts.value: finger stopers, or chutes with flow-control doors in modern installations

children.note: Drawpoint rates are mine-specific; medium confidence on the range.

children.name: Tertiary porphyry intrusion
children.description: The leaf: a granodiorite or quartz monzonite stock, once liquid and now frozen, with the copper-bearing sulphide veins filling fractures and disseminated grains through it. Under a 100 m of leached, iron-stained capping lies the transition ore and then the primary sulphides, so the pit's first 50-150 m of material is nearly worthless and has to be hauled anyway.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: granodiorite / quartz monzonite porphyry with hydrothermal alteration

facts.label: Oxidation profile
facts.value: leached zone, then mixed sulphide-secondary enrichment, then primary sulphide

children.name: The haul road, the ramp and the truck cycle
children.description: The economics of an open pit are a haulage problem. A 130-tonne truck on a 2 km round trip from the loading point to the crusher, at about 25 km/h loaded and 40 km/h empty, takes 3-5 minutes per cycle including spotting and loading, so a shovel with a 4-second loading cycle needs about 6-8 trucks to keep it fed. The ramp grade matters enormously - every 1% of extra grade costs roughly 1-2% of the truck's payload - and so does where the crusher is put. A large porphyry pit moves 100,000-400,000 tonnes a day, and the fleet is 100-400 trucks.

facts.label: Truck
facts.value: 100-150 t payload, 25 km/h loaded

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 3-5 min, so 6-8 trucks per shovel

facts.label: Ramp grade
facts.value: 8-10% typical; every extra 1% costs payload

facts.label: Fleet
facts.value: 100-400 haul trucks at a large porphyry pit

children.note: Medium confidence on the cycle times and the grade penalty; both are well documented in mining engineering but vary by operation.

children.name: Suppress the pit dust on the haul road
children.description: A 100,000 t/day pit with unsuppressed haul roads produces a very large tonnage of airborne dust, and by the 1970s that had become a legal problem: the Clean Air Act of 1970 and the 1974 federal mine-safety inspection regime both applied to metal mines, and the pit had to water its roads, restrict the speed on unpaved haulage, and in the worst cases stop blasting in a high wind. So the environment is a genuine node in the middle of the ore chain, not a decoration at the end of it, and it is the same regulation that produced the sinter-plant dust precipitator in the steel branch.

facts.label: Control
facts.value: road watering, speed limits on unpaved haulage, blast restrictions in wind

facts.label: Regime
facts.value: Clean Air Act 1970 and the federal mine-safety inspection regime of 1977

children.note: Medium confidence on the specific US regulatory application to metal mines; the controls themselves are standard.

children.name: Crushing and grinding to 100-150 um
children.description: The ore arrives at 1 m. It goes through a gyratory crusher, then a semiautogenous mill (which uses the ore itself as the grinding medium, so no steel balls to pay for at that stage), then one or two ball mills in a closed circuit with a spiral classifier and then a cyclone. Autogenous grinding came in during the 1970s and was fully established by 1982 because it both saved the grinding media cost and produced a much cleaner surface - less steel contamination matters when you are about to float it. Before the mill a 1500-4000 t/h gyratory with a screen at 25-50 mm does the primary crushing, and a 100 g charge goes to the fire assay for total copper while a leach assay of the fines gives the recoverable copper - the difference between the two, the oxide and the locked-up copper, is the number that becomes the contract between the mine and the mill. The grind has to be fine enough to liberate chalcopyrite but not so fine that the froth washes out.

facts.label: Product size
facts.value: P80 of 100-150 um for a porphyry flotation feed

facts.label: Typical circuit
facts.value: one 1.2-1.8 m semiautogenous mill plus two 1-1.2 m ball mills, or SAG plus ball in series

facts.label: Power
facts.value: order 35-55 kWh per tonne of ore ground

facts.label: Steel contamination
facts.value: why autogenous was adopted: iron in the concentrate poisons the smelter

facts.label: Primary crushing
facts.value: 1500-4000 t/h gyratory, screened at 25-50 mm

children.name: Forged steel grinding balls
children.description: Even in an autogenous circuit the ball mills need some steel, and the balls themselves are a ferroalloy product: rail steel or scrap forged and quenched. Hardness matters more than anything - a 1982 ball mill ran 100-150 mm balls in the harder grind, and the wear rate was the plant's second-biggest cost after power. Nickel and chromium in the steel were deliberately kept low here, unlike in a crusher liner.

facts.label: Ball size
facts.value: 100-150 mm for a coarse grind in 1980s practice

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.05-0.2 kg of balls per tonne of ore ground

children.note: Consumption depends heavily on the abrasive index of the ore; medium confidence.

children.name: Froth flotation of chalcopyrite
children.description: The slurry is conditioned with lime to a pH of 8-9.5 and with a xanthate collector, then aerated in a bank of 20-50 cubic metre rectangular cells. Air bubbles pick up the particles of chalcopyrite that the collector has made water-repellent and float them into a froth; the gangue stays in the water. Each cell in a bank is stage-controlled, with a froth of 100-300 mm. In 1982 the workhorse collector was sodium or potassium ethyl xanthate, made from carbon disulphide, caustic soda and ethanol, and the frother was pine oil or a synthetic such as methyl isobutyl carbinol.

facts.label: pH
facts.value: 8.0-9.5, set with lime or soda ash

facts.label: Cell size
facts.value: 20-50 m3 rectangular cells, 5-15 in series

facts.label: Concentrate grade
facts.value: 20-30% Cu; about 0.3 t of concentrate per tonne of Cu metal

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 85-92% in a porphyry circuit

facts.label: Collector
facts.value: potassium ethyl xanthate, 5-30 g/t

children.name: Ethyl xanthate collector (SIPC)
children.description: Xanthate is the workhorse flotation reagent, and it is a petrochemical in disguise: carbon disulphide (from natural gas or from coke-oven gas and methane) reacts with ethanol and caustic soda. Potassium and sodium ethyl xanthates were the standard 1980s collectors for sulphide copper, with a frother on top. So the flotation chemistry that recovers copper in 1982 depends on a sulphur-and-alcohol chain that ends in a gasworks, not a mine.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CS2 + C2H5OH + KOH -> C2H5OCS2K + H2O

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: 5-30 g/t of concentrate collector

children.note: Dosage varies with mineralogy and water chemistry; medium confidence on the range.

children.name: Carbon disulphide (CS2)
children.description: Carbon disulphide, the feedstock for every xanthate collector and for the rayon and cellophane industries, was made in 1982 almost entirely from natural gas or from methane recovered from coke-oven gas: the gas and a fraction of hydrocarbon oil are passed over a silica or alumina gel at 600-700 C, and the carbon disulphide is condensed out. So the flotation collector that separated copper from a porphyry in Nevada was made from gas, and the same molecule went into the rayon that was in the 1980s' idea of a flame-retardant textile. It is a leaf of the copper branch that is unambiguously a chemical plant rather than a mine.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: methane plus naphtha over a silica or alumina gel at 600-700 C

facts.label: Product
facts.value: carbon disulphide, condensed out of the gas stream

children.note: Medium confidence; the CS2-from-methane route is well documented.

children.name: Lime and soda ash as pH regulators
children.description: Flotation needs the ore surfaces clean of slime and the water at a controlled alkaline pH, or the xanthate decomposes to xanthic acid and carbon disulphide and evaporates. Lime from a limestone kiln is the cheapest and most common regulator; soda ash where lime is unavailable; and in the deep concentrators of Chile and Arizona the process water has to be lime-treated hard before use because the Andean water is very soft and very acid.

facts.label: Water treatment
facts.value: lime softening to remove carbonate hardness where process water is soft

children.name: Pine oil and MIBC frothers
children.description: Frothers are oily surfactants that stabilise the air-water interface. Until the 1970s the standard was pine oil distilled from pine stumps and mill residues - a forestry residue, not a mineral. Pine oil was being displaced by methyl isobutyl carbinol, a petrochemical, precisely because the natural supply was limited and the synthetic one gave a more stable froth.

facts.label: Pine oil
facts.value: alpha-terpineol-rich fraction, from kraft and sulphite pulp-mill residues

facts.label: Synthetic
facts.value: MIBC (methyl isobutyl carbinol), fully synthetic by the 1980s

children.note: The pine oil to MIBC transition is well documented in mineral processing literature; medium confidence on exact 1982 split.

children.name: Copper flotation concentrate (~25-30% Cu)
children.description: A damp, fine, almost black powder shipped by rail or truck to the smelter. What the smelter really wants is not the copper but the sulphur, because that is what makes the smelter a sulfuric acid plant. A 25% Cu concentrate is roughly 50% sulphur and 10% iron, and the smelter's job is to burn out the iron, keep a copper-iron matte, and send every tonne of SO2 to an acid plant.

children.name: Thicken, filter and ship the flotation concentrate
children.description: The flotation concentrate at 25-30% Cu arrives as a pulp at 10-20% solids and has to be dewatered to 8-12% moisture to be shipped, because shipping water is shipping money. A 30,000 t/day concentrator produces 1,000-3,000 t of concentrate a day, and it is thickened in a 30-50 m diameter tank, filtered on a vacuum belt or a plate-and-frame press, and often dried to 8% on a steam belt dryer so it does not cake in a railcar. Copper concentrate that arrives wet is worth less per tonne and smelters charge for the water.

facts.label: Moisture in
facts.value: 10-20% solids by weight from the flotation circuit

facts.label: Moisture out
facts.value: 8-12%, or dried to about 8%

facts.label: Dewatering
facts.value: thickener, then vacuum filter or filter press, then a belt dryer

children.note: Medium confidence on the specific flowsheet; the practice is standard.

children.name: Flash smelting of concentrate to copper matte
children.description: Concentrate, silica flux and limestone are dropped into a vertical reverberatory shaft where a hot gas blast, 40-60% oxygen-enriched, burns the concentrate as it falls. Three reactions happen simultaneously: the sulphides oxidise to copper oxide and iron oxide, the oxides react with each other to form a copper-iron matte, and the iron oxide reacts with the silica flux to make a slag. The furnace runs at 1250-1400 C and the products settle into three layers - matte at the bottom, slag above it, and offgas above that - which are tapped separately. By 1982 the flash furnace had largely displaced the reverberatory furnace: it is smaller, faster and needs less fuel, and it works on concentrate straight from the flotation circuit with only a small amount of dried concentrate added as fuel.

facts.label: Dried concentrate as fuel
facts.value: order 0.15-0.35 t per tonne of charge

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: CaO/SiO2 held around 1.0-1.5 so the slag stays fluid

facts.label: SO2 strength
facts.value: 10-14% SO2 in the flash furnace offgas, which the acid plant takes

children.note: Copper smelting has barely changed since the 1980s; the industry still runs flash furnaces and Peirce-Smith converters today. The changes since are in slag cleaning and in higher oxygen enrichment.

children.name: Silica flux from a sand quarry
children.description: The smelter adds sand or quartzite so that the iron in the concentrate can be thrown off as a slag instead of entering the matte. The quartz is often a cheap nearby dune sand - which is exactly the same material the glass industry buys, and the reason a copper smelter in the 1980s had a sand dryer and a small silica prep plant. The flux is dosed so the slag's silica content matches what the concentrate brings.

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: quartz sand or quartzite, sized 0.1-1 mm

facts.label: Addition
facts.value: order 5-15% of the dry concentrate weight

children.name: Industrial silica sand (quartz dune sand)
children.description: Siliceous sand from a dune or a beach, washed, screened and often magnetically separated to take out the heavy mineral concentrates that would be a nuisance. This is a distinct node from the silicon-grade quartzite: the purity required here is far lower, and this sand is a commodity that the foundry, the glass and the copper industries all pull on. The quartzite that goes into the silicon furnace is a different, much rarer rock.
places: map of the Mississippi valley dune sands

facts.label: Processing
facts.value: wash, screen, dry, magnetite separation; <150 um for foundry and smelter use

facts.label: Vitrified silica
facts.value: used in foundry moulds and in fused silica, at 99.9%+

children.name: Aeolian dune sand and beach placer
children.description: The leaf: quartz grains rounded by wind or wave, in an unconsolidated surface deposit a few metres to tens of metres thick sitting on older sediment. Dunes along the Mississippi valley, the Great Lakes shorelines and the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States were the standard sources, mined with bucket-wheel or dragline dredges - a sand mine is the commonest kind of open pit in the world.

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: surface dune and beach sand, over bedrock or older sediment

children.name: The flash furnace, its tuyeres and the concentrate burn
children.description: The furnace is a 20-25 m tall, 5-7 m diameter vertical shaft with a refractory lining, fed by a few hundred tonnes an hour of dried concentrate through a hopper, and blown at the bottom by 30-60% oxygen-enriched air through tuyeres. The concentrate burns as it falls - it is the fuel as well as the charge - so the furnace needs almost no external heat. The reaction happens in the first metre above the tuyeres, the particles are spent, and the matte and slag settle into the two-deep bath at the bottom. The shaft above is used to preheat the charge with the rising offgas, and a flash furnace treats more tonnage in less volume than anything else in smelting.

facts.label: Shaft
facts.value: 20-25 m tall, 5-7 m diameter, refractory lined

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: 200-600 t/h of dried concentrate

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: two layers: matte at the bottom, slag above

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: the concentrate is both the charge and the fuel, so the furnace is close to thermoneutral

children.name: Peirce-Smith converter to blister copper
children.description: The matte from the flash furnace is charged into a horizontal cylindrical steel converter with refractory lining and is blown with air through tuyeres along the side. The iron in the matte oxidises preferentially and goes into a slag that is skimmed off the top every few hours; once the iron is gone the copper sulphide itself oxidises to copper metal and gives off SO2. The blow takes 4-8 hours and takes 1 t of 60% matte to roughly 0.85 t of blister copper at 98-99% purity, still containing iron, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. The converter is a batch process and by the 1980s it was the target of the new continuous technologies (Noranda, Inductokemco) that were not yet commercial.

facts.label: Converter diameter
facts.value: 3.5-4.8 m, holding 30-120 t of charge

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: iron silicate, skimmed through the converter mouth

children.note: The Peirce-Smith converter remained the dominant technology into the 2020s, accounting for roughly 90% of world matte refining.

children.name: Fire-refine the blister copper
children.description: Blister copper still carries arsenic, antimony and bismuth, and every one of them is a nightmare for the electrolytic tankhouse because they float to the cathode and destroy the deposit. So the blister is ladle-refined: an oxidising slag of sodium carbonate with the impurities skims off, and then the copper is under-oxidised by dropping in green charcoal to reduce the whole mass back to copper, with the arsenic floatationised out. Where the arsenic is high, the refinery buys a second, smaller furnace.

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: As, Sb and Bi down to 0.02-0.1% before anode casting

facts.label: 1982s practice
facts.value: outright refining in the converter or in a tilting launder furnace; anode casting with a low-As anode became the later route

children.note: There was real variation in refinery strategy between operators in this era; medium confidence on specifics.

children.name: The Peirce-Smith converter and its tuyeres
children.description: The converter is a cylindrical steel shell, 3.5-4.8 m inside diameter and 8-10 m long, on trunnions so it can be tilted, lined with magnesite brick, with 20-40 tuyeres along one side at the trunnion line. Air at 30-50% oxygen is blown in at 5-10 bar through water-cooled tuyeres that must be cleared and re-cleared by hand every few hours as the lining erodes - and a tuyeres that is not cleared becomes a plug and the whole heat is lost. The operator tilts the converter so the slag runs out of the mouth, then charges back, and there is no continuous process anywhere else in smelting with quite that much manual involvement. It is the machine that has been unchanged since 1865, and it is still the standard.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: 3.5-4.8 m diameter, 8-10 m long, on trunnions

facts.label: Tuyeres
facts.value: 20-40, water-cooled, hand-cleaned of lining several times a heat

facts.label: Lining
facts.value: magnesite brick, eroded by the oxidising slag

facts.label: Slag removal
facts.value: the converter is tilted so the slag pours out of the mouth

children.note: Medium confidence; the Peirce-Smith converter geometry is very well documented.

children.name: Blister copper anode, 99.9%+
children.description: Blister is poured into a horizontal straight-mould casting machine - a ladle of molten copper that pours into a row of cast-iron moulds on a moving chain, giving a rectangular anode of 200-500 kg, roughly 700-1000 mm long, 400-800 mm wide and 30-50 mm thick, with a hanging loop cast on top. In 1982 the standard anode assay was 99.5-99.9% copper, and the gold and silver in it - typically 5-30 g/t gold equivalent - is why anodes are not made to 99.99%: that would be throwing away money.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 200-500 kg per anode, 25-50 mm thick

facts.label: Casting method
facts.value: horizontal straight-mould casting machine with a water-cooled chain

children.name: Electrolytic refining of copper to 99.99%
children.description: The refinery's tankhouse is a building a couple of hundred metres long containing rows of concrete or rubber-lined steel cells. Each cell holds a 150-250 g/L copper, 200-250 g/L free sulfuric acid solution at 55-65 C, with one or two anodes and one cathode per cell. Current at 20,000-40,000 A per cell is passed through; copper dissolves off the anode and plates onto the cathode at 98-99% efficiency, and gold, silver, selenium, tellurium and the platinum group fall out as a sludge on the bottom of the cell - the anode slime - which is worth more per tonne than the copper. A refinery producing 100,000 t a year has 300-500 cells and about 100,000 MWh of DC power.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: 40-60 g/L free Cu2+, 180-230 g/L free H2SO4, 10-25 ppm Fe/As/Bi

facts.label: Current density
facts.value: 10-30 A/m2; 1980s plants commonly 20-25

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 0.15-0.35 V; power about 200-250 kWh per tonne of copper

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) cathode, LME Grade A 99.9935%, one cathodic plate ~1 m x 1 m, 50-125 kg

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: anode 4-28 days, cathode 4-14 days, by plate weight

children.note: Tankhouse technology has changed very little since 1982; the later innovation was more automation and the move to higher current density with ion-exchange purification.

children.name: Starter sheets, seeding and the tankhouse floor
children.description: Everything in a tankhouse depends on nucleation. The cathodes start on stainless steel or titanium starter sheets, or on copper seed plates that have been roughened. If too many nuclei start, the deposit is dull and soft and hard to strip; if too few, it is bright and hard and needs a big shear force. The whole art is seeding the right number. The electrolyte is also circulated at 200-400 mm/s across the cell face, because the anode slime would otherwise build up and short.

facts.label: Starters
facts.value: stainless steel or titanium, or roughened copper seed plates

facts.label: Circulation
facts.value: 200-400 mm/s across the cell face

facts.label: Slime removal
facts.value: a travelling scraper on the cell floor

children.note: Medium confidence; the seeding practice is proprietary.

children.name: Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts
children.description: Tin is the metal that made electronics solderable. On a 1982 C64 board there are roughly 3,500 through-hole joints and most of them are joined with a lead-tin alloy, so there is a couple of hundred grams of tin per machine. Tin also does two other jobs in the machine: it is the coating on tin-plated steel (tinplate, though a home computer case is not canned food) and it is the facing on tin-plated copper-alloy switch and connector contacts, where it stops the copper from tarnishing and gives a low and stable contact resistance.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.9-99.97% Sn; electrolytic refining reaches 99.97-99.99%

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: cassiterite, SnO2, at 0.2-1.5% Sn in alluvial and lode deposits

children.name: Tin smelting: reduction of SnO2 with carbon
children.description: Cassiterite is one of the easiest oxide ores to reduce: SnO2 + C -> Sn + CO2 goes at only 1200-1400 C, far below copper or iron, because tin's oxides are unstable. The Malaysian and Indonesian smelters in 1982 were reverberatory or electric furnaces on 5-20 t capacity, fired with coke, charged with concentrate and about 15% limestone as a flux, and tapped a crude tin at 99.5-99.8% in maybe eight hours. The furnace is a long, narrow, brick-lined box with a step grate at the firebox end, so the charge moves gradually forward and meets rising temperatures - a reverberatory used for a purely solid-solid reaction, which is why tin smelting smells of SO2 only when the concentrate is sulphide.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: SnO2 + 2C -> Sn + 2CO; below 1200 C the reduction is too slow

facts.label: Reagent
facts.value: coke or anthracite, 15-25% of concentrate mass

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: 15% limestone, to take silica into the slag

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: iron and silica with some tin left in it - the usual tin smelter loss is 1-3%

children.note: Tin smelting is one of the few pyro-metallurgical processes that did not move to electric furnaces until well after 1982.

children.name: Roasting of fluorine-bearing Bolivian concentrate
children.description: Bolivian concentrates carry fluorine, which would carry through into the tin as a stubborn impurity. So they are roasted at 600-800 C before smelting to drive off the fluorine as HF and the arsenic as arsenic oxide, and the hot gas is scrubbed with lime to make calcium fluoride before release. That lime scrub is a genuine environmental control fitted in the 1970s and 1980s, and it is one of the reasons the smelters are the only tin plants with a scrubber.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 600-800 C in a rotary or fluidised-bed roaster

facts.label: Offgas scrub
facts.value: limestone slurry neutralises the HF, giving calcium fluoride

children.note: Applied mainly to Bolivian and Brazilian concentrates; medium confidence on the exact scrub chemistry.

children.name: Dry, sieve and mix the smelter charge
children.description: Cassiterite concentrates are roasted if they carry fluorine or arsenic, dried to remove the 8-12% moisture, and sieved - because a reverberatory furnace with fine charge in it just makes dust. The charge is then mixed with the limestone flux and the coke, in the ratio that gives 15-20% flux and 15-25% reductant. Nothing about this is clever and everything about it is critical: an Indonesian smelter that got the coke ratio wrong lost a few percent of its tin into the slag, which at 3% is a third of its margin.

facts.label: Moisture in concentrate
facts.value: 8-12%, dried before charging

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: 15-20% limestone

facts.label: Reductant
facts.value: 15-25% coke or anthracite

children.note: Medium confidence; the ratios are typical of Southeast Asian practice.

children.name: The tin smelter's slag and its tin loss
children.description: A tin smelter loses 1-3% of its tin into the slag, and the slag is a silicate of iron and silica with tin locked up in it. Recovering that tin is a separate business: the slag is crushed and re-smelted, or in Malaysia and Brazil it was re-smelted in a small furnace to recover the tin. A tin smelter therefore has a second, smaller smelter, and the discipline of a tin plant is judged by its recovery, which is why the industry published recovery figures with a seriousness that most primary metals do not.

facts.label: Loss to slag
facts.value: 1-3% of the tin in the charge

facts.label: Recovery route
facts.value: slag retreatment, historically by resmelting

children.note: Medium confidence on the loss figure; it varies with the slag basicity and the furnace.

children.name: Fluid-bed reduction of fine cassiterite (post-1982 route)
children.description: Worth noting as the direction the industry went in rather than as 1982 practice: the fine concentrates that a gravity circuit now produces reduce easily in a fluidised bed at 850-1000 C, which is a temperature no reverberatory furnace can hold at its hearth. This process is why the modern tin industry uses much less coke and produces much less CO. In 1982 essentially none of this existed.

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: lower carbon and lower reductant per tonne; adopted after 1985

children.note: Deliberately a sibling of the smelting step rather than part of it, and kept at era=modern: fluid-bed reduction did not exist in the 1982 window, when the reverberatory and electric furnaces were the industry's actual practice. CHECKLIST 7 wants later practice labelled, not hidden.

children.name: Refine the crude tin to 99.9%
children.description: Crude tin at 99.5-99.8% still carries iron, copper and arsenic, and the difference between 99.5% and 99.9% matters enormously for solder because iron is a solder poison and raises the liquidus. Two routes. Liquation, the old one, melts the crude tin at about 400 C: tin melts at 232 C, so the iron and copper stay solid and bottom out, and the clean tin is drawn off. Electrolysis, the modern one, uses a stannic chloride or a fluorostannate bath and gives 99.97-99.99%. Malaysia ran electrolysis; Bolivia's low-grade concentrate still used liquation.

facts.label: Liquation
facts.value: melt at 380-400 C; iron and copper stay solid

facts.label: Electrolysis
facts.value: SnCl2/SnCl4 or Na2SnF6 bath; 99.97-99.99% Sn

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: iron above ~0.1% wets badly and raises the melting range of solder

children.name: Lead: the base metal of 63/37 solder
children.description: Lead is the soft, low-melting, cheap half of the solder alloy, and it is the reason soldering works at all: pure tin wets copper badly and has no strength, and pure lead does not wet anything. Lead also has its own huge pre-electronics industrial life - storage batteries, cable sheath, pigment - and its 1982 smelting industry is the oldest continuous industrial process in the book. The C64 carries a couple of hundred grams of it, which is why the machine is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.99% (4N); 'corroding lead' at 99.99% was the standard for 1980s solder manufacture

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: galena PbS at 2-15% Pb

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~100 t of 5% Pb ore -> ~15 t of 60% Pb concentrate -> ~5 t of crude lead -> ~4.7 t of refined lead

children.name: Roasting/sintering of galena to PbO
children.description: The concentrate is roasted in a sinter plant: a travelling grate on which a 1-2 m bed of concentrate is ignited and slowly drawn through with the gas being pulled after the fire. The sulphide oxidises to lead(II) oxide: 2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2. The point of sintering rather than fluidised-bed roasting is that the heat can be high and localised enough to sinter the fine particles into a coherent porous cake, which is exactly what the blast furnace needs to breathe. The sinter is 50-60% Pb and the SO2 - at 10-14% - goes to the acid plant, the same one the copper smelter uses.

facts.label: Sinter machine
facts.value: Dwight-Lloyd travelling grate, ~60-90 m2 of grate area, 1-2 m bed

facts.label: Bed temperature
facts.value: 1100-1250 C in the burn-down zone

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 50-60% Pb, 8-15% SiO2, self-fluxing with 15-25% CaO

facts.label: SO2
facts.value: 10-14% to the acid plant

children.note: The sinter plant is where lead's energy cost sits; it is a genuinely old process and the dominant sinter machine type in 1982 was the Dwight-Lloyd.

children.name: Dwight-Lloyd sinter strand
children.description: A continuous chain of cast-iron pallets on an endless track about 1.2-1.5 m wide, with the ignition hood at the discharge end. Feed is a mix of concentrate, sinter returns, flux and coke spread to exactly 1-2 m - there is nothing clever about it and it works. The strand advances 1-2 m/min, the fire burns through the bed in about 20 minutes, and the hot sinter is broken off by a set of crusher jaws at the end and tipped into the blast furnace. One machine makes 200-400 t of sinter an hour and runs continuously for years.

facts.label: Grate width
facts.value: 1.2-1.5 m for a single-width strand; multi-width for large smelters

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 200-400 t of sinter per hour per strand

facts.label: Feed moisture
facts.value: 8-12% - the bed has to hold together

children.name: Self-fluxing sinter mix
children.description: Sinter is not simply roasted concentrate. The mix is designed so the sintered cake is its own flux: the silica that comes with the concentrate is balanced with limestone so the blast furnace slag has a basicity near 1.5-2.0. Anything between about 1.0 and 2.0 works; outside that range the slag either freezes in the furnace or dissolves too much lead. The smelter's metallurgist is balancing silica, iron, calcium and lead every shift.

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: CaO/SiO2 of 1.5-2.0 in the blast furnace

facts.label: Limestone in the mix
facts.value: 15-25% of the mix

children.note: Slag basicity range varies with the ore; medium confidence.

children.name: Lead blast furnace reduction to crude lead
children.description: A lead blast furnace looks like an iron blast furnace but is only 4-7 m tall, because lead reduces so easily. Self-fluxing sinter, coke and limestone are charged at the top; a blast of 200-350 C air is blown in at the hearth; the PbO is reduced to lead by CO at 1000-1100 C and the metal runs out. The sinter, coke and limestone charge comes down a shaft that is deliberately kept chilled so the metallic lead freezes before it goes further down - if it melted it would run into the tuyeres. Two outputs: crude lead bullion at 950-1050 C at the bottom, and a slag carrying off the iron and silica.

facts.label: Furnace height
facts.value: 4.7-7.5 m (much shorter than an iron furnace)

facts.label: Blast
facts.value: 200-350 C, wet or filtered

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: PbO + C -> Pb + CO, at 1000-1100 C

facts.label: Chilling
facts.value: the shaft is cooled by sprays so the lead freezes as a sponge above the tuyeres

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: CaO-FeO-SiO2, 15-20% of the sinter charge, sometimes tapped separately

children.name: Crude lead bullion with silver and gold
children.description: Tapped at 950-1050 C, the bullion is about 95-98% lead with 1-3% silver, a little gold, and copper, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. Silver at 1-3% is not a trace - it is often the difference between a viable mine and a marginal one, and the Parkes process that recovers it is the reason lead smelters have a refinery at all. By 1982 crude lead was increasingly sold as a low-grade bullion to the refinery and the smelter/ refinery was one continuous plant.

facts.label: Wealth in the bullion
facts.value: order 250-800 g/t Ag equivalent

children.name: Parkes process: zinc drossing and desilverisation
children.description: The genius step, invented in 1850 and still standard in 1982. The molten bullion is stirred with a few tenths of a percent of zinc, which has a much stronger chemical affinity for silver than lead does, so a zinc-silver intermetallic (AgZn2, Ag2Zn5) migrates to the zinc 'dross' floating on top. The dross is skimmed, and the now-silver-poor lead is treated again with fresh zinc until it is down to 10-30 g/t silver. The dross is then distilled in a retort: zinc boils at 907 C and is condensed, and the silver and gold stay behind, to be cupelled. The zinc is a sacrificial reagent and goes back into the alloy.

facts.label: Zinc addition
facts.value: 0.2-0.8% of the bullion mass

facts.label: Cycles
facts.value: 3-5 drossing and skimming stages

facts.label: Desilverised lead
facts.value: 10-30 g/t Ag (the 'corroding' grade)

facts.label: Retort distillation
facts.value: zinc distilled off at 800-950 C and condensed

facts.label: Second reagent
facts.value: the Parkes process is sometimes followed by the Harris 'throat' blow, which adds 0.1% Na and 0.06% Mg for copper and for the last of the silver

children.note: The Parkes process is essentially unchanged since 1850 and is still in use today; that is unusual enough to be worth stating.

children.name: Betts process: electrolytic refining
children.description: The rival to the Parkes process, and the answer for the last fraction of a gram of bismuth. Anodes of impure lead are dissolved in a caustic soda solution containing sodium plumbite (Na2PbO3), and pure lead plates onto the cathode. The chemistry is unusual - the anode dissolves as plumbite and the deposit forms by the reaction of plumbite with metal, which is why the bath has to be kept in a narrow alkaline window. Cost is high, energy is high, so it was used only as a finishing step on top of the Parkes route, and in the 1980s it was being displaced by the Betterton-Krastchkow continuous drossing tower.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: Na2PbO3 in caustic soda at 35-45 C

facts.label: 1982s position
facts.value: falling out of favour in favour of continuous drossing towers

children.note: The decline of the Betts process in the 1980s is well documented; medium confidence on the specific replacement technologies used by any given smelter.

children.name: Vacuum-degass and dross the lead bullion
children.description: The modern version of both processes in one machine: a 6-10 m tall cylindrical steel vacuum vessel with an internal fractionating column. Molten lead is sprayed into the vacuum; the volatiles - hydrogen, oxygen, zinc, and the remaining silver on its way out - distil out and are fractionated, so the silver comes off as a separate metal rather than as a dross. It replaces two steps with one, cuts the labour, and gives 99.99% lead with under 5 g/t silver. It was the technology that spread through the lead industry in the 1980s, and it is a good marker for what was changing in smelting and what was not.

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: 0.1-1 mbar

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: lead at 700-850 C in a tall vessel

children.note: The drossing tower was a genuine 1980s innovation in lead refining; medium confidence on the precise vacuum figures.

children.name: Retorting the Parkes dross to recover the zinc
children.description: After the silver has been skimmed off as dross, the dross itself has to be processed, and it is done in a cast-iron retort: the dross is mixed with charcoal and a little limestone, charged into a retort at 800-950 C, and the zinc distils out - it boils at 907 C - into a condenser where it is collected as a crude zinc metal. The silver and gold stay in the retort. A dross retort holds 100-500 kg and takes 8-20 hours, and a refinery had six to a dozen of them. The recovered zinc is dirty and goes back into the next drossing cycle, which is why the Parkes process consumes no net zinc even though it uses some every time round.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 800-950 C, above the 907 C boiling point of zinc inside the retort

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 100-500 kg of dross with charcoal and limestone

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 8-20 h per retort

facts.label: Zinc balance
facts.value: the recovered zinc is returned to the drossing cycle, so net zinc consumption is small

children.note: Medium confidence; the retort practice is well described in the historical and metallurgical literature.

children.name: The dross retort and its condenser
children.description: A cast-iron or steel tube, 1.5-3 m long, charged at one end and heated in a coke-fired setting, with a condenser of iron pipes at the cool end into which the zinc vapour condenses and runs out as a crude metal. The retort has to be skimmed of oxide and it is a batch process, so a refinery ran a bank of them in shifts. It is an object that is essentially unchanged since the 1850s, which makes it one of the oldest continuous processes in this file.

facts.label: Retort
facts.value: 1.5-3 m long cast iron, fired in a coke setting

facts.label: Condenser
facts.value: iron pipe condenser, crude zinc metal collecting in a pot

children.note: Medium confidence; the retort geometry is standard historical practice.

children.name: Hot-dross the copper out of the lead bullion
children.description: Before the Parkes zinc drossing, the bullion is hot-drossed for copper. The blast-furnace bullion comes out at 950-1050 C holding copper, which is insoluble in lead at that temperature and forms a separate copper matte that floats on top; the refinery skims it off, cools it, and recovers the copper and its precious metals by further processing. It is the same physical principle as the zinc drossing - a metal that mixes preferentially with another - and it is done first because the copper dross would otherwise interfere with the silver dross.

facts.label: Order
facts.value: hot copper drossing at 950-1050 C, then the Parkes zinc drossing at 400-500 C

facts.label: Bullion copper
facts.value: 0.2-1.5%, dropping to 0.02-0.06% after hot drossing

children.note: Medium confidence; the sequence is standard and the copper figures are typical.

children.name: 63/37 Sn-Pb solder: wire, bar, paste
children.description: The alloy that makes electronics manufacturable. 63% tin, 37% lead is a true eutectic, so it melts and freezes at one temperature, 183 C, with no mushy interval - which means a joint goes from solid to liquid in milliseconds and the reflow time window can be measured in seconds. That property is why a decade of copper thicknesses and lead-free anxiety has not displaced it from the bench. A C64 has roughly 3,500 through-hole joints; at about 30 mg of solder per joint that is around 100 g of alloy per machine, in wire fed from spools and in a few kilos of bar in the wave-solder tank.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 63% Sn, 37% Pb by weight

facts.label: Liquidus and solidus
facts.value: 183 C exactly - a eutectic

facts.label: Tensile strength
facts.value: 30-45 kg/mm2 annealed

facts.label: Forms
facts.value: solid-core wire 0.3-1.0 mm, cast bar, and paste

children.name: Casting the 63/37 bar
children.description: The alloy is made in a handful of ways, all of them embarrassingly simple. The best is the cored wire method: rods of high-purity tin are cast inside a steel tube pre-filled with molten lead at exactly 37%, so the tube's own wall meters the lead; the tube and the core are then rolled and drawn out to wire in one operation, and the core forms down the middle as the flux. This is how most electronics solder wire is still made. The alternative, and what the solder manufacturer would do for its own bar stock, is simply to melt the two ingots together in a grease pot with a little antimony or phosphorus and pour into ingot moulds.

facts.label: Composition control
facts.value: to +/-0.5%; the liquidus is steep enough that 2% off composition moves the melting point by 10-20 C

facts.label: Antimony
facts.value: 0.1-0.5% Sb added to raise fluidity and prevent the solder sticking to the pot

facts.label: Oxide control
facts.value: a covering flux of resin or glycerine prevents tin oxide dross

facts.label: Forms
facts.value: 1-10 kg bars, and 'sticks' or 'pigs'

children.name: Antimony addition to stiffen the alloy
children.description: Pure Sn-Pb solder creeps. A 1982 instrument or a through-hole joint under a hot component would push itself out of the joint over a few years, and the classic failure was a capacitor that walked out of its pads. Two tenths of a percent of antimony, as an Sb-Sn hardener or as a lead-antimony master alloy, makes the alloy's creep resistance about an order of magnitude better with only a small rise in melting point. So the solder in the C64 very probably contained 0.1-0.5% antimony, and none of it is on the bill of materials.

facts.label: Level
facts.value: 0.1-0.5% Sb for general electronics work

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: much better creep resistance; melting point up a few degrees

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: below the fluid point, so 60/40 and 63/37 differed more by creep than by melt

children.note: Antimony level is a supplier specification, not something visible on a C64; 0.1-0.5% is the normal commercial range for electronics-grade Sn-Pb.

children.name: The cored-wire manufacturing method
children.description: The standard way to make electronics solder wire, and the reason the alloy composition is so consistent. A steel tube with a wall thickness calculated for 37% lead by volume is filled with molten high-purity tin - actually with the exact alloy, but the wall does the metering - and the tube is cold-drawn and then drawn to wire in the same multiwire machine the copper industry uses. The core forms down the middle as the tube collapses. The result is a wire in which the flux core is in the middle of the metal rather than smeared along it, which is what stops the flux from being wiped off during handling. The alternative - extruding a bar of flux and then jacketing it in molten alloy - gives a worse wire and was being displaced by the cored method through the 1980s.

facts.label: Metering
facts.value: a steel tube wall of controlled thickness meters the lead, or the melt ratio is set in the fill

facts.label: Drawing
facts.value: multiwire drawing, as for copper

facts.label: Flux fraction
facts.value: 10-25% of the diameter by volume

children.note: Medium confidence; the cored-wire method is well established in the solder industry literature.

children.name: Fill the flux core with activated rosin
children.description: The flux core is a paste, not a powder: rosin dissolved in a solvent - turpentine, or in the 1980s increasingly a mild-rosin paste - with the zinc chloride activator, made viscous enough to hold a column.
