It is injected into the tube with a hydraulic filler in a batch, and the tube's ends are crimped and drawn closed. The viscosity and the shrinkage matter, because the core has to survive being drawn to 0.5 mm without either splitting out of the wire or shrinking away from the axis. So the flux chemistry in a C64's solder wire is a colloid and a rheology problem as much as it is a chemical one.

facts.label: Vehicle
facts.value: rosin dissolved in a terpene solvent, or a mild rosin paste

facts.label: Filler
facts.value: hydraulic injection, batch, into a drawn steel tube

children.note: Low confidence; the cored-wire fill process is proprietary and I am describing the general shape of it, not a specific machine.

children.name: Wave soldering with the alloy pot
children.description: The board assembly method for a 1982 C64. The bottom of the board is swept across a standing wave of molten 63/37 at 250-280 C, the excess drains through a hot-air knife, and the whole board lives in a hood full of the vapour of flux decomposition products. A few kilograms of solder in the pot are held at a temperature just above the 183 C liquidus, and the pot is kept clean with a rotating skimmer. Wave soldering is why solder consumption in electronics manufacturing was measured in kilograms per day per line rather than grams per board, and why the flux vapour was a genuine occupational exposure that the electronics industry was only beginning to quantify in the late 1980s.

facts.label: Wave height
facts.value: 3-8 mm

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: pre-fluxed board via a foam or spray fluxer, then preheated at 100-150 C

facts.label: Dwell
facts.value: 2-5 s in the wave

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 3-8 s per board; a 1982 line ran a few hundred boards an hour

children.note: The 1982 wave-solder process for a large through-hole board is well documented; wave time and pot temperature ranges are typical rather than from a specific manual.

children.name: Intermetallics and lead leaching in the solder joint
children.description: A good 1982 through-hole joint is a shallow concave meniscus filling the pad hole about 70-90%, with a fillet at the lead. The metallurgical reason it works is the intermetallic: copper and tin react to form Cu6Sn5 and Cu3Sn, and the joint is a composite of unreacted solder and intermetallic compound. On the PCB side the pad is tin-plated and forms a Cu-Sn intermetallic too. What nobody in 1982 was measuring was how much lead leached out of a solder joint into the copper land when the joint was at 200 C for an hour - and it is a lot, which is the mechanism behind the later 'solder fatigue' literature.

facts.label: Intermetallics
facts.value: Cu6Sn5 and Cu3Sn form at the interface

facts.label: Phases
facts.value: Sn-rich matrix plus brittle intermetallic skeleton

children.note: The microstructural description is standard; the specific metallurgy of a Commodore board in 1982 would need the actual board. Medium confidence.

children.name: The hot-air knife and the solder wave
children.description: A pump throws molten solder up a nozzle to form a standing wave 3-8 mm high, and the board is dragged across it on a conveyor with fingers. As the board leaves, a 'hot-air knife' - a duct blowing 200-300 C air across the solder line - blows the excess solder off the pads and off the solder side of the board, and what runs off goes back into the pot through a trough. The whole operation is a temperature profile in space: preheat, flux activation, wave, drain, and the knife. Getting the four temperatures right - preheat, pot, board and cleaning - is the entire craft.

facts.label: Hot-air knife
facts.value: 200-300 C, high-velocity air

facts.label: Conveyor
facts.value: 1.5-3 m/min for a large through-hole board

children.note: The temperature windows are standard; medium confidence on the conveyor speed range.

children.name: Preheater, fluxer and the thermal profile
children.description: Before the wave, the board goes through a preheater - infrared lamps, a hot plate or hot air - to 100-150 C, and through a fluxer that lays a foam or sprayed layer of flux on the solder side. The reason for preheating is thermal expansion: a FR-4 board with a big hole pattern expands by a different amount in different directions, and if the solder side heats faster than the component side the board warps and the joints crack. A C64's mainboard is a large single-sided board with a lot of heat-generating parts on one side, so warp was a real yield problem. The preheater is the cheapest fix and it is a temperature-control problem.

facts.label: Preheat
facts.value: 100-150 C for 1-2 min

facts.label: Fluxer
facts.value: foam or spray, 10-30 g of flux per board

facts.label: Why
facts.value: to control the through-thickness thermal gradient and stop the board warping

children.note: Medium confidence; the temperatures are standard, the warp mechanism is well established.

children.name: Board warp, thermal stress and the epoxy
children.description: Why preheat exists at all. A single-sided 1.6 mm FR-4 board with a large hole pattern expands and contracts with a coefficient of about 14-18 x 10^-6 per K, and it is not isotropic - the copper layer and the epoxy cloth have different coefficients, and the weave gives the board different stiffness in the warp and weft directions. Warm the solder side faster than the component side and the board bows; cycle it and the board stays bowed; and on a double-sided board it can delaminate the copper from the epoxy. So the preheater is really an epoxy-handling device, and the epoxy is the resin agent's problem while the solder pot is the metals one, and they meet at the warp.

facts.label: CTE of FR-4
facts.value: 14-18 x 10^-6 per K in-plane; anisotropic between warp and weft

facts.label: Copper
facts.value: 17 x 10^-6 per K; epoxy cloth 50-70 x 10^-6

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: bow if the solder side heats faster; delamination if the gradient is severe

children.note: Medium confidence on the coefficient ranges; the mechanism is textbook.

children.name: Solder paste: powder in flux
children.description: Solder paste is a mixture of atomised alloy powder at 60-90% by weight in a flux vehicle, and in 1982 it was the technology for surface-mount parts, which Commodore did not really use on the mainboard but which every other electronics maker in the world was. The powder particle size is controlled by the printing stencil: a 0.5 mm gap needs 20-45 um powder so the powder does not bridge the gap with two particles. Alloy powder is not made by atomising finished solder; it is made by atomising the melt and then the 63/37 particles are aged so they develop an oxide shell of a controlled thickness, so that paste sits on a pad for minutes without the paste shrinking or the surface going dull.

facts.label: Powder fraction
facts.value: 60-90% by weight

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: type 2 (25-45 um) to type 4 (15-25 um) in 1982 practice

facts.label: Paste consistency
facts.value: classified by viscosity, e.g. solder paste Type 1 through 6

children.note: Paste is mostly a surface-mount story rather than a through-hole story; included because it is the other half of the solder industry in 1982 and because Commodore's own subsidiaries used it.

children.name: The leaded-solder problem in the 1980s
children.description: Lead in solder was the first workplace poison to arrive with electronics. It was already deeply regulated for the smelter workers - the whole lead industry is under air-monitoring and blood-lead surveillance - and by the early 1980s occupational-health attention had turned to the solder bench: solder fume is an aerosol of lead oxide particles, and the flux fumes carry it. The US OSHA lead standard covered soldering. The C64 is the emblem of this because it was sold by the million with a leaded-solder supply chain: the solder manufacturer, the wave-solder pot, the washing machines that washed the flux off, the drain water, and finally the landfill. Every one of those is a different regulatory jurisdiction and none of them was solved in 1982.

facts.label: Fume mechanism
facts.value: PbO aerosol from the reaction of lead oxide in the flux with rosin acids

facts.label: Exposure limit
facts.value: an airborne lead limit existed in the US under the OSHA lead standard from the 1970s

facts.label: Later developments
facts.value: lead-free solder (Sn-Ag-Cu SAC305, Sn-Ag-Bi) only took commercial share after about 2000-2010, driven by RoHS

children.note: Lead-free alternatives existed as patents and laboratory melts in the 1980s-90s; nothing displaced 63/37 in commercial manufacture until the 2000s. High confidence.

children.name: Silver-bearing solder and silver paste
children.description: A distinct and important thing in the 1980s electronics industry, which is easy to confuse with the lead-tin eutectic: high-temperature silver solder - 62Ag/38Cu, 50Ag/50Cd, 70Ag/30Sn - melts at 600-750 C and is brazed, not soldered. Silver-tin solder melts at 217-220 C and is used where lead-free behaviour is wanted. Silver brazing is how the heat sinks and the chassis joints were made. And separately there is the silver-filled epoxy and silver-filled ink of the electronics industry: real silver powder at 60-80% by weight in an epoxy or an organic vehicle, screen-printed or stencil-printed and fired, used for die attach and for the conductive ink of the keyboard membrane. That is a genuine and separate use of silver in a C64, and it is a chemistry, not a metallurgy.

facts.label: Ag-Sn solder
facts.value: 95.5Sn/4.5Ag or 96.5Sn/3.5Ag, melts 217-221 C

facts.label: Silver brazing
facts.value: Ag-Cu or Ag-Cd, 600-750 C, with a flux

facts.label: Silver epoxy
facts.value: 60-80% Ag powder in epoxy, cured at 150-250 C

facts.label: Silver ink
facts.value: a fine silver flake powder in an organic vehicle, screen-printed onto the flexible membrane

children.note: The keyboard membrane of a 1982 C64 is a triple-layer flex circuit with printed conductive ink - whether that ink was silver-filled or carbon/graphite is the keyboard agent's call. Silver-filled epoxy die attach was a specialised 1980s technology used mostly in power devices and in some hybrid ICs.

children.name: The wave-solder pot and its dross
children.description: A 5-20 kg pot of 63/37 at 250-280 C with a pump and a wave-forming nozzle, plus a rotating skimmer and an oil skimmer. The surface of a working solder pot accumulates a metre of black oxide dross - tin oxide, lead oxide and flux residue - and it has to be skimmed off every shift and every night, and it is a genuine metallurgical waste stream: the dross contains most of the lead and a lot of the tin, and in 1982 the recovery options were poor. A dross reclaimer sold a few percent of the metal back and the rest went out as lead-containing waste. This is the point at which the solder chain and the lead chain close on each other.

facts.label: Pot size
facts.value: 5-20 kg of alloy on a small line, 200 kg on a large one

facts.label: Dross rate
facts.value: order 0.2-1% of the solder used per shift, plus a oxide skim

facts.label: Dross composition
facts.value: mostly SnO2 and PbO with entrained flux; the lead is the problem

children.note: Dross recovery in 1982 was poor and the residue was a recognised waste problem; medium confidence on the rates.

children.name: The dross oxide film on the solder pot
children.description: At 250-280 C the surface of molten Sn-Pb oxidises continuously - tin oxide forms preferentially because it has the lower oxidation potential - so the pot grows a skin of SnO2 with lead oxide and flux in it. The skimmer takes it off, but the formation is unavoidable, which is why wave-solder lines had a person whose whole job was pot maintenance and why the flux was designed to keep the oxide mobile and floatable rather than letting it crust over.

facts.label: Oxide
facts.value: SnO2 with PbO, on the pot surface at 250-280 C

facts.label: Control
facts.value: a cover flux, a rotating skimmer, and frequent skimming

children.note: Standard soldering practice; medium confidence on the quantitative rates.

children.name: Cleaning the flux residue off the board
children.description: A rosin-fluxed board is covered in a sticky, slightly acidic film of flux decomposition products that will corrode the copper and will not accept a conformal coating. In 1982 it was removed in an aqueous machine - a conveyor with spray bars and drying ovens - often followed by a trichloroethane or perchloroethylene vapour degreaser. The cleaning water left the factory through the drain with the lead in it, which is the other half of the 1982 leaded-solder problem and the reason the electronics industry spent the late 1980s arguing about what to do about it.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: aqueous wash with detergents, then trichloroethane or perchloroethylene vapour degrease

facts.label: Water
facts.value: 50-200 litres per board on a heavy-duty line

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: the wash water carried lead and tin; the varnish and resin types were the difficult ones

children.note: The water consumption and the solvent choice are representative; medium confidence.

children.name: The solder wash-water waste stream
children.description: A C64 assembly line's cleaning water carried dissolved lead, tin, flux residues and a lot of suspended solids. In 1982 the standard practice was dilute and discharge: a settling tank and a pH adjustment, then to the drain. The lead was almost all in the sludge, so the sludge went to a hazardous-waste landfill and the liquid went out. This is the last place the C64's lead leaves the factory, and it is the reason leaded solder became a regulatory object rather than merely an occupational one.

children.name: Lead in landfill leachate
children.description: Landfill leachate is where the lead problem stops being a factory problem. Dross and baghouse dust that could not be recycled went to a hazardous-waste landfill, and a landfill that takes metal-bearing waste generates leachate in which lead concentrations are routinely orders of magnitude above the drinking-water limit, so the liner, the leachate collection sump and the treatment plant are the last line of defence. By the early 1980s this was the reason several countries began classifying lead-bearing wastes separately from general industrial waste.

facts.label: Speciation
facts.value: lead as sulphate and as carbonate in an anoxic sludge

facts.label: 1980s control
facts.value: landfill-liner standards existed but were young and widely bypassed

children.note: Low confidence on any specific site's performance; the general chemistry is well established and the 1980s regulatory position is the point being made.

facts.label: Volume
facts.value: a hand-soldering station used a few litres an hour of water for flux-residue rinsing and tip cleaning

children.name: The solder factory's own waste streams
children.description: A solder pot, a dross heap, a flux residue stream, a wash-water drain and a baghouse for the flux fumes. The dross goes to a reclaimer or to a hazardous-waste disposal contract; the baghouse dust is lead oxide and rosin and is genuinely hazardous; and the wash water goes to the drain with the lead in it. In 1982 this was the least regulated part of the whole electronics industry, and it is the reason the United States' lead exposure limits for electronics workers - which were set at a time when electronics was not a regulated industry - exist at all. The waste stream is a leaf of this tree and a genuinely uncomfortable one.

children.name: The flux fume baghouse and its dust
children.description: The wave-solder hood has an extraction duct and a baghouse, because the fume is an aerosol of lead oxide and of rosin-acid degradation products. The dust is 30-60% lead oxide and it is collected as a hazardous waste. A big 1982 line threw away tens of kilograms a week. The control measure was local exhaust ventilation with a capture hood about 100 mm from the wave, and the compliance measure was an area respirator, which was why electronics assembly was one of the more heavily respirated occupations of the period.

facts.label: Dust
facts.value: 30-60% lead oxide with rosin-acid residues

facts.label: Capture
facts.value: local exhaust at about 100 mm from the wave, plus a baghouse

children.note: Medium confidence on the dust composition; the lead oxide figure is representative.

facts.label: Fractions
facts.value: flux-cork dross, baghouse dust off the flux fume, wash-water and spent degreasing solvent

children.name: Zinc: die-cast alloy, plating, brass, varistor
children.description: Zinc is the fourth non-ferrous metal and the most recycled one. In a 1982 C64 it appears as a die-cast zinc alloy for the case-mounted parts and the key plungers, as a plating on steel for EMI shields and chassis fasteners, as brass (copper-zinc) for the bus-bar and connector bodies, and as zinc oxide in the varistor that clamps the supply spikes off the mains input. The smelting industry in 1982 was in the middle of its biggest change in a century: the roast-leach-electrowin zinc-iron plant was replacing the horizontal retort furnace.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.995% (SHG), the standard grade for galvanising and die casting

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: sphalerite ZnS at 3-20% Zn; the ore is often mined as a lead-zinc deposit

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~100 t of 6% Zn ore -> ~18 t of 55% Zn concentrate -> ~5 t of zinc metal in the concentrate

children.name: Roasting of sphalerite to zinc oxide
children.description: The concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed or on a sinter strand, 850-1000 C, with the result 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. The 1980s plant that grew out of this is the roaster-sinter plant, in which the hot ZnO and Fe2O3 sinter together into a porous 'dead roast sinter' that is a much better feed for an acid leach than a fine powder. The SO2 at 8-12% goes to the acid plant. This roasting step is where a zinc smelter became a sulfuric acid producer of the same order as a copper smelter, and where the sinter plant's dust catch and its dewpoint control - keep the gas above about 150 C or the zinc and lead fume plasters the plant - became a real engineering discipline.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2

facts.label: SO2 to acid
facts.value: 8-12%, captured; a zinc plant makes 3-5 t of 100% acid per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Dewpoint control
facts.value: offgas held above roughly 150 C to keep zinc and lead oxides out of the gas

facts.label: By-products
facts.value: cadmium and lead fume captured from the roaster gas; mercury in the fume is a modern problem, largely uncontrolled in 1982

children.name: Fluidised-bed roaster
children.description: Concentrate is fed into a bed of 1-3 m of the roast itself on a distributor of tuyeres, held at 850-950 C by the fluidising air, and the bed overflows continuously into a hot cyclone and then a sintering conveyor where the last 100-150 C of roast and the sintering happen together. The whole thing was invented at the Balotelawezwa plant in South Africa and Canadian Calumet in the 1960s and was standard new-plant practice by 1982. An older plant would instead have used a multiple-hearth roaster or a sinter strand and produced a fine, un-sintered ZnO.

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 50-60% Zn, 6-10% Zn soluble, rest in the silicate matrix

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: flotation concentrate, 4-12% moisture

children.note: Roaster design details vary; medium confidence.

children.name: Catch the cadmium and lead in the roaster gas
children.description: The roaster gas carries a fine zinc oxide fume and, in the vapour phase, the cadmium and the lead. Economically the cadmium is the point: the fume goes to a baghouse, and the cadmium is recovered in a separate cadmium plant. The lead in the same gas is a nuisance and an occupational hazard, and in 1982 the zinc plants of North America were beginning to worry about it for exactly the reason they would later worry about it in the environmental context. The dust is one of the more awkward solid wastes in metallurgy because it is both valuable and toxic.

facts.label: Collection
facts.value: baghouse or electrostatic precipitator after a cooling tower

facts.label: Fume
facts.value: ZnO with Cd, Pb and Cl compounds

facts.label: Cadmium recovery
facts.value: the fume goes to a cadmium distilling plant

children.note: The cadmium recovery route is well documented; medium confidence on the 1982 collection efficiency.

children.name: Zinc oxide sinter: the smelter's intermediate
children.description: The dead-roast sinter is the actual feed to the leach circuit, and its specification is a compromise between the roast and the leach. It wants to be as completely roasted as possible so that the zinc is all in the oxide, but it also wants to be porous enough for the sulphuric acid to reach it, which is what the sintering stage of the roaster-sinter plant is for. Between 5 and 10% of the zinc stays locked up in the silicate matrix and is lost in the leach residue, which is the second big reason a zinc plant's recovery is not higher than it is.

facts.label: Zinc soluble
facts.value: 90-95%; the rest is locked in the silicate

facts.label: Loss
facts.value: 1-3% of the zinc reports to the leach residue

children.note: Medium confidence; the sinter quality figures are typical rather than specification values.

children.name: Acid leach and purification of the zinc sulphate solution
children.description: The dead-roast sinter is leached in spent electrolyte diluted with water, at pH about 4.5 and 40-60 C, in a series of leaching tanks. Then the solution must be purified, because almost every impurity that reaches the cell either consumes current or plates out on the cathode as a short circuit. Iron is removed by air oxidising the pH up to 5.2 so it precipitates as jarosite or goethite - a step that consumes zinc as well and is where most of the zinc plants' zinc loss is. Then copper, cadmium and cobalt are removed by adding zinc dust, which by cementation throws those metals out of solution. Chloride is kept down by jarosite precipitation. Every one of these is a chemistry rather than a metallurgy, and every one of them costs zinc.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: spent electrolyte + water, pH 4.5, 40-60 C

facts.label: Iron removal
facts.value: air oxidisation to pH 5.2, precipitating jarosite or goethite; costs 3-8 kg Zn per tonne of Zn

facts.label: Cementation
facts.value: zinc dust removes Cu, Cd and Co down to mg/L

facts.label: Chloride
facts.value: kept below about 500 mg/L; chloride drives anode corrosion

facts.label: Ajar residue
facts.value: the iron precipitate is a residue stream of 1-3 t per tonne of zinc

children.note: The zinc loss in iron removal is the single biggest reason zinc plants' recoveries sit at 85-92% rather than higher; medium confidence on the exact figure range.

children.name: Zinc dust for cementation
children.description: The purification step uses zinc metal itself, atomised from a small kettle, as the reagent that throws out copper, cadmium and cobalt. The cemented metals - a black sludge heavy with copper and cadmium - is filtered off and shipped to a cadmium refinery, which is where the world's cadmium came from in 1982. So the zinc plant's purification residue is a cadmium ore in all but name.

facts.label: Dust size
facts.value: atomised, 75-150 um

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 3-10 kg of zinc dust per tonne of zinc

children.note: Dust consumption depends on the impurity load; medium confidence on the range.

children.name: Copper-cadmium residue
children.description: A 1980s cadmium plant roasted the residue in a retort at 600-800 C: the cadmium volatilised off (it boils at 767 C) and was condensed in a condenser, giving 99.9% cadmium metal, while the copper stayed behind. This is the only major industrial source of cadmium, and it is a zinc by-product. It matters here only as a consequence of zinc refining; a C64 has no cadmium.

facts.label: Retort
facts.value: 600-800 C, cadmium distilled and condensed

children.note: Cadmium is included as a consequence of the zinc chain; medium confidence on retort detail.

children.name: Jarosite residue and the zinc it costs
children.description: The iron precipitation step that makes the zinc plant's chemistry work is also its biggest single loss. Oxidising the iron out at pH 5.2 throws down jarosite or goethite, and both of them carry zinc in their lattice - typically 4-10% Zn. At 1-3 tonnes of residue per tonne of zinc made, and 5-10% of the contained zinc never recovered, the iron removal step is where a zinc plant loses a million dollars a year. It is also a waste stream: acidic, iron-rich, and in the 1980s dumped in a lined pond. This is the residue the modern jarosite and goethite processes are designed to shrink.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 1-3 t of residue per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Zinc lost
facts.value: 4-10% of the contained zinc in the residue

facts.label: Overall plant recovery
facts.value: 85-92%, limited mostly by this step

children.note: The 5-10% zinc loss figure is a rule of thumb; medium confidence.

children.name: Iron removal by the jarosite and goethite routes
children.description: The purification chemistry in one process. The leach liquor's pH is raised with limestone and the iron is oxidised with air in a bank of aeration tanks at 90-100 C. Whether the precipitate is jarosite (the older route, at pH 5.2 with sodium sulphate added, at 90-100 C over 10-20 hours) or goethite (the newer route, at 80-95 C with less retention time) decides how much zinc the residue holds and how much sulphate the plant makes. Every zinc plant in 1982 had made a choice between these two, and the choice is the single biggest determinant of its cost.

facts.label: Jarosite
facts.value: pH 5.2, 90-100 C, 10-20 h, needs added sulphate

facts.label: Goethite
facts.value: 80-95 C, shorter retention, no added sulphate

facts.label: Neutralising reagent
facts.value: limestone, from the same quarry as the blast furnace flux

children.note: The jarosite versus goethite split is a real and well-documented 1980s process choice; medium confidence on the specific temperature windows.

children.name: Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless
children.description: Nickel is small in mass and enormous in function. In a C64 it is the plating on the connector shells and the gold-plated edge connector fingers' underlayer, the constantan and nichrome of the thin-film resistors on the board, the Invar of the composite-video circuit's chroma delay, and the bulk of AISI 304 and 430 stainless in the audio jack and the shield cans. 1982 was the year nickel was in a price crisis - the 1982-83 LME collapse, following the Escondida-adjacent and the Sherritt expansions of the late 1970s, took nickel from about $4/lb in 1980 to under $1.30/lb by 1983.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.8% cathode nickel; 99.9% for plating and for 304 stainless

facts.label: 1982 price context
facts.value: the LME nickel price collapsed from over $4/lb in early 1980 to under $1.50/lb by 1983 - a factor of three in three years

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: sulphide at 1-3% Ni (Sudbury, Thompson, Ranko Inlet) or laterite at 1.5-3% Ni (Cuba, Philippines, New Caledonia, Queensland)

children.name: Sherritt-Gordon ammonia leach and hydrogen reduction
children.description: The process that unlocked the laterites in the 1970s and 1980s. The slurry is leached at atmospheric pressure with concentrated ammonia and oxygen at 50-70 C: nickel and copper form soluble ammine complexes while the iron precipitates as hematite. The pregnant liquor is heated in a pressure autoclave with hydrogen and more ammonia, and the nickel comes out of solution as a metal powder while the copper stays in solution as the ammine, so the two separate in one vessel. The powder is filtered, washed and dried in a rotary vacuum dryer. This is genuinely a 1980s technology - the first commercial laterite plant, at Browns River in Queensland, started in 1974 and Sherritt licensed the process to the Cubans and the Japanese in the second half of the decade.

facts.label: Ammonia leach
facts.value: 50-70 C, atmospheric pressure, concentrated NH3, aerated

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: Ni2+ and Cu2+ as [Ni(NH3)6]2+ and [Cu(NH3)4]2+; Fe precipitates as hematite

facts.label: Hydrogen reduction
facts.value: 150-200 C, 20-35 bar H2, in a stirred autoclave

facts.label: Product
facts.value: nickel powder 99%+

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: copper stays in solution and is electrowon separately

facts.label: First commercial plant
facts.value: Browns River, Queensland, 1974

children.name: The ammonia-hydrogen autoclave
children.description: A 10-15 m long, 3-5 m diameter, titanium or 316L-lined pressure vessel in a 6-10 stage cascade. In each stage the liquor is contacted with hydrogen and stirred, and the nickel comes out onto the walls and the cooling surfaces. The whole chemistry depends on the fact that ammonia complexes nickel and copper so strongly that hydrogen alone cannot reduce them at atmospheric pressure; the autoclave gives the extra pressure to push the equilibrium over. Removing the ammonia and boiling the slurry then precipitates basic nickel carbonate, which is calcined to nickel oxide.

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: 3-5 m diameter, 10-15 m long, 6-10 stages

facts.label: Material
facts.value: carbon steel with titanium or stainless lining

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: a cobalt-nickel or iron-based slurry catalyst seeds the deposition

children.note: Sherritt's own patents cover the details; medium confidence on the vessel dimensions.

children.name: Nickel oxide (NiO)
children.description: The commercially traded intermediate. The pregnant solvent is stripped of ammonia and boiled, basic nickel carbonate NiCO3.2Ni(OH)2.4H2O drops out, it is filtered and washed, and it is calcined at 400-600 C to green-black nickel oxide at 99.0-99.5% Ni. In 1982 the overwhelming majority of nickel oxide went to ferronickel smelting; pure nickel oxide was a smaller but growing market for stainless steel and for plating.
children.note: The later hydrometallurgical routes (Murrin Murrin, using a sulphate/chloride pressure leach) came after 1982; medium confidence.

children.name: Ferronickel, the laterite iron-nickel alloy
children.description: The dominant way nickel actually became metal in 1982. Dried laterite and quartzite are fed with coke into a large submerged arc furnace, 30-60 MW, three electrodes, running at 1350-1500 C. The laterite's iron is already present as hematite, so the whole charge reduces together and the product is not nickel metal but an alloy of about 60-75% Ni and 25-40% Fe, plus a slag of magnesium, silicon and aluminium oxides. The ferronickel is tapped and either refined in the same operation to pure nickel or - more commonly in the 1980s - sold straight to a stainless steel mill as a charge, which is why the whole ferronickel industry is really a stainless steel industry.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 30-60 MW, three electrodes, 1350-1500 C

facts.label: Product
facts.value: ferronickel, 60-75% Ni / 25-40% Fe

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 1.5-2.5 t of dried laterite per tonne of Ni in the alloy

facts.label: Charge drying
facts.value: suspension or rotary dryer to reduce the 30-45% moisture of laterite to below 1-2% before the furnace

children.name: Nickel electrowinning from a pure sulphide circuit
children.description: Where the ore is sulphide rather than laterite, Sherritt's original ammonia-pressure process dissolves the concentrate in ammoniacal ammonium sulphate at 160-190 F (70-90 C) with oxygen, and then electrowins the nickel directly out of the pregnant liquor onto titanium cathodes in diaphragm cells at a very low voltage, about 0.5-1.0 V, because hydrogen evolution competes and the current efficiency is only 70-85%. This is the Sherritt-Gordon route as it was licensed in 1969-1972, and it is why the company is called after two towns in Manitoba. The cathodes are stripped, briquetted and remelted.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: ammoniacal ammonium sulphate, 70-90 C, aerated

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: titanium starter sheets, stripped and briquetted

children.note: The 160-190 F optimum is from Sherritt's own published leach chemistry for sulphide concentrates; medium confidence on the current efficiency range.

children.name: Nickel sulphide concentrate (Sudbury)
children.description: The Sudbury basin of Ontario was the world's nickel capital and it is a genuinely strange deposit: an impact structure full of shock-melted, metal-rich breccia at the base of a 1.8 billion year old impact crater, with pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8 and millerite NiS. The INCO operation mined both underground and, from 1962, from the open pit at the south end of the basin, and roasted the ore in fluidised beds to make 'fines' - a nickel-copper matte rather than a concentrate - before smelting. The tree therefore continues down through the Sudbury ore to a shocked sulphide breccia in an impact melt sheet, which is as geologically interesting an endpoint as this tree has.

facts.label: Minerals
facts.value: pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8, millerite NiS, pyrrhotite

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: a 1.85 billion year old meteorite impact structure; the ore sits in and below the melt sheet

facts.label: Route
facts.value: fluidised-bed roasting to sinter fines, then smelting to a matte, then converting

children.name: Impact melt sheet at the base of the Sudbury crater
children.description: The leaf: a foot-thick to 20 m layer of rock melted and shock-altered by the impact, in which the nickel and copper sulphides were disseminated as droplets. It is a metamorphic and melt rock, not an igneous intrusion, and it is a band about 60 km long and 20 km wide across northern Ontario. The mining is ordinary room-and-pillar or open-pit on a sheet that lies only a few hundred metres below the Huronian cover.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: impact melt and suevite breccia, disseminated Ni-Cu sulphide

children.name: Mond carbonyl refining (nickel from 99.9 to 99.999)
children.description: Ludwig Mond's 1890s process, still used in the 1980s for the last nines. Nickel carbonyl Ni(CO)4 is formed at 50-60 C in a saturator, distilled off as a colourless liquid boiling at 43 C, and decomposed in a decomposer column at 200-230 C onto 99.99% nickel pellets. The trick is that the carbonyl of cobalt is much less volatile and iron forms a non-volatile carbonyl, so the distillation separates the three metals in one operation - the same volatility trick as the trichlorosilane column in the silicon branch. Cobalt is recovered from the residue as Co2(CO)8.

facts.label: Carbonyl
facts.value: Ni(CO)4, liquid, boils 43 C at atmospheric pressure

facts.label: Decomposer
facts.value: 200-230 C, produces high-purity nickel pellets

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% nickel - the Mondcarbonyl process still supplies the very pure nickel used in plating chemistry

facts.label: Safety
facts.value: extremely toxic; the vapour is the reason Mond refineries had continuous air monitoring from the 1970s

children.name: Dicobalt octacarbonyl, Co2(CO)8
children.description: The cobalt in the Mond residue is a genuine industrial source of cobalt: the residue is treated with copper at 200 C under hydrogen to reduce the cobalt and copper carbonyls, and then re-carbonylated to Co2(CO)8, which is filtered out and decomposed. In 1982 the two leading producers - INCO in Canada and OUTOKUMPU in Finland - between them controlled most of the world's cobalt from their nickel operations, and a period of low cobalt stocks in 1982-83 contributed to a real shortage.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: reduction with copper under hydrogen, then carbonylation

facts.label: 1982 context
facts.value: a genuine cobalt shortage in 1982-83 driven by Zaire's production problems and by the INCO/OUTOKUMPU cutbacks

children.note: The 1982-83 cobalt shortage is well documented; medium confidence on attributing a specific share to the nickel carbonyl plants.

children.name: Why nickel carbonyl is the deadliest room in metals
children.description: Nickel tetracarbonyl is a colourless, volatile liquid that boils at 43 C and is lethal by inhalation at concentrations far below anything that can be smelled. A Mond refinery therefore runs on a rule that no one enters a carbonyl area without a respirator, that the vapour is continuously monitored at the floor and at breathing height, and that the whole plant is vented through a high-temperature incinerator that destroys the carbonyl before releasing it. The 1980s occupational-hygiene literature on nickel carbonyl is a case study in how a process can be kept running at all when the material is that toxic, and the number of fatal poisonings in nickel refineries over the century is a reminder that this is one of the most dangerous processes in the metals industry.

facts.label: Boiling point
facts.value: 43 C at atmospheric pressure

facts.label: Exposure limit
facts.value: of the order of 0.1 ppm as an 8-hour TWA in most jurisdictions by the 1980s

facts.label: Control
facts.value: closed process, continuous air monitoring, and high-temperature incineration of the offgas

children.note: The exposure limit varies by jurisdiction; medium confidence on the specific 1982 figures.

children.name: Manganese: the steel deoxidiser
children.description: Manganese has no visible place in a C64, but without it the steel the case and the shielding are made from would have inclusions and blowholes in it. Almost all manganese ore is used to make ferromanganese, which is added to the steelmaking furnace as a deoxidiser and desulphuriser and as an alloying element. It is a branch included because the steel branch cannot honestly stop without it.

facts.label: Refined form
facts.value: ferromanganese, most commonly high-carbon at 6-8% C

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: pyrolusite MnO2 at 30-50% Mn; the 'manganese nodules' on the abyssal plains held most of the world's reserve

children.name: Charge the ferromanganese into the steel ladle
children.description: A ladle of steel is a bad place to drop a lump of ferromanganese, because the lump floats, the reaction is violent and the steel is left with unreacted alloy inclusions. So the FeMn is added in sized lumps and, increasingly in the 1980s, in cored wire - a steel tube filled with powdered ferromanganese and flux, fed into the ladle on a lance and dissolved by the passage of the steel through it. Cored-wire charging was a genuine 1980s development in secondary metallurgy and it improved the yield of the manganese, because it puts the metal into the steel rather than onto it.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sized lumps, or cored wire on a ladle lance

facts.label: Why
facts.value: a lump floats and reacts only at the surface; cored wire dissolves below the surface and gives a higher yield

facts.label: Typical addition
facts.value: order 1 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel

children.note: Medium confidence; cored-wire charging of ferroalloys is well documented in secondary-metallurgy practice.

children.name: Chromium: stainless, ferrochrome, hard chrome
children.description: Chromium does three separate jobs: it makes stainless steel stainless, it is the alloying element in the NiCr film resistors on the board, and as hexavalent chromium it is the hard chrome plating on switch contacts, the keyboard frame hinges and the RF shielding. The plating chemistry is the one with a body of regulation attached to it, and the ferrochrome industry is a South African monopoly that gave apartheid-era South Africa its nickname 'Chrome City'.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: chromite FeCr2O4, 30-45% Cr2O3

facts.label: Refined form
facts.value: ferrochrome, 60-70% Cr, and chromium metal

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: ~95% of world ferrochrome capacity was in South Africa in the early 1980s

facts.label: Electrolytic chromium
facts.value: a few thousand tonnes a year of 99.9% metal, for plating chemistry and sputtering targets

children.name: Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts
children.description: A C64 contains perhaps 0.2-1 g of gold. It is the flash on the edge-connector fingers, the plating on the IC leads, the ball or wedge bond from the die pad to the package, and the contacts in the 'jewel' switch mechanisms. Gold is the only metal that does not tarnish and does not form an insulating oxide, which is the entire reason it is used where an electrical contact has to survive years untouched. All of that gold is refined to 99.99% from an ore averaging a few grams per tonne, and in 1982 essentially all of it came out of a cyanide leach.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) minimum for plating; 99.9995% (5N) for bonding wire

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.5-8 g/t for open-pit and heap leach operations; underground veins run 5-30 g/t

facts.label: Leachant
facts.value: 0.01-0.05% NaCN in solution (100-500 mg/L)

facts.label: 1982 route
facts.value: cyanide leaching and carbon adsorption, plus amalgamation and gravity in older small operations

children.name: Low-grade gold ore (0.5-5 g/t)
children.description: Gold at a few parts per million is not visible and not dense in a hand specimen - it is in the ore as discrete grains, often only microns across, or in tellurides. Most of it is in quartz veins, often with sulfides. The 1982 world had two completely different industries: the deep underground Witwatersrand, where a 15 cm face of reef at 10-40 g/t gave 100,000 tonnes a day through mills, and the Carlin trend and the Nevada heap leaches, where 0.5-2 g/t in oxide rock was stacked in 10 m heaps and leached in place. The heap leach was a genuine 1970s invention and by 1982 it had become a third of Nevada's production.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 0.5-8 g/t open pit and heap leach; 5-30 g/t underground vein

facts.label: Host
facts.value: quartz veins (lode gold), disseminated in carbonate and jasperoid (Carlin-type), and reef conglomerate (Witwatersrand)

facts.label: Precious-metal credits
facts.value: typically 1-3% of the ore's gross value is silver

children.name: Heap leaching with cyanide, 10 m pads
children.description: Run-of-mine ore, after a cyanide spray test, is crushed to a few centimetres and stacked in 100,000-tonne heaps on an impermeable pad. It is flooded with 0.02-0.05% NaCN solution, allowed to percolate for 30-60 days, and then drained and sprayed again. The pregnant solution is sent through a carbon bed and then an electrowinning cell. A heap-leach pad is a piece of civil engineering first and a chemical plant second: the entire economics depend on the liner holding and the pad draining properly, and the cyanide inventory on a large heap is the largest single cyanide hazard in mining. After the leach the cyanide is destroyed with lime and ferrous sulphate and the pad is detoxified before closure.

facts.label: Solution
facts.value: 0.02-0.05% NaCN (200-500 mg/L), with lime to pH 10-11

facts.label: Heap
facts.value: 50,000-400,000 t, 6-12 m high, irrigated for 30-60 days

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 50-75% for a well-oxidised ore

facts.label: Detoxification
facts.value: lime plus ferrous sulphate to convert CN- to cyanate

children.name: Witwatersrand underground gold mining
children.description: The other end of the industry. A 15 cm to 3 m band of gold-bearing conglomerate called 'the reef' lies at 1000-6000 m below the Witwatersrand, and from 1886 to 1982 the industry sank shafts and drove long decline haulages and ventilation and cooling galleries into it. Ventilation was the limiting factor: rock at 3000 m is at 40-50 C because of the geothermal gradient and because the rock is 3-6 C warmer than surface, so a mine 4 km deep needed refrigeration and a shaft fan development that took hours to boost air through the raises. Each shift broke perhaps 30,000 tonnes of reef in the mine and treated 100,000 tonnes in the plant, so the metallurgy was crushing a very hard quartzite and recovering maybe 60-70% of a 10-40 g/t ore.

facts.label: Mine production
facts.value: order 20,000-40,000 t of ore broken per shift

facts.label: Rock temperature
facts.value: geothermal gradient of ~3 C per 100 m, giving 40-50 C at depth

facts.label: Mining method
facts.value: long-wall stopes, stepped, backfilled with a sand-and-cement fill from a hydraulic stope

children.name: Witwatersrand gold reef conglomerate
children.description: The leaf: a 2.9 billion year old quartzite with rounded pebbles of quartz and jasper in a fine matrix - a fossil beach. The gold is in the matrix, as discrete grains a few microns across, and the deepest part of the deposit has the highest grade because it is the oldest and the most distal. It is one of the largest gold concentrations ever formed and it is a sediment.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: quartzite with quartz and jasper pebbles, 2.9 Ga

facts.label: Gold
facts.value: fine grains in the matrix, 5-40 g/t in the Far West Deep

children.name: The uraninite in the Witwatersrand reef
children.description: The gold reef is also the world's largest gold-uranium conglomerate, and the same reef that was being mined for gold was being mined for uranium by a separate set of shafts from the 1950s onwards. The uraninite is present as discrete grains on the carbon seams, and it recovers in the gold plant's gravity circuits and in the tailings retreatment plants. So the uranium in the C64's power supply - in a 1982 it might have been a South African or Canadian utility's grid, but the fuel cycle is the same one - began in the same bed as the gold on the edge connectors. It is the single best example in this tree of one layer of rock supplying two unrelated metals.

facts.label: Uranium grade
facts.value: roughly 0.5-3 kg of U per tonne of reef in the uranium-bearing zones

facts.label: Form
facts.value: uraninite grains on the carbon seams, released by weathering

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: with the gold, in the gravity and flotation circuits and later in tailings retreatment

children.note: Medium confidence on the uranium grade figures; the co-occurrence of gold and uranium in the Witwatersrand is very well established but the grade varies enormously between reefs.

children.name: Cyanide leaching of gold ore at pH 10-11
children.description: The reaction is 4Au + 8NaCN + O2 + 2H2O -> 4Na[Au(CN)2] + 4NaOH, and it needs three things: cyanide, lime to hold the pH at 10-11 so the cyanide does not protonate into deadly hydrogen cyanide gas, and dissolved oxygen. The pulp - ground ore plus lime, at 25-50% solids by mass - is agitated in an aerated pachuca tank or a Dorr agitator for 12-48 hours. The design variables are all about cyanide consumption, most of which is not gold dissolving but the cyanide reacting with the copper, iron and zinc minerals in the ore. In 1982 the plant that won was the one that kept the concentration as low as possible and the oxygen pressure as high as possible, which is the lesson of the 1986 Carbonin/Small's Pouso Bello mine disaster in Brazil, where 5-6 tonnes of cyanide went into the environment through a tailings dam failure and poisoned a river.

facts.label: NaCN
facts.value: 0.01-0.05% (100-500 mg/L), matched to the ore

facts.label: pH
facts.value: 10.0-11.0, held with lime or soda ash

facts.label: Solids
facts.value: 20-50% by mass

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 60-95% depending on the ore; refractory carbonaceous ores much less

children.name: Pachuca tank and the Dorr agitator
children.description: The 1982 standard leach vessel was either a Pachuca tank - a tall cylindrical tank with a cone at the bottom and a compressed-air rising pipe that boils the pulp like a carbonated drink - or a Dorr agitator, a vertical tank with a rotating central shaft and radial arms and baffles. A typical circuit was 4-8 tanks of 30-60 m diameter in series, 6 m deep, with the air line serving as both the agitator and the oxygen supply. Life before the mid-1980s the industry moved to Dorr thickeners and to the large rectangular Dorr-Oliver leach tanks.

facts.label: Tank
facts.value: 30-60 m diameter, 5-8 m deep, 4-8 in series

facts.label: Air
facts.value: 0.3-1.5 Nm3 per m3 of slurry per minute

children.note: Air consumption figures are class values from mineral processing textbooks; medium confidence.

children.name: Carbon-in-pulp and activated carbon adsorption
children.description: Gold is present in the pregnant solution as the cyanide complex at only about 1 mg/L, far too dilute to precipitate or to recover directly. The industry fix is adsorption onto activated carbon: the slurry after leaching goes through a bank of 4-8 tall columns of 1.5-3 mm coconut-shell carbon, which takes up the gold. In carbon-in-pulp the carbon is instead added directly to the leach tanks and separated by a static or centrifugal screen. The carbon is then stripped in a hot caustic solution - with a few parts in a million of cyanide and, from the late 1970s, acetonitrile, which is what makes the strip efficient - and the gold is electrowon off a lead or stainless cathode, or smelted.

facts.label: Pregnant solution
facts.value: typically 0.5-5 mg/L Au in cyanide

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: 0.6-1.6 mm activated coconut or coal carbon, 5-10 kg/m3 of carbon

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 1,000-6,000 g Au per tonne of carbon

facts.label: Elution
facts.value: 1-2% NaOH at 90-120 C, with 100-500 ppm CN-; acetonitrile used from the late 1970s

facts.label: Stripped solution
facts.value: 20-200 mg/L Au, electrowon to a 99.5% melt

facts.label: Carbon loss
facts.value: carbon is regenerated by acid and steam at 700-1000 C and reused

children.name: Activated carbon from coconut shell
children.description: The adsorbent is a botanical product, not a mineral: coconut or palm-kernel shell, or coal, carbonised at 500-900 C and steam-activated at 800-1000 C until the pore volume is about half the material's bulk volume. The pore structure is what holds the gold cyanide. So the carbon in the carbon-in-pulp column is a plantation or coal-mill product, and by the 1980s activated carbon was becoming an industrial commodity in its own right.

facts.label: Activation
facts.value: steam at 800-1000 C

facts.label: Surface area
facts.value: 700-1200 m2/g for the best grades

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: coconut shell, wood, hard coal, and in 1982 increasingly petroleum coke

children.note: The 1980s activated carbon industry shifted toward coal and later petroleum coke because coconut shell became scarce and expensive; medium confidence on the timing.

children.name: Hard coal and petroleum coke as activated carbon feed
children.description: By 1982 the industry was moving off coconut shell, which had become scarce and expensive as the plastics and activated-carbon markets grew, onto hard coal and - as the process matured - onto delayed petroleum coke, which has the right isotropic pore structure and essentially no ash. The activation is the same: carbonise, then blow steam at 800-1000 C to burn out the carbon and open the pores, giving a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. So the carbon in a carbon-in-pulp gold plant in the 1980s was often made from the same coke as the aluminium anode and the coke battery electrode, which is one of the more unexpected places this tree's carbon converges.

facts.label: Feedstocks
facts.value: coconut shell, hard coal, and increasingly petroleum coke

facts.label: Surface area
facts.value: 700-1200 m2/g for the best grades

facts.label: Ash
facts.value: coke-derived carbon is essentially ash-free, which is why gold plants wanted it

children.note: The shift to petroleum-coke feed for activated carbon was a genuine 1980s trend; medium confidence on the timing.

children.name: Activate the carbon with steam at 800-1000 C
children.description: The step that makes charcoal into activated carbon. A bed of coke or coal is held at 800-1000 C while steam and carbon dioxide are passed over it, and the gas burns the carbon away, opening a pore structure with a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. The rate of the burn is the whole process: too fast and the structure collapses, too slow and the pores are too small to admit the gold cyanide complex. The gold is adsorbed as the ion-pair Au(CN)2- at the carbon surface, so the carbon's chemistry is an ion-exchange chemistry rather than a physical adsorption, which is why the carbon has to be chemically clean and why it has to be regenerated before its capacity falls too far.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 800-1000 C with steam and carbon dioxide

facts.label: Adsorption
facts.value: the Au(CN)2- ion pair, i.e. an ion-exchange mechanism

children.note: Medium confidence on the mechanism being ion exchange rather than purely physical; it is the standard description but the mechanism is genuinely not fully settled.

children.name: Miller chlorination and the Aubure process
children.description: The refinery end. Gold doré - typically 90-95% gold with 5-10% silver - is fluxed with borax and litharge and blown with chlorine gas in an MRL (Mineral Resources Limited) chlorinator, heated by a propane torch, for 1-3 hours. The chlorine dissolves the gold as AuCl3 and the silver as AgCl, and the silver chloride precipitates as a crust. The gold is then stripped of the silver by the Aubure process - a hot parting - which reduces the silver chloride with wet wood chips and wet clay, a piece of technology that had not changed since the Middle Ages: the organic matter reduces the AgCl to metallic silver. What is left is gold at 99.5-99.9%, which is then electrorefined to 99.99% or cast directly into an anode.

facts.label: Chlorinator
facts.value: MRL/Merrill type, 350-1000 kg of doré per charge, propane-heated to 1000-1200 C

facts.label: Chlorine
facts.value: a continuous stream through a hollow lance into a molten salt flux

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 1-3 h per charge

facts.label: Parting
facts.value: Aubure: AgCl reduced by wood chips and clay

children.name: Electrorefine the gold to 99.99%
children.description: The Doré is cast into anodes and dissolved in an aqueous solution of gold chloride in hydrochloric acid at 50-60 C. The electrolyte is the Wohlwill process electrolyte, with a little silver nitrate added to make the silver chloride stay solid and drop out. Gold plates onto a pure gold or platinum cathode at 99.99% and the whole refinery runs at 2-5 V with a very high current efficiency. Every gold refinery in the world in 1982 used the Wohlwill process and it is essentially unchanged today.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: AuCl3 in HCl, with 5-20 g/L AgNO3 added

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) cathode, 99.9995% (5N) possible

children.name: Melt the dore bars
children.description: Before the gold can be chlorinated it has to be melted, and the doré - whatever mixture of gold and silver the refinery is holding - is melted with a little borax and litharge in a clay or graphite crucible to 1000-1200 C and poured into a dore ingot weighing 20-50 kg. The litharge is what makes the dore pour cleanly, because it fluxes the oxide skin; it also means a little lead comes along, which is harmless because the next step takes it out. The dore is weighed and assayed, and that assay is the number on which the refinery is paid for the month's production.

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 20-50 kg of doré with borax and litharge

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: borax plus litharge; the lead is removed in the chlorination step

children.note: Medium confidence; dore melting practice is standard and was unchanged from the 19th century.

children.name: Sodium cyanide from natural gas
children.description: Cyanide is an industrial chemical, not a mined material, and its feedstock is the same natural gas that makes hydrogen cyanide for acrylonitrile. The Andrussow process is the cheap one: natural gas plus ammonia plus oxygen over a platinum-rhodium catalyst at 900-1000 C gives hydrogen cyanide, which is absorbed in caustic to give sodium cyanide. So the cyanide that leaches the gold that plates the connector comes out of an ammonia-and-air reactor fed with methane.

facts.label: Andrussow reaction
facts.value: CH4 + NH3 + 1.5 O2 -> HCN + 3H2O at 900-1000 C over Pt-Rh

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: HCN + NaOH -> NaCN + H2O

facts.label: Form sold
facts.value: solid briquettes or flakes of 80-85% NaCN; bulk solution at mines

children.note: Also a very high confidence node: sodium cyanide manufacture from HCN is exactly this reaction.

children.name: Ammonia (NH3)
children.description: The nitrogen source for the cyanide that dissolves the gold. Ammonia is made in enormous tonnage for fertiliser and the cyanide plant buys a small part of it: natural gas and steam are reformed to hydrogen and nitrogen, the mixture is shifted, and about 15-20 MPa of hydrogen with nitrogen passes over a promoted iron catalyst at 400-500 C to give ammonia. The ammonia is then oxidised with air over a platinum or manganese dioxide catalyst to hydrogen cyanide and hydrolysed to sodium cyanide. The same ammonia is what the Sherritt-Gordon nickel leach and the potash-ammonia Solvay works buy.

facts.label: Haber-Bosch
facts.value: 400-500 C, 200-300 bar, iron catalyst, order 20-40 GJ per tonne of NH3

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: fertiliser ammonia ran to tens of millions of tonnes a year in 1982; a cyanide plant used tens of tonnes

children.note: Medium confidence on the numbers; the Haber-Bosch conditions are standard.

children.name: Iron catalyst for ammonia synthesis
children.description: The hydrogen in the cyanide comes from ammonia, and the ammonia's Haber-Bosch reaction runs over a promoted iron catalyst made from magnetite or from mill scale. So the cyanide that leaches the gold, and the chlorine that makes the hydrochloric acid, and the aluminium in the case all hang off an iron-ore-derived catalyst in a gas works. This is the last of the deliberate cross-branch loops in this file, and it is a real one: the Haber-Bosch catalyst is a 1980s version of the same magnetite that this tree mines for steel.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: magnetite reduced to alpha-iron, promoted with K2O and Al2O3

facts.label: Link
facts.value: the same magnetite mined for iron ore in this tree

children.note: The Haber-Bosch catalyst is manufactured from natural magnetite or from mill scale; medium confidence on which predominated in 1982.

children.name: Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing
children.description: Silver is the most electrically conductive of any element, and it is used in a C64 where the contact has to carry current at low force: the contacts of the rocker switches and of many of the keyboard switches, the silver-bearing solder and brazing alloys for the heat sinks and chassis joints, the silver-filled epoxy and silver ink of the keyboard membrane, and the silver that comes out of the lead and copper refineries as a by-product. Most of the world's silver is mined as a by-product - of lead, of copper, of zinc - and only about a fifth comes from a primary silver mine.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.9% (2N) minimum; 99.99% (4N) for contacts

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: native silver, argentite Ag2S, at 100-2000 g/t; the great districts were Freiberg, Potosi, Guanajuato, Cobalt, Broken Hill

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: ~75% of silver production is a by-product of lead, zinc and copper refining

children.name: Silver ore and the by-product sources
children.description: Silver behaves chemically like lead, so it substitutes for it in galena, and the world's most productive silver mines are really lead mines. The primary ores are native silver, argentite Ag2S, pyrargyrite Ag3SbS3 and stephanite Ag5SbS4 - the last two are why silver is also a lead-bysulphide metallurgy problem. The Cordillera Real of Potosi in Bolivia and Zacatecas in Mexico were the great producers, and Cobalt in Ontario is the historical outlier where silver was the target. Silver at 500-1000 g/t is a very good ore and at 5-50 g/t it is a credit.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 100-2000 g/t Ag in primary veins; 20-200 g/t as a lead-zinc credit

facts.label: Minerals
facts.value: native Ag, argentite Ag2S, pyrargyrite Ag3SbS3, stephanite, and solid solution in galena

children.name: The Zacatecas-Potosi silver vein mines
children.description: Mines like the Fresnillo, the Zacatecas and the San Luis Potosi: an underground operation on steeply dipping epithermal quartz veins carrying native silver, argentite and the antimony sulphides, worked in the Spanish colonial era by water-driven mills, mercury amalgamation and patio amalgamation, and by 1982 by mechanised narrow-vein mining and flotation. The Fresnillo mine is a silver mine that also happens to be the world's largest producer of antimony, which is a neat illustration of the interpenetration of these branches.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: underground narrow-vein, sublevel or conventional stoping; flotation of the antimony sulphides

facts.label: Dating
facts.value: Zacatecas was producing silver from 1548

children.note: Amalgamation was still in use for small operations in the 1980s; the mid-1980s saw a strong shift to cyanide. Medium confidence.

children.name: Mercury amalgamation of small silver operations
children.description: Before cyanide, silver was recovered by amalgamating the crushed ore with mercury: 4Au + 8Hg -> 4AuHg4 and 4Ag + 4Hg -> 4Ag2Hg, then squeezing the amalgam in a heated press and retorting the sponge at 500-700 C to drive the mercury off and recover the metal. The process left 10-100 grams of mercury per tonne of ore behind in the tailings, and it is one of the largest anthropogenic mercury dispersals in history. In 1982 it was in decline in the large mines and still widespread in artisanal operations; in the small artisanal miners' union of Guanajuato it outlived the century.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Ag + Hg -> amalgam; retort at 500-700 C recovers the metal

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 10-500 g of Hg per tonne of ore, most of it lost

facts.label: 1982 status
facts.value: declining in industry, persisting in artisanal mining

children.name: Mercury: cinnabar from Idrija and Almaden
children.description: Amalgamation consumes mercury and does not give it back, so a silver mine that amalgamated needed a mercury supply. Cinnabar, HgS, the vermilion pigment mineral, came from Idrija in Slovenia - the largest mercury mine in the world for 500 years - and from Almaden in Spain, and from the New Idria and New Almaden mines in California. The leaf is a mercury deposit, which is itself a strange one: cinnabar forms in shallow hydrothermal systems, and the Spanish and Yugoslav mines are in exactly the kind of fractured carbonate and volcanic rocks that the precious-metal branches of this file have already been through.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: cinnabar HgS, scarlet, with metacinnabar (black cubic)

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: epithermal and structurally controlled, in carbonate and volcanic host rocks

facts.label: 1982 supply note
facts.value: Idrija was still producing; the Idrija mercury plant closed in 1995

children.note: The Idrija and Almaden mercury mines are well documented; medium confidence on the 1982 production split.

children.name: The cinnabar vein
children.description: The leaf: a scarlet vein of cinnabar in brecciated limestone, sometimes 10 m wide, worked by open pit and by fire-setting underground since Roman times. It is the only mercury ore that has ever mattered commercially, and it is a beautiful and rather grim example of a metal that exists in one mineral, in one setting, in a few places on Earth.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: brecciated and faulted carbonate rock, with clay and chalcedony

children.name: Silver mill: crushing, grinding and flotation
children.description: Ore at 300-1500 g/t is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground in a ball mill to 50-100 um, and floated with a xanthate or a thio compound collector at pH 8-10. Silver sulphides float with the lead and zinc sulphides they are intergrown with, so the circuit produces a bulk concentrate that the smelter treats as a lead concentrate. The recovery is 60-85% and the tailings are the reason the Zacatecas and Guanajuato districts look the way they do - a very large volume of finely ground rock in long, engineered tailings impoundments.
children.note: Silver flotation is not well served by generic numbers because the mineralogy is so varied; medium confidence.

children.name: Why silver concentrate goes to a lead smelter
children.description: A silver concentrate is not a product anybody wants to buy; it is a concentrate to ship to a lead smelter 500 km away, because the only economical way to separate silver from lead is the Parkes process, and that needs a lead smelter. So the silver chain leaves the mine, joins the lead chain inside a smelter that may be in a different country, and comes back out at 99.9%. This is the practical meaning of silver being a by-product metal, and it is why the silver price has so little to do with the silver mines.

children.name: Refine the silver to 99.9-99.99%
children.description: Most silver never gets a refinery of its own. It is separated inside the lead smelter and refinery, or the copper anode slime, and refined there. The copper route: the slime is dissolved in nitric acid or in an aqua-regia type circuit, silver precipitates as silver chloride which is then reduced with copper and melted, and gold is recovered separately. The lead route: the Parkes process and the cupellation furnace described in the lead branch deliver silver at 96-99%, and it is electrorefined in a small silver tankhouse with a silver anode and a silver cathode in a nitric acid or a copper nitrate electrolyte at 2-4 V. In 1982 perhaps 60% of the world's refined silver was made at a handful of silver refineries and the rest was by-product metal refined alongside lead and copper.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: nitric acid with a little silver nitrate, or copper nitrate

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.9% cathode; 99.99% by re-electrorefining

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: order 300-600 kWh per tonne of silver

children.name: Electrolyse the silver and the dore loop
children.description: The silver from the Parkes cupellation or from the anode slime is cast as anodes and dissolved in a nitric acid electrolyte with a little silver nitrate, at 2-4 V with a pure silver cathode. The electrolyte's job is to hold the silver as the nitrate while the gold and the base metals either stay in the anode mud or fall out as slime. A small refinery might have 20-40 cells and make 5-20 t a month. The silver cathode is then melted and cast, and the whole cycle - cupell, electrorefine, cast, cupell again - can run three times to get five nines.

facts.label: Cells
facts.value: 20-40 per small refinery

facts.label: Passes
facts.value: 2-3 electrorefining passes for 99.99%

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 300-600 kWh per tonne of silver

children.note: Medium confidence on the cell counts and the energy figure; the process itself is standard.

children.name: Silver contact powder: Ag-SnO2 and Ag-graphite
children.description: A switch contact is not silver metal. It is a powder metallurgy composite: 80-95% silver powder mixed with 5-15% of a refractory oxide - tin oxide, cadmium oxide or graphite - pressed at 200-400 MPa and sintered at 700-950 C. The oxide breaks up the silver grain boundaries and suppresses the metal transfer that otherwise builds up on a small, low-force contact, at the price of some conductivity. Silver-graphite is the same idea for sliding contacts, and silver-graphite in a rotary encoder or a potentiometer is the single most common use of silver powder in electronics.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 80-95% Ag, 5-15% SnO2 or CdO or graphite

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 700-950 C in a hydrogen atmosphere

facts.label: 1982 competition
facts.value: Ag-SnO2 and the gold-plated contact were already displacing Ag-CdO on cost and toxicity grounds

children.note: The cadmium oxide contact alloy was being phased out on toxicity grounds through the 1980s; medium confidence on the timing of that shift.

children.name: Fire assay with borax and litharge
children.description: A refinery that also assays needs a cupellation furnace and a borax flux, because silver is assayed by cupellation: the sample is mixed with borax and litharge, cupelled, and the silver bead that is left is weighed. So the assay and the refining process are the same process, which is why a small refinery has a cupel furnace whether or not it refines. It is also why the assayer's skill and the refiner's skill are the same skill, and why the price of silver has always been set by a weighing scale on a furnace roof.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: cupellation with a borax-litharge flux, weighing the silver bead

facts.label: Fusion assay
facts.value: the alternative, for ores where the silver reports to the lead button

children.note: Medium confidence; cupellation as an assay method is well documented.

children.name: Tantalum powder for electrolytic capacitors
children.description: A 1982 C64 has a handful of tantalum capacitors on the mainboard, in the analogue filter section, and tantalum beads in small packages. Each one is a sintered porous tantalum anode with a tantalum oxide dielectric and a solid manganese dioxide or a liquid electrolyte. The tantalum metal is won from columbite-tantalite, a refractory oxide ore, through a hydrofluoric-acid digestion that is one of the most corrosive industrial processes in existence. In 1982-83 there was a real tantalum supply crisis - the Congo and Brazil supply, the Botswana and Zimbabwe expansions, the US stockpile, and a price that doubled - and it is the one place in this tree where a commodity shock from a mining country touched a home computer.

facts.label: Metal purity
facts.value: 99.9%+; capacitor powder is made from very high-purity metal

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: columbite-tantalite (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 at 10-40% Ta2O5

facts.label: Market 1982-83
facts.value: a genuine supply disruption in 1982-83; the price roughly doubled and the electronics industry began substituting niobium

facts.label: Capacitor grade
facts.value: capacitor-grade powder, 99.9%+ Ta, particle size controlled by milling and by sodium reduction

children.name: Columbite-tantalite concentrate
children.description: A hard, black, sub-conchoidal mineral - (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 - that in practice is never a pure species but a solid solution, and that is the whole problem of the tantalum industry: tantalum and niobium are chemically almost identical and always occur together, with the tantalum content ranging from a few percent to more than 50% of the total. The separation is the entire industry. The main 1982 sources were the Greenbushes and Wodgina pegmatites in Western Australia, the Cat Creek and Oarkopper operations in Brazil, and the columbite-tantalite concentrates from the Congo, Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Tantalum-bearing tin slags from Malaysia and Brazil were a secondary source.

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 20-60% Ta2O5 in the tantalum-rich fraction; lower for ordinary columbite

facts.label: Host
facts.value: granitic pegmatite; the Greenbushes pegmatite is a lithium-tantalum-columbite body

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: the ore is chemically a refractory oxide locked in a silicate rock

children.name: Pegmatite open pit with sluicing
children.description: The tantalum ore is in a pegmatite dyke, a very coarse-grained granite intrusion, and the extraction in the small operations is almost artisanal: the dyke is blasted, the rock is crushed and hand-sorted, and the heavy tantalum minerals are concentrated on a sluice or a jig. The Greenbushes operation, at the time one of the largest, mined a 3 km pegmatite by open pit with a 200,000 t/year plant. So the tantalum in a 1982 C64's capacitors very plausibly came out of an Australian open cut in a pegmatite, hand-sorted and sluiced.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit, drill and blast, coarse crushing, hand sorting, gravity concentration, or a dense-medium plant

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: coltan at 20-30% Ta2O5 from a 0.05-0.1% Ta2O5 pegmatite

facts.label: Predecessor technology
facts.value: cassiterite and wolframite were the original 1940s products of these same operations

children.note: Greenbushes was already a tin mine before it was a tantalum mine and then a lithium mine - a genuinely rare example of one pit changing commodities. Medium confidence on the production figures for 1982.

children.name: Granitic pegmatite dyke
children.description: The leaf: a coarse-grained, quartz-feldspar-mica rock so coarse that individual crystals are centimetres across, with the tantalum-bearing minerals in small pockets of rare-metal enrichment. Pegmatites are the last-crystallising fraction of a granite magma, so they are the natural home of every incompatible element - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, rare earths. There is no more apt end point for the tantalum chain than a dyke of crystals bigger than your fist.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: granitic pegmatite: quartz, albite, potassium feldspar, mica, with coltan pockets

facts.label: Grain size
facts.value: commonly 1-100 mm crystals

children.name: The crystals and the rare-metal pockets
children.description: The leaf of the tantalum branch. A pegmatite is the last thing a granite magma crystallises, and because it is water-rich and volatile-rich it can hold elements that have no business being in a granite at all - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, tin, the rare earths - at hundreds of times their normal concentration. Those elements concentrate in the last pockets to crystallise, and a pocket 30 cm across can hold a few kilos of coltan worth more than the whole pegmatite around it. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor came out of small pockets in a last-stage granite pocket, hand-sorted out of a rock whose crystals are bigger than your fist, in a pegmatite that is less than 0.1% tantalum.

facts.label: Enrichment
facts.value: volatile elements concentrate in the final crystallising pockets, at 100-1000x background

facts.label: Pocket size
facts.value: cm to tens of cm, holding grams to kilograms of coltan

facts.label: Host
facts.value: a granitic pegmatite dyke

children.name: Coltan concentrator: gravity, magnet and electrostatic
children.description: The coltan upgrade in a small operation is a classic three-stage gravity and magnetic plant: a shaking table or a jig throws away the quartz and mica, a magnetic separator takes off the magnetite and ilmenite, and a second gravity stage with a dense-medium separator makes a 20-30% Ta2O5 concentrate from a 0.05-0.1% pegmatite. Electrostatic separation takes out the zircon. The mass yield is under 1%, so the concentrator's job is mostly to throw away 99.5% of the rock, which is why a coltan operation is a small, cheap, labour-intensive plant sitting next to the pit rather than a large mill.

facts.label: Stages
facts.value: jig or shaking table, magnetic separator, dense medium, electrostatic

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: 0.05-0.1% Ta2O5 pegmatite

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 20-30% Ta2O5, at 60-80% recovery

children.note: Recovery figures for artisanal coltan operations vary enormously; medium confidence.

children.name: Coltan tailings
children.description: A coltan concentrator throws away over 99% of the mass it treats, and in the artisanal operations of the 1970s and 1980s that was put into the creek bed without any attempt at settling, and the creek carried it away. The ecological consequence of that was small compared to what followed - the coltan rush of 2000-2008 - but the mining itself was the problem and the tantalum industry spent most of the 1980s designing a better process and a better tailings facility precisely because it was planning for exactly the kind of scrutiny it eventually got. A node whose importance is only visible in hindsight.

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: over 99% of the feed mass, as a fine quartz-mica-feldspar slurry

children.note: Low confidence; the 1980s artisanal tailings practice is poorly documented and I am reasoning from the mass balance rather than from a source.

children.name: Hydrofluoric acid digestion at 100-200 C
children.description: The concentrate is digested in a mixture of hydrofluoric acid, nitric acid and hydrochloric acid at 100-200 C in a Teflon-lined or Monel vessel with a condenser to keep the HF in the loop. Ta2O5 and Nb2O5 both dissolve as pentafluorides, while iron, tin, thorium and most of the rare earths stay as insoluble fluorides or oxides and are filtered off. Thorium in particular is a problem: it is a radioactive alpha emitter that comes with the coltan and has to be separated and disposed of carefully. The mixed HF/HNO3/HCl digestion was the industry standard for decades; the Bayer process digest, using anhydrous HF with calcium fluoride at 150-200 C, arrived later.

facts.label: Medium
facts.value: HF/HNO3/HCl, or HF with CaF2 (the Bayer process digest)

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: Monel or Teflon-lined, with a reflux condenser - HF attacks glass

facts.label: Refractory waste
facts.value: 5-15% of the mass leaves as insoluble fluoride sludge; the hardest waste stream in the industry

children.note: The Bayer-process alternative digest came into commercial use in the 1980s and 1990s; the acid digestion below is the 1982 norm.

children.name: Thorium in the coltan: a radioactive by-product
children.description: Columbite-tantalite carries thorium and uranium in solid solution, typically 0.01-0.5% Th as ThO2, and because thorium's chemistry is so close to the rare earths it follows them through the whole fluoride circuit and reports with the rare-earth product. It is an alpha emitter, so the refinery's thorium residue is a radioactive waste that has to be stored, and in 1982 the disposal arrangements in most producing countries were informal. The leaf is a radioactive waste site, which is a legitimate if slightly grim terminus for a branch of the metals tree.

facts.label: Thorium content
facts.value: 0.01-0.5% Th as ThO2 in coltan concentrate

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: follows the rare earths through the fluoride circuit

facts.label: 1982 handling
facts.value: thorium nitrate sold as a 'fertile material' for a thorium fuel cycle that never arrived; the rest was stored

children.note: The thorium content of coltan is well documented; medium confidence on the 1982 commercial handling arrangements.

children.name: Monazite, the thorium and rare-earth carrier
children.description: Monazite, (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4, is a heavy placer mineral from the same beach sands as the ilmenite and the rutile - the Kerala and Queensland and Cape Breton sands. It is the world's main thorium source and, after a very difficult separation, a rare-earth source. In the tantalum circuit monazite is an impurity that has to be filtered off the fluoride solution. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor, the titanium dioxide in its casing, and the thorium residue all come out of the same Queensland beach sand.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4 with 5-30% ThO2

facts.label: Occurrence
