facts.value: heavy placer concentrates from a beach sand

children.note: The co-occurrence of ilmenite, rutile, zircon and monazite in one beach sand is well established; medium confidence on individual mine tonnages.

children.name: The heavy-mineral beach and its dredge
children.description: The leaf of the tantalum branch's by-product chain: a beach on the east coast of Queensland or on the Malabar coast of Kerala where the wave has concentrated ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite and xenotime into a dark, 1-10% heavy-mineral band a metre or two thick in the sand. It is worked by a suction dredge on a barge that pumps the sand onto a floating concentrator with shaking tables, spirals, a magnetic separator and an electrostatic separator. Everything in this file that is 'derived from a beach sand' - the titanium dioxide, the coltan, the thorium, the rare earths, the zircon - came out of a band like this one.

facts.label: Band
facts.value: 0.5-5 m of heavy-mineral sand at 1-10% HM

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: cutter-suction dredge or a walking dredge on a barge

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: gravity tables and spirals, then magnet and electrostatic separation

children.name: The fluoride digestion vessel
children.description: The digestor is the most aggressively corrosive piece of equipment in the metals tree. Anhydrous hydrofluoric acid at 100-200 C attacks glass, attacks most metals, and attacks concrete; so the vessel is Monel, nickel, or Teflon-lined, with the condenser and the piping also in Monel, and there is a continuous fluoride leak problem because HF is off-gassing from a boiling slurry. The industry answer through the 1980s was the Monel plant, with a steam stripping system to recover the HF and a caustic scrubber on the vent, and it was the single largest reason the industry needed a process chemist rather than a metallurgist.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: Monel, nickel, or PTFE-lined steel

facts.label: Why
facts.value: anhydrous HF at 100-200 C attacks glass, most metals and concrete

facts.label: Fluoride recovery
facts.value: steam stripping of the offgas, then a caustic scrubber

children.note: Medium confidence; the materials of construction for HF service are well established in chemical engineering handbooks.

children.name: Monel: nickel with copper
children.description: The alloy that made the fluorine chemistry of the 1980s possible: 60-70% nickel with 30% copper, and sometimes molybdenum, made in the same vacuum-melted, cast-and-rolled route as any nickel alloy. Monel resists hydrofluoric acid better than almost anything because the nickel fluoride film that forms is protective while aluminium fluoride and steel fluoride are not. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor was separated in a vessel made of a nickel alloy that came out of the nickel branch of this same file, and the aluminium capacitor in the power supply is made with an acid that would destroy it.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 60-70% Ni, 25-35% Cu, sometimes 1-5% Mo

facts.label: Why it survives HF
facts.value: the nickel fluoride film is protective; aluminium and iron fluorides are not

children.note: Medium confidence; Monel's composition is well documented and the mechanism is the standard explanation.

children.name: Separation of tantalum from niobium: K2TaF7
children.description: From the fluoride solution the tantalum is selectively precipitated as potassium heptafluorotantalate, K2TaF7, by adding potassium chloride and hydrofluoric acid at 70-90 C - and this is the step that separates it from niobium, because K2TaF7 is far less soluble than K2NbF7. The K2TaF7 crystals are filtered, washed and dried. Then the metal is won from it in one of two ways. The potassium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with liquid potassium metal, or with sodium, at 700-800 C, giving a coarse tantalum powder. The aluminium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with aluminium in an induction furnace, and the charge is self-separating by particle size - the tantalum comes out as the finer powder and the aluminium-fluoride slag on top. The capacitor industry wanted the sodium-reduction powder specifically, because it could be made much finer.

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: K2TaF7 from the fluoride solution by KCl at 70-90 C; niobium stays in solution

facts.label: Potassium/sodium reduction
facts.value: K2TaF7 + 7Na -> Ta + 7NaF at 700-800 C; the standard capacitor-grade route

facts.label: Aluminium reduction
facts.value: K2TaF7 + 5Al -> Ta + 5AlF3, at 700-900 C in an induction furnace

facts.label: Product form
facts.value: tantalum powder; capacitor grade needs a controlled particle size and a high surface area

children.note: The sodium reduction of K2TaF7 at 700-800 C is the standard capacitor-grade route and is still the industrial norm; the aluminium reduction is for bulk metal.

children.name: Recycling the potassium and fluorine
children.description: The potassium in K2TaF7 and the fluorine in it both come back. The mother liquor from the precipitation is evaporated and the potassium is recycled, and the fluoride is recovered from the aluminium fluoride slag in the metal reduction by hydrolysing it to fluoride and re-fluorinating. A modern tantalum plant's fluorine and potassium consumption is a small fraction of its theoretical requirement because of this loop, and the 1980s plants were learning it. It is a small detail that says something about how tight the tantalum business economics were - and the answer is that they were tight enough to make the 1982-83 supply crisis severe.

facts.label: Streams
facts.value: KCl from the mother liquor; fluoride from the AlF3 slag

children.note: Low confidence on the 1982s recovery efficiencies; the flowsheet is standard but the plant data is proprietary.

children.name: Coke and coke oven gas: the reducing agent
children.description: Coke is the black, porous, 90% carbon solid that makes the blast furnace possible, and it is also the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, manganese, ferrochrome and ferrosilicon furnaces. A tonne of coke is roughly 70% of the fuel and 30% of the reductant in a blast furnace charge, and nothing works without it. By 1982 the coke oven was a mature and much-diagnosed industry: the air pollution from coking, and the fact that a coke oven is the largest single source of coal tar and benzene in the industrial world, were the reasons the Clean Air Act of 1970 and its amendments hit coal and coke first.

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 88-92% carbon, <1.5% sulphur, <10-12% ash, 5-9% volatile matter

facts.label: Blast furnace use
facts.value: order 0.3-0.5 t of coke per tonne of hot metal; ~70% as fuel, ~30% as reductant

facts.label: Metallurgical grade requirement
facts.value: CSR (cold strength) and CRI (reactivity) indices; 55-70 CSR was typical

facts.label: Other reductant uses
facts.value: tin, lead and zinc smelting, ferrosilicon, ferrochrome, ferromanganese, and the silicon furnace

children.name: Coking coal, caking and prime coking blends
children.description: Not any coal: a blend of coals that fuse and solidify into a coherent cellular cake when heated. The caking power comes from the vitrinite, and the best coking coal is a low-volatile, medium-bituminous coal that goes plastic around 350-450 C. The 1982 sources were the Appalachian basin (the US steel industry ran on Appalachian coal shipped up the Great Lakes and the Mississippi), the Ruhr, the Donbass, the Kuzbass, the Bowen Basin in Queensland, and the Gondwana coals of India, which are so low in caking power that India had to import coking coal to make coke for its own steel - a good illustration of how coal rank, not just coal carbon, is the relevant property.

facts.label: Rank
facts.value: medium bituminous, 25-35% volatile matter, 1.2-1.7% sulphur at best

facts.label: Caking
facts.value: the coal must soften and fuse; the assessment is the Gieseler audibert dilatation or the BS swelling index

facts.label: Yoke
facts.value: order 1.3-1.4 t of coking coal per tonne of coke

facts.label: A problem coal
facts.value: the Gondwana coals of India and Australia (a) are non-caking, (b) have high phosphorus, and (c) ship long distances

children.name: Longwall coal mine at 300-1000 m
children.description: A coking coal mine in 1982 was almost always a mechanised longwall: a shearer cuts a 1.5-3 m thick seam across the face, the roof is allowed to collapse, the coal is loaded onto a pan chain conveyor and a main belt carries it to a preparation plant and up the shaft. The seam is a few metres thick, so the mine is a thin dark ribbon of coal a kilometre wide. Pennsylvania, the Ruhr and the Kuzbass are the three great coking coal provinces, and they are the geological reason those three places have both the coke ovens and the blast furnaces - the coal is too bulky to ship, so the steel industry grows where the coal is.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: mechanised longwall with shearer and roof bolting

facts.label: Seam
facts.value: 1-4 m thick; multiple seams mined in series

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: 300-1000 m in the US, up to 1200 m in the Ruhr

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 40-70% recovered after including development coal

children.name: Bituminous coal seam (Middle and Lower Kittanning)
children.description: The leaf: a 2-3 m band of bright, banded, caking bituminous coal lying within a cyclothemic sequence of sandstone, shale and fireclay - the same sequence that holds the Pennsylvanian iron ore, coal and limestone together in the Appalachian basin, and the reason Pittsburgh is the steel capital of America. The Kittanning and the Freeport seams were the premium coking coals; the coal is Carboniferous, about 320 million years old, and it was deposited in a swamp.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: Middle Pennsylvanian, ~320 Ma

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: cyclothemic sequence of coal, sandstone, shale and fireclay; a coastal plain swamp

children.name: Coal preparation: crushing, washing, blending
children.description: Run-of-mine coking coal is crushed to under 50 mm and washed, because the ash that matters is the mineral matter - clay bands and pyritic nodules - that can be taken off by a dense-media wash at about 1.4-1.6 specific gravity. The washed coal then goes to a blending yard, because a coke oven wants a consistent blend and no single seam is consistent. Blending is done by a stacker-reclaimer in a yard, and the recipe is a metallurgical decision that is still made on the basis of the dilatation and the sulphur.

facts.label: Crush
facts.value: to under 50 mm, usually on a double-roll crusher

facts.label: Wash
facts.value: dense media at 1.4-1.6 specific gravity, or a jig on the smaller seams

facts.label: Blend
facts.value: stacker-reclaimer yard; ash below 10% and sulphur below 1.5% for a good blend

children.name: The wash plant tailings and the creek
children.description: The other end of the coal preparation. Dense-medium washing rejects 15-30% of the mined tonnage as a fine waste with a high ash content, and in the Appalachian coal country in the early 1980s that waste was routinely placed in the creeks. The valley fills and the stream failures - the Buffalo Creek disaster in West Virginia in 1972 killed 125 people - were the reason the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 exists and why by 1982 a coal mine had to have a reclamation plan and a bond. So the coke chain in a 1982 C64 has, at its far end, one of the first major environmental regulations in the United States.

facts.label: Rejection rate
facts.value: 15-30% of the mined tonnage

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, 1977, with a per-tonne reclamation bond

facts.label: Precedent
facts.value: the Buffalo Creek failure of February 1972, which killed 125 people, was the event that produced the law

children.note: The Buffalo Creek death toll is well documented; medium confidence on the exact 1982 enforcement regime.

children.name: Rehabilitate the spoil by valley fill
children.description: The deep end of coal preparation's waste problem. In a contour mine the seam outcrops along a hillside, the coal is taken off along the contour and the overburden is pushed into the valley below, so the terrain ends up as a stream of grey waste from the highwall to the toe. It is cheap mining - no stripping, no trucks - and it is the reason the Appalachian coalfield has a hundred kilometres of dead grey creeks. In 1982 the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 required the mine to backfill and revegetate, with a bond per tonne, and that is the direct ancestor of the reclamation practices that the rest of the extractive industries adopted later.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: coal taken off along the contour of the outcrop, overburden pushed into the valley

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: backfill and revegetation required under the 1977 Act, with a per-tonne bond

children.note: Medium confidence; the contour-mining practice and the 1977 Act are both well documented.

children.name: Coking in a battery of by-product ovens
children.description: Two hundred and fifty horizontal chambers, 5-6.5 m long, 0.4-0.6 m wide and 3.5-5 m high, arranged in a brick battery 40-100 m long, heated in the flues between them by coke oven gas and reheated to 1100-1300 C. A charging car pushes 20-30 tonnes of crushed coal through a hopper into each chamber in about 30 seconds; the chambers are then sealed, and 16-20 hours later the doors are opened and the red-hot coke is pushed out by a pusher machine onto a quenching car. That cycle, 16-24 hours, is the heartbeat of the plant and it never stops. In the meantime the gas coming off the coal - the raw coal gas, typically 15-20% hydrogen, 20-25% methane, 15-20% CO, 5% CO2, 20-30% nitrogen - has been drawn off, cooled, and cleaned of tar and ammonia.

facts.label: Chamber
facts.value: 5-6.5 m long, 0.4-0.6 m wide, 3.5-5 m high

facts.label: Battery
facts.value: 50-100 ovens in a refractory-bonded brick battery

facts.label: Coking temperature
facts.value: 1100-1300 C in the coke; the oven itself 1000-1300 C

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 16-24 h; charge 20-30 t; yield 65-72% by mass

facts.label: Volatiles
facts.value: 25-35% of the coal mass leaves as gas, tar, ammonia and benzene

facts.label: By-products per tonne of coke
facts.value: ~0.4 t raw coal gas, ~30-50 kg crude tar, ~4-8 kg ammonia, ~10 kg benzene

children.name: Quench the hot coke, wet or dry
children.description: The coke comes out of the oven at 1000-1100 C and must be cooled fast or it will keep burning. Wet quenching sprays it with 3-4 m of water in a 30-60 s tower; the water flashes to steam, the coke is cooled to about 200 C and comes out wet with 3-8% moisture, which the blast furnace operator hates. Dry quenching pushes the coke into a sealed horizontal chamber and cools it with nitrogen or recirculated coke-oven gas. In 1982 nearly every coke plant in the world was wet, and the change to dry came later, mostly driven by the same air-pollution regulation that hit the oven itself.

facts.label: Wet
facts.value: ~4 m3 of water per m3 of coke; coke leaves at 150-250 C with 3-8% moisture

facts.label: Dry
facts.value: indirect chamber cooling with N2 or gas; no moisture, no steam plume

children.note: Wet quenching was near-universal in 1982; German practice had led the switch to dry by then and the rest of the world followed in the 1980s-90s.

children.name: The coke quench blow tank and its drain
children.description: Quenching has three products, not one: the coke, the water with the fine carbon in it, and the coke breeze - the 3-10 mm fraction that the blast furnace cannot use because it would be blown through the burden. Breeze is worth something: a coke plant sells it for sinter-plant fuel, for foundry moulding sand, and in 1982 increasingly for the electrode and anode pitch trade as a cheap carbon filler. So the coke oven's smallest product feeds three of the other branches in this file, and the water carries 1-3 kg of suspended carbon per tonne of coke quenched.

facts.label: Breeze yield
facts.value: 2-5% of the coke

facts.label: Quench water
facts.value: ~4 m3 per m3 of coke, carrying suspended carbon

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: sinter plant fuel, foundry sand additive, carbon filler

children.note: Medium confidence on the breeze yield; it depends on the crusher settings and the quenching practice.

children.name: Coke oven gas and its by-products
children.description: The gas is the profit centre as well as the fuel. After cooling it goes through a primary cooler and a benzol washer, which strips out benzene, toluene and xylenes; then a saturator removes tar and ammonia; then a Quinolining or electrostatic precipitator removes the last of the dust. What is left is coke oven gas, which is burnt in the battery flues to supply exactly the heat the ovens need - the plant is roughly self-sufficient - and the surplus goes to the steelworks as fuel and to a chemical works as a benzene and ammonia feedstock. Crude benzene from the benzol washer is one of the most valuable by-products in the plant, and it is where the aromatic chemistry of the plastics agent's chain starts.

facts.label: Gas yield
facts.value: 0.35-0.45 Nm3 per kg of coke, gross, before purification

facts.label: Benzene from the benzol washer
facts.value: 8-12 kg per tonne of coke

facts.label: Ammonia
facts.value: 3-6 kg per tonne of coke, as ammonium sulfate

children.name: The quench tower and the coke push
children.description: The physical heart of the battery: a tall steel tower with spray nozzles fed by a 300 mm main, a receiving pan, and a surge hopper from which a 2-3 m pusher car pushes the cooled coke onto a belt. Behind it stands the battery, bricked with about 20,000 refractory bricks per oven chamber in the modern design and castable in the older one, all of which has to survive 1300 C cycling every twenty hours forever. The doors are the coke-side door on top and the charging door below, and the charging machinery is driven by a single large winch.

facts.label: Ovens per battery
facts.value: 50-100 in 1982; 200+ in later designs

facts.label: Refractory
facts.value: silica brick or castable, replaced in rotation

facts.label: Push
facts.value: every 16-24 h, a 2-3 m stroke of the pusher car

children.note: Battery and push machinery design details; medium confidence.

children.name: Coal tar and pitch: the binder under everything
children.description: The tar that comes off a coke oven condenses as a dense black liquid, and it is the source of three of the most important carbonaceous materials in this file. Distilled, it gives crude tar, heavy creosote oil, and pitch - the binder in the carbon anode, the coke-battery electrode, the extrusion die lubricant and the aluminium pot lining. A tonne of coke gives roughly 30-50 kg of crude tar, and a tonne of that tar gives a few tens of kilos of soft pitch. So the coke oven is upstream of the aluminium pot, the coke battery and the graphite electrode, and the carbon-anode branch of this file is not an independent industry at all - it is the coke oven's tar still.

children.name: Soft pitch and hard pitch
children.description: Pitch is classified by softening point: soft pitch around 40-70 C, medium 70-110 C, hard pitch above 110 C. The carbon anode wants a medium-to-hard pitch for the extrusion binder; the pot lining wants a softer grade that can be rammed hot. Pitch is also a dense, black, aromatic, carcinogenic material that has to be kept hot at every stage, so the anode plants had their own pitch melting and storage tanks. It is one of the dirtiest materials in the metals tree and one of the least replaceable.

facts.label: Softening point
facts.value: soft 40-70 C, medium 70-110 C, hard above 110 C

facts.label: Binder use
facts.value: 25-30% by mass in a green carbon anode, 20-30% in an electrode

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: aromatic, carcinogenic, and it has to be kept above its softening point in storage

children.note: Medium confidence on the softening point classifications; they vary between suppliers.

children.name: Crude coal tar and creosote
children.description: The tar is separated into a light fraction (benzol wash oil and crude benzene), a middle fraction of heavy oils used as a coking-plant quench medium and a wood preservative, and a heavy pitch fraction. Creosote as a wood preservative is a genuinely large market and it is the same molecule family as the pentachlorophenol and the coal-tar pitch that the board and case coatings used. So the coke branch of this tree touches the plastics, the coatings and the timber-preservation branches as well as the metals one.

facts.label: Tar yield
facts.value: 30-50 kg of crude tar per tonne of coke

facts.label: Fractions
facts.value: light oil, heavy creosote oil, and pitch

children.note: Medium confidence on the tar yield; it varies with the coal and the oven design.

children.name: The coke oven feeds six branches of this tree
children.description: Putting the carbon branch together as one loop. Coal is distilled for rosin and turpentine on one side and for tar and pitch on the other; the pitch becomes the binder in the carbon anode, which becomes aluminium; the coke from the same oven becomes the fuel for the silica reduction that becomes the metallurgical silicon that becomes the polysilicon; the coke breeze becomes the sinter plant's fuel; and the benzene becomes the styrene and the phenol and the epoxy resin. One oven on a 1982 coking plant therefore feeds at least six branches of this tree, and it is the single most connected node in the file after the quartzite.

facts.label: Tar yield
facts.value: 30-50 kg of crude tar per tonne of coke

facts.label: Products
facts.value: crude tar, heavy creosote oil, and soft and hard pitch

children.name: The battery, its flue and the chimney
children.description: A coke battery is a long brick building - 50-100 ovens in a row, 40-60 m long, with a 60-70 m chimney at one end and a quenching tower at the other. Between every pair of ovens is a heating flue, so there are twice as many flues as ovens, and the gas from the ovens is burned in those flues and the hot gas is then drawn up the chimney. The chimney is the tall thing on the coke works skyline, and it is there for the combustion products, not for a draft. A battery is a piece of 1880s engineering that has been continuously rebuilt ever since and is essentially the same machine today.

facts.label: Chimney
facts.value: 60-120 m, 4-7 m diameter at the top

facts.label: Flues
facts.value: one between every pair of ovens

facts.label: Heat
facts.value: the coke oven gas is burned in the flues to supply the ovens' heat

children.name: The cold-strip push and the bench
children.description: The hottest, ugliest machine in the coking plant: a horizontal bar on a chain, 3-5 m long, permanently red, that pushes red coke out of the chambers onto the collecting bench. Its life is measured in weeks and its water-cooling is the operator's main concern. Everyone who worked on a battery in the 1980s had a job that was hot enough to need its own PPE rotation, which is the reason the whole industry has a 'coke oven man' occupational category and a very specific set of burn scars.

facts.label: Coke temperature
facts.value: 900-1100 C as it leaves the chamber

facts.label: Bar
facts.value: 3-5 m long, water-cooled, replaced every few weeks

children.note: Medium confidence on the consumable life; it varies with the coal.

children.name: Steel: sheet, stainless, tin plate, tool steel
children.description: Steel is the machine's frame, its shields, its fasteners and its tooling, and in mass it dominates everything else in the C64. The route is: iron ore plus coke plus limestone into a blast furnace for hot metal; hot metal plus oxygen plus scrap into a steelmaking vessel; steel through a continuous caster into a slab; slab through a hot mill and a cold mill into sheet. Then three specialties matter for this tree: grain-oriented electrical steel for the power supply transformer, stainless for the jack and the shields, and hardened tool steel for the injection moulding dies and the extrusion dies.

facts.label: 1982 routes
facts.value: BOF was ~70% of world steel; open hearth was in steep decline, in the US open hearth output fell from ~50% in 1970 to near zero by the mid-1980s

facts.label: Crude steel 1982
facts.value: roughly 650-700 Mt worldwide

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 1.4-1.6 t of hot metal and 0.2-0.4 t of scrap per tonne of steel

facts.label: Scrap
facts.value: ~30% of US steelmaking was electric arc furnace scrap-based by 1982; world-wide about 20%

children.name: Blast furnace hot metal (4.3% C)
children.description: A 25-30 m tall, 8-11 m wide stack, charged at the top with sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke and limestone, and blown at the bottom through 3-4 tuyeres with 1000-1300 C blast at a pressure of 2-4 bar. The iron oxide is reduced in stages on the way down - hematite to magnetite at 400-600 C, magnetite to wüstite at 700-900 C, wüstite to iron below 1000 C - and the carbon goes out as CO. The iron arrives at the hearth as a liquid at about 1450-1550 C, containing 3.5-4.5% carbon, 0.3-1% silicon, 0.1-0.2% manganese, 0.05-0.1% phosphorus and about 0.5% sulphur, and it is tapped every 4-6 hours. The slag floats on top and is tapped separately. A 1982 furnace made 5,000-15,000 t of hot metal a day on 3,000-4,500 m3 of volume and consumed about 400,000 m3 of blast a minute.

facts.label: Hot metal temperature
facts.value: 1450-1550 C at the tap

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: CaO-SiO2-Al2O3, 30-35% by mass, tapped at ~1500 C

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 5,000-15,000 t/day of hot metal

facts.label: Coke rate
facts.value: 0.3-0.5 t of coke per tonne of hot metal

facts.label: Tuyere zone
facts.value: the only place a furnace can fail catastrophically; a tuyere burn-through means 500 t of hot metal on the floor

children.note: The blast furnace has changed very little in the last fifty years: the great technical changes were the pellet plant and the oxygen enrichment of the blast, both of which were complete before 1982.

children.name: The furnace stack, throat and bustle pipe
children.description: The 20-30 m stack is lined with 1,000-2,000 mm of refractory and carries the burden down through a rotating throat seal into a stock column. The burden rests on a 'ledge' in the wall where the gas changes from upward to horizontal flow - the place every blast furnace operator watches, because if the burden descends too fast the gas gets through and the furnace races. At the bottom, the bustle pipe wraps the furnace and delivers the blast through the tuyeres, with the hot blast stoves - Cowper stoves, 8-12 per furnace, each 8-12 m tall - heating the air to 1000-1300 C on the gas from the previous cycle. A 1982 furnace is a machine about 25 m tall and 9 m wide with a 3,500 m3 working volume, and it holds about 100 tonnes of burden in flight at any moment.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: 25-30 m to the top of the stack

facts.label: Hot blast stoves
facts.value: 8-12 Cowper stoves per furnace, 1000-1300 C

facts.label: Refractory
facts.value: carbon-impregnated brick in the hearth and bosh; the hearth stave cooling is the critical maintenance

children.name: Copper stave hearth cooling
children.description: The stave coolers that protect the hearth from 1500 C molten iron are made of copper or copper alloy with a water passage cast into them, because copper conducts heat far better than cast iron. They are a copper industry product, and they are one of the more elegant cross-links in this tree: the blast furnace cannot survive without a copper casting technology. On a modern furnace the stave is cast as a composite with a cast-iron backing and a copper water-cooled front, and about 400-900 staves are fitted.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: copper or copper-iron composite with an internal cooling waterway

facts.label: Count
facts.value: 400-900 staves per furnace

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: years to decades; they fail by fatigue at the waterway

children.name: Basic oxygen furnace steelmaking
children.description: Hot metal is charged into a 40-60 t vessel - a pear-shaped converter with a refractory lining - together with about 20-30% scrap, and then a lance lowered into the bath on a boom blows 99.5% oxygen at 40,000-80,000 Nm3/h for 15-25 minutes. Three things happen at once: the carbon burns, the silicon and phosphorus oxidise, and the carbon monoxide boils the bath. The phosphorus removal is the reason the process is called basic: the lining is doloma, calcined dolomite, and the phosphorus ends up as calcium phosphate in the slag, which is why BOF slag is a genuine phosphorus fertiliser. The chemistry is violent and self-accelerating - the bath heats itself to about 1600 C from the oxidation reactions alone, so no fuel is added at all.

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: 40-60 t (up to 250 t by the late 1980s)

facts.label: Oxygen
facts.value: 40,000-80,000 Nm3/h through a submerged lance, 15-25 min

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 1580-1650 C; self-heating, no fuel

facts.label: Scrap
facts.value: 15-30% of the charge

facts.label: Lime
facts.value: 50-90 kg per tonne of steel, for the slag basicity

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: hot metal at 4.3% down to 0.05-0.1% or lower

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: CaO-FeO-SiO2, basicity 2.5-3.5, 100-150 kg per tonne of steel

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 80-90% on a good heat

children.note: In 1982 the BOF was around 70% of world steel. The open hearth, which needed fuel and hours and gave worse chemistry, was disappearing: US open hearth steelmaking had essentially ended by the mid-1980s. The open hearth was still significant in India, Japan and parts of Europe.

children.name: Open hearth furnace steelmaking, in decline
children.description: A 200-500 t rectangular basin of refractory with a hearth at 1300-1400 C, in which pig iron and scrap were melted while fuel gas or oil was burned above them and air was blown across the surface. It was dominant in 1920-1960 and it took 6-10 hours for a heat, produced a lot of nitrogen (so it could not easily make low-carbon steel) and consumed a lot of fuel. In 1982 it was a historical footnote in most of the world, still running in India, in Japan at a few works, and in a handful of Eastern European plants. It is included because it is the process the industry left, and because the heat-transfer engineering of the open hearth was the same furnace that the BOF was designed to eliminate.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: 200-500 t per furnace

facts.label: Heat time
facts.value: 6-10 hours per heat

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke oven gas, producer gas or fuel oil

facts.label: By 1982
facts.value: gone from North America and Europe, still present in India, Japan and Eastern Europe

children.name: Electric arc furnace on scrap
children.description: The other route, and the one that was growing fastest in the 1980s. Three carbon electrodes are lowered into a 30-100 t shell furnace and an arc struck, melting scrap with 600-1,500 A at 30-50 V - a physically brutal heat transfer that lets a small furnace melt steel quickly. In 1982 the units were mostly the smaller, older 'three-phase' EAFs of 30-50 t; the 100 t+ DC furnace that transformed the industry came at the end of the decade. The EAF makes about 20% of US steel and rather less of world steel, and it is the route that makes the recycling loop of car scrap back into new sheet possible.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: 30-100 t; most 1982 units were 30-50 t three-phase

facts.label: Arc
facts.value: 600-1,500 A per electrode at 30-50 V, ~30-60 MW

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: ~90% scrap, 10% direct reduced iron or pig iron

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: oxygen lances added later in the heat to burn off C, P and S

facts.label: US share 1982
facts.value: roughly 20-25% of US raw steel

children.name: Carbon electrodes from needle coke and pitch
children.description: The EAF, the submerged arc furnaces of the ferroalloy industries, the aluminium pot anodes and the large carbon blocks of the blast furnace all consume the same two materials: calcined petroleum coke or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as a binder. An electrode is milled green - coke, pitch and sometimes a sulphur or metal additive - extruded, and baked at 800-1200 C in a graphitising furnace to above 2500 C. The 1980s problem was exactly the nickel crisis showing up here: the EAF plants had no electrodes of their own in Japan, and when the 1979-80 nickel spike also hit electrode prices, Japanese steelmakers found that making steel required nickel, in the electrodes. UHP electrodes and the shift to larger electrode sizes was the industry response.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: 75-700 mm; 1982 EAF electrodes mostly 175-350 mm

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 kg of electrodes per tonne of EAF steel

facts.label: Baking
facts.value: 800-1200 C for carbon electrodes; 2500-3000 C for graphite

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 20-30% coal-tar pitch

children.note: The electrode/nickel cross-dependency of the early 1980s is well documented in the steel industry literature; medium-high confidence.

children.name: Choosing the steelmaking vessel in 1982
children.description: Three vessels made the world's steel in 1982 and only one of them was winning. A short parent node so the basic oxygen furnace, the dying open hearth and the scrap-based electric arc furnace sit side by side instead of inside one another.

children.name: Ladle treatment, degassing and the steel's last chemistry
children.description: In 1982 the most important development in steelmaking was not the furnace but the ladle. A 1980s steel ladle is a 100-200 t vessel on a rotating turret, and it is where three things happen in sequence. Secondary metallurgy: argon is stirred in to homogenise the temperature and composition and to flush hydrogen and nitrogen. Desulphurisation: calcium or a calcium-bearing reagent is added and stirred, taking the sulphur out as calcium sulphide in a basic slag. Deoxidation and inclusion control: aluminium is added as the last deoxidiser, and in a bottom-pour ladle the whole ladle is streamed through a nozzle to collect the inclusions in the nozzle. This is the technology that made clean, low-inclusion, low-carbon steel a reproducible product, and it is why modern sheet steel for tinplate and for deep drawing exists at all.

facts.label: Ladle
facts.value: 100-200 t on a rotating turret

facts.label: Stirring
facts.value: argon at 0.1-0.5 Nm3/min/t

facts.label: Deoxidation
facts.value: 0.5-2 kg of aluminium per tonne

facts.label: Desulphurisation
facts.value: CaO-Flux or Ca-Si, to below 0.005% S in a few minutes

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: 0.03-0.08% for deep drawing and for tinplate base

children.note: Secondary metallurgy was genuinely new in the 1980s and I am confident about the mechanisms and less about the exact reagent dosages at any specific plant. Medium confidence.

children.name: Continuous-cast the steel slab
children.description: Steel is not poured into moulds one heat at a time; it is cast continuously. Liquid steel at 1600 C is fed from a tundish through a nozzle into a water-cooled copper mould 1-2.5 m long, where the shell freezes in seconds. The strand then passes through a series of spray headers that remove the rest of the heat, and finally through a torch-cut or a flying shear, and is coiled. The whole point is yield: continuous casting replaced ingot casting in the 1980s across the industry, and a modern continuous caster turns out better than 95% of its steel while ingot casting threw away the 10-20% of each ingot that was the crop - the ends, the segregation, and the shrinkage void. The C64's steel exists because of this machine.

facts.label: Mould
facts.value: 1-2.5 m long, copper or copper alloy, water-cooled, 900-1350 mm wide for slab

facts.label: Secondary cooling
facts.value: mist spray along the roller table, taking the strand from about 1000 C to 300-400 C

facts.label: Cutting
facts.value: torch cut or flying shear, into 10-30 t slabs

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: >95% versus 80-90% for ingot casting

facts.label: Adoption
facts.value: essentially universal in the developed world by the mid-1980s

children.note: The adoption of continuous casting between 1970 and 1985 is one of the genuine revolutions in steelmaking and it is the direct reason tinplate could be made from 0.15-0.25 mm base steel at all.

children.name: The copper mould wall of the continuous caster
children.description: The copper alloy plate - phosphor bronze in most designs - that does the single hardest job in the whole of steelmaking, withdrawing heat from 1600 C steel at a rate that makes a millimetre of metal freeze in a second, and doing it hundreds of thousands of times. The plates are thin, 5-30 mm, and are cooled internally by high-pressure water, and they are plated and re-ground as they wear. Their thermal-fatigue cracking is the plant's central maintenance problem, and every crack means a slab defect that a tinplate maker will find on the inspection line.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: phosphor bronze or copper-zirconium, 5-30 mm

facts.label: Cooling
facts.value: high-pressure water at 30-50 bar inside the plate

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: thermal-fatigue cracks, marked with dye and then re-machined

children.note: Mould plate alloy and thickness vary; medium confidence on the specific figures.

children.name: Hot and cold rolled sheet steel
children.description: The slab goes to a reversing hot rolling mill at 1150-1250 C - first through a roughing stand, then a rail mill or a continuous mill - and comes out as strip 2-12 mm wide. Then the cold mill, a Sendimir or a multi-high cluster mill with a Sendzimir Z-High line upgrade, takes it to 0.2-0.5 mm, with the rolling oil and the annealing line in between. Annealing in a hydrogen or hydrogen-nitrogen atmosphere gives the recrystallised, equiaxed grain structure that makes a stamping possible. Cold-rolled sheet at 0.3-1 mm is the C64's case panel, the shield cans, the brackets and the heat-spreader, and the tinplate branch below is the same mill with a different end.

facts.label: Hot rolling
facts.value: 1150-1250 C, scale is descaled with a high-pressure water jet

facts.label: Cold rolling
facts.value: to 0.2-0.5 mm, with an anneal between passes

facts.label: Tensile of cold-rolled low carbon steel
Surface finish
facts.value: a bright rolled finish; oiled or pickled

children.name: Steel rolling oil: emulsion and hydraulic oil
children.description: Hot rolling of steel uses water emulsion; cold rolling uses a neat oil or a water-in-oil emulsion, chemically similar to the aluminium rolling lubricant but with a much higher base oil viscosity and a lot of boundary additives. So the C64's steel mill and its aluminium mill are the same kind of lubricant plant, and both are quietly downstream of crude oil.

facts.label: Hot rolling
facts.value: water emulsion, 0.5-5% oil

facts.label: Cold rolling
facts.value: neat mineral oil or water-in-oil emulsion, 1-10% emulsion concentration

children.note: Rolling oil formulations are proprietary; medium confidence on the ranges.

children.name: Anneal and temper the sheet to its specification
children.description: Cold-rolled low-carbon steel is hard and full of internal stress, so it is annealed in a continuous line - a few seconds to a few minutes at 700-850 C in a hydrogen-nitrogen atmosphere - to recrystallise it into soft equiaxed grain, and then, if it is going to be drawn rather than stamped, given a temper mill pass to raise the yield point by 50-150 MPa. The temper mill is a roll that puts in a deliberate rolling reduction that the temper roll locks in as a dislocation structure the anneal will not remove. The 1982 temper mill was a three-high Sendimir with a work-roll diameter of about 300 mm, and it is the reason a can and a deep-drawing panel are different products from the same mill.

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: 700-850 C in hydrogen-nitrogen, seconds to minutes

facts.label: Temper mill
facts.value: a deliberate 0.1-1.5% reduction, raising the yield point by 50-150 MPa

facts.label: Work roll
facts.value: hardened tool steel, about 300 mm, in a three-high Sendimir

children.note: Medium confidence; the temper-mill principle is standard, the specific 1982 mill geometry varies.

children.name: Pickle, oil and specify the surface
children.description: Cold-rolled sheet is covered in mill scale and must be pickled in hydrochloric or sulfuric acid to remove it, or the next operation cannot stick to it. Then it is oiled or lacquered so it does not rust in storage. On the 1980s tinplate line the acid was hydrochloric, which put a genuinely dangerous hydrogen into the atmosphere, and the 1982 line ran its pickling tanks under a hood with an acid fume scrubber using sodium carbonate - which is another place the sodium chain of this file enters. The surface specification is a contract: roughness, cleanliness, and oil film weight in grams per square metre.

facts.label: Pickle
facts.value: hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, 70-90 C

facts.label: Scrub
facts.value: the acid fume is neutralised with sodium carbonate

facts.label: Oil film
facts.value: specified in g/m2; on tinplate, 0.05-0.15

children.note: Medium confidence on the oil film weights; they are line-specific.

children.name: Tinplate: the tin-coated steel sheet
children.description: Tinplate is 0.15-0.3 mm of low-carbon steel with 1.1-11.2 g/m2 of tin on both sides, made on a continuous electrolytic line at 4-8 m/s. The strip is degreased and pickled in hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, rinsed, then tinned in a stannous sulphate bath with a fluoroborate additive, rinsed, and either given a food-can passivation in chromic acid or - in the electronics and tinplate trade - an electrolytic passivation in a chromate or tin-oxide bath. A C64 uses a few square metres of tinplate a year at most, in switch bodies and shields, but tinplate is worth a node because it is the one place where tin and steel and electrochemistry all meet, and because the chromate passivation is the same chemistry as the zinc chromate passivation in the plating branch.

facts.label: Base steel
facts.value: 0.15-0.3 mm, low carbon, low phosphorus

facts.label: Tin coating
facts.value: 1.1-11.2 g/m2 (2.8-28.2 g per 100 cm2); the food can standard is 5.6-11.2

facts.label: Tin consumption
facts.value: a 1 t tin can does about 250,000-400,000 400 g cans - which is why food can dominated the tin market

children.name: The tinning line: greening, tinning, soaking
children.description: The line has four electrolytic tanks in series - a 'greening' or pretreat tank to strip the last oxide, two or more tinning tanks with soluble tin anodes, and a 'soaking' tank to heal any bare spots. The strip runs through as a ribbon, and the tin is applied at a controlled thickness by the current and by how long the strip spends in the stannate bath. The mechanical complexity is in the handling: a 0.2 mm ribbon travelling at 6 m/s has to be threaded, cleaned and welded end to end several times a shift.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: SnSO4 with tin sulfate or fluoroboric acid additive; soluble tin anodes

children.note: Electrolytic tinning line parameters are well documented; medium confidence on the exact ranges.

children.name: Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain
children.description: The bottom of the steel branch. Iron ore is dug, concentrated, reduced and never appears in a C64, and this branch exists so that the steel branch terminates in a mine rather than in an abstraction. The 1982 iron ore trade was dominated by three names: Mount Whaleback and the Pilbara in Western Australia, the Carajas and Quadrilatero Ferrifero in Brazil, and the Labrador Trough and the Mesabi range in North America. The ore is hematite, or magnetite, or both in a metamorphic banded iron formation - a rock that is 2 billion years old and was originally a chemical precipitate out of seawater.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 60-66% Fe for the Pilbara direct-shipment ore; 30-45% for the Mesabi taconite that had to be beneficiated

facts.label: Sulphur
facts.value: <0.05% for a good steelmaking ore; sulphur above 0.1% is a penalty

facts.label: World production 1982
facts.value: roughly 800-900 Mt of ore and concentrate

children.name: Ferrite: transformer and choke cores
children.description: The C64's power supply transformer, the filter chokes, the RF modulator coil and the ferrite beads on the board are all ceramic magnetic materials, not metal. A power ferrite is a spinel - either MnO.Fe2O3.ZnO or NiO.Fe2O3.ZnO - pressed as a powder and fired to 1200-1300 C, which is powder metallurgy in the truest sense: the magnetisation is not in the metal particles, it is in the magnetic domain walls of a ceramic. This is the branch where the metals tree stops being about metal and starts being about oxide chemistry, and the raw materials are iron oxide, manganese carbonate, zinc oxide and nickel oxide.

facts.label: MnZn power ferrite
facts.value: ~50% Fe2O3, 20-30% MnO, 10-20% ZnO; sintered at 1200-1300 C in air

facts.label: NiZn ferrite
facts.value: ~50-55% Fe2O3, 10-30% NiO, balance ZnO; useful to about 100 MHz

facts.label: Two families
facts.value: MnZn for 10 kHz to 1 MHz and high flux; NiZn for 1 to 200 MHz and low loss at high frequency

children.name: Ferrite raw materials: the oxide blend
children.description: The three powders that get blended, and each one has its own industrial route. The iron oxide is either mill scale from the aluminium or the steel mill - washed, dried and milled, and the cheapest source - or a precipitated oxide made by acid leaching hematite. The manganese is manganese carbonate, a chemical precipitate from a manganese sulphate solution. The zinc is zinc oxide, made by roasting zinc ore or by burning zinc metal. The blend has to be accurate to about 0.2% in each component, because the magnetic properties are extremely sensitive to it, and by the 1980s the oxide suppliers were selling pre-blended 'master mixes' to the smaller ferrite makers precisely because the blending was the hard part.

facts.label: Fe2O3
facts.value: mill scale (5-30% Fe2O3, the rest magnetite/FeO, needs magnetic separation) or a precipitated high-purity oxide

facts.label: MnCO3
facts.value: precipitated from manganese sulphate solution; 1-2% Fe is the usual impurity

facts.label: ZnO
facts.value: from the zinc smelter, 99.0-99.7% ZnO

facts.label: Blend tolerance
facts.value: better than +/-0.2 wt% on each oxide for a good power ferrite

children.name: Iron oxide from mill scale or from a precipitate
children.description: The cheapest ferrite iron oxide is the mill scale from an aluminium rolling mill or a steel mill - but it comes as a mix of FeO, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 plus the alumina or silica the original metal carried, so it is milled and then passed over a strong magnetic separator to take out the magnetite, and the residue is calcined in air to convert all the iron to Fe2O3. The higher-purity route is to leach fine hematite in sulfuric acid and precipitate goethite or ferric hydroxide, wash it, and calcine it to a very pure Fe2O3 of 0.02% or less impurity - which is what the RF NiZn grades and the high-permeability grades need.

facts.label: Mill scale route
facts.value: magnetic separation of Fe3O4, then air calcination at 700-900 C to Fe2O3

facts.label: Precipitate route
facts.value: H2SO4 leach of hematite, precipitate Fe(OH)3, calcine at 700-900 C

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: the final oxide is milled to 0.5-2 um before blending

children.note: Ferrite raw-material routes are well documented in the ceramics literature; medium confidence on the temperature window.

children.name: Manganese carbonate
children.description: Not a mined material: a chemical precipitate. High-purity manganese sulphate solution is treated with sodium or ammonium carbonate at 60-90 C and pH 5-7, and manganese carbonate drops out as a pale pink powder. The iron must be kept out because MnCO3 with 1-2% iron pushes the ferrite's Curie temperature up and its permeability down. So the manganese chemistry of the ferromanganese branch in this file and the manganese chemistry of the ferrite branch share a plant but not a product, and a manganese mine does not touch either.

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: Na2CO3 onto MnSO4 at 60-90 C, pH 5.5-7

facts.label: Purity target
facts.value: Fe below 0.02% for high-permeability grades

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: pale pink to buff; brown if oxidised

children.note: Manganese carbonate for ferrites is commonly specified at 99% with iron limits; medium confidence on the exact precipitation window.

children.name: The mix house and the recipe book
children.description: The place where a ferrite formula is actually executed. A blend of perhaps 300 kg of oxide is weighed into a mixer - a ribbon blender or a ball mill - to 0.1 kg, sampled, analysed, and then the result is used to correct the next batch. The correction logic is where the manufacturer differs: some makers blend to the analysis and some blend to the recipe, and the argument between them is an old one. The mix house also holds the master recipes, and the confidentiality around them is a matter of pride rather than of deep mystery. A 1980s small ferrite factory had one mix house, one kiln line and one grinding room, and made a few hundred tonnes a year.

facts.label: Batch
facts.value: 100-500 kg of oxide per blend

facts.label: Correction
facts.value: blend-to-analysis or blend-to-recipe; the industry splits on this

facts.label: Small factory output
facts.value: a few hundred tonnes a year

children.note: Medium confidence; the mix-house practice is standard but proprietary in detail.

children.name: Ferrite powder metallurgy from blend to fired core
children.description: Five steps, all of them inherited from the ceramic industry, none of them changed since the 1950s. Blend: the oxides are mixed wet in a ball mill or a vibrating mill to a few tenths of a percent. Calcine or pre-sinter: the blend is heated in air to about 900-1100 C, which drives off the moisture and the carbonate carbon dioxide and starts forming the spinel; the material comes out as a hard, sintered cake. Granulate: the cake is crushed and screened, and about 1-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or polyethylene binder is added with a little water so the powder will press. Press: a dry press - a 100-250 tonne hydraulic press - forms the shape at 100-200 MPa, with the tool steel die giving the final dimensions. Fire: the pressed part is sintered in air at 1200-1350 C, and the part shrinks about 1% linearly, which is why the die is made oversize and why every ferrite part in the world is ground afterwards. Finish: the fired part is ground on a double-disc or planetary grinder to final dimension, because the press cannot hold the tolerance.

facts.label: Calcination
facts.value: ~940 C in air for a typical MnZn blend

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1200-1300 C in air for MnZn; 1150-1250 C for NiZn

facts.label: Pressing
facts.value: 100-200 MPa in a 100-250 t dry press; shrinkage ~1% linear

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 0.5-2% PVA or PVA-polyethylene glycol

facts.label: Green density
facts.value: ~2.0-2.2 g/cm3 for MnZn, against ~5.0 fired

children.note: The firing schedule - the temperature, the ramp, and the oxygen partial pressure - is where the entire performance of a ferrite lives, and it is the most closely guarded secret in the industry. The 1980s practice was a sinter belt furnace with a controlled atmosphere over several hours; the tight-oxygen and fast-fire schedules came later.

children.name: Wet mixing and the ceramic ball mill
children.description: The oxide blend is mixed wet in a rubber-lined ball mill or a vibrating mill, because water is the only way to get all three oxides into intimate contact within half a percent. A 1982 MnZn blend ran in a 1-3 m vibratory mill at 25-50 Hz, or in a ball mill with a few hundred kilos of zirconia or rubber-lined steel balls. The wet slip is then dried on a spray dryer or a rotary dryer to a granulated powder with the right moisture and the right particle size. The whole discipline of the ceramic industry is really about this step, and the blending tolerances of the finished core are set here.

facts.label: Mill
facts.value: 1-3 m vibratory mill at 25-50 Hz, or a rubber-lined ball mill

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: better than +/-0.2 wt% on each oxide

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: spray dryer for a granulated free-flowing powder

children.note: Medium confidence; the process is standard ceramic practice.

children.name: Granulation and the binder
children.description: Free powder flows; a pressed ferrite part needs the powder to fill the die uniformly, so the powder is granulated with 0.5-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or a PVA-polyethylene glycol binder and 8-12% water, on a spray granulator or a pan granulator, into 100-400 um granules. The granule has to survive being filled at a few grams per stroke and being pressed at 200 MPa, which is a tough mechanical requirement for a granule of ceramic powder.

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 0.5-2% PVA or PVA-PEG

facts.label: Water
facts.value: 8-12% of the green granule

children.note: Medium confidence; granulation practice is proprietary and varies between manufacturers.

children.name: Calcination and the spinel formation
children.description: The chemical heart of the branch. Below the calcination temperature the blend is a mechanical mixture; by 900-1100 C the oxides have reacted and the cubic spinel lattice - which has three cation sites and eight for every 32 oxygen atoms - has formed, with the zinc on the tetrahedral sites, the manganese on the octahedral sites and the iron distributed across both. That distribution is why MnZn has a high permeability: Mn2+ and Fe2+ on opposing sublattices give an antiparallel but nearly equal spin arrangement, so the magnetisation can be tipped by a small field. It is an oxide chemistry result, and it is why a C64's transformer is ceramic and not iron.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 900-1100 C in air

facts.label: Product
facts.value: partly formed MnZn or NiZn spinel, still porous and crushable

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: cubic spinel, AB2O4; 8 formula units per unit cell

children.name: Dry pressing in a tool steel die
children.description: The pressed shape is the finished shape - an E, an EE, a toroid, a drum core - and the tool is a hardened steel die in a 100-250 tonne press. Ferrite presses in 1982 were 100-250 t, usually with a single or double action upper punch, and the cycle time for a small E core was 0.3-2 s. The part is pressed dry, which is why the powder has to be granulated first: free powder flows, granulated powder fills a die uniformly. The tooling is the same tool steel as an extrusion die, so the SKD61/H13 branch serves the ferrite industry too.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: 100-250 t, cycle 0.3-2 s per part

facts.label: Green density tolerance
facts.value: +/-2%, which is what sets the finished permeability tolerance

facts.label: Die life
facts.value: order 100,000-1,000,000 shots depending on the abrasive behaviour of the powder

children.note: Medium confidence on die life; abrasive wear of the powder is highly formulation-dependent.

children.name: Firing at 1200-1300 C and the shrinkage
children.description: The pressed part is fired on a belt or in a tunnel kiln in air, and in the last stage of the sintering it goes through the Curie temperature - about 200-250 C for MnZn - which is a magnetic transition, and above it the permeability of the material is irrelevant because it is paramagnetic. That is why a fire that goes too fast or spends too little time above the Curie point produces a core with poor low-frequency properties even though its density looks fine. During firing the part shrinks about 1% linearly, so a 20 mm E core comes out of a 20.2 mm die, and the finished dimension has to be set by grinding.

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1200-1300 C in air for MnZn

facts.label: Shrinkage
facts.value: ~1% linear, 3% by volume

facts.label: Curie temperature
facts.value: 200-250 C for MnZn

facts.label: Hold
facts.value: 30 min to several hours above 1000 C, atmosphere and ramp critical

children.name: Grinding the fired part to size
children.description: Because the fired part cannot be held to a useful dimension by pressing, it is lapped and ground. An E core is face-ground and the bore is ground; a toroid is OD and ID ground. In 1982 this was a double-disc or a planetary grinder with a diamond wheel, and it was expensive enough that a great many ferrite parts were still sold with a loose dimension tolerance and machined by the customer. The final steps are the coating: a thin epoxy or phenolic coat, or a dry lacquer coat and bake, which holds the core together, insulates it from the winding, and gives it a corrosion-resistant surface.

facts.label: Grinding
facts.value: double-disc or planetary, diamond wheel, to about +/-0.1 mm

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: epoxy or phenolic coat and bake at 150-200 C, or a dry coat

facts.label: 1982 economics
facts.value: for small E cores it was often cheaper to sell an oversize core and let the transformer builder grind it

children.note: Medium confidence on the cost trade-off; it depends entirely on the part size and the volume.

children.name: Control the firing atmosphere and the schedule
children.description: The most closely guarded part of the whole ferrite industry is the firing curve: the ramp rate, the hold times, and the oxygen partial pressure through a 12-30 hour cycle. Too fast through the Curie point and the grain boundaries form in the wrong order and the core is lossy; too oxidising and Mn2+ becomes Mn3+ and the losses double; too reducing and the Fe becomes FeO and the permeability collapses. The kiln in 1982 was a tunnel kiln or a continuous belt with a controlled-atmosphere section and a dewpoint-controlled atmosphere, and the recipe was the plant's only real asset.

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 12-30 h through a tunnel or continuous belt kiln

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: dewpoint-controlled; the oxygen partial pressure through the Curie point is the critical variable

facts.label: Oxidation states
facts.value: Mn2+/Mn3+ and Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio set the loss

children.note: The mechanism is well established; the specific schedules are proprietary and I am not reproducing them.

children.name: Hard ferrites and permanent magnet materials
children.description: The same pressed-and-fired powder metallurgy as the power ferrite, but with no permeability requirement and a coercive force instead. Barium and strontium hexaferrite, BaFe12O19 and SrFe12O19, are sintered into magnet blocks for small motors and, in this tree, for the permanent magnets inside a magnetic ore separator. None of it is in the C64; it is here because the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace is full of ferrite magnets, and because the separator is the one place the barium branch and the ferrite branch meet.

children.name: Strontium ferrite magnet
children.description: SrFe12O19 pressed and fired like a power ferrite, then cooled through the Curie point in a magnetic field so the hexferrite grains line up. It is brittle, it is an oxide, and its key property is that it does not need any rare earth at all - which is exactly why barium and strontium ferrite are the standard cheap magnet, and why the two-share-the-mill argument makes this branch's economics obvious.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 (strontium hexferrite)

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: above the Curie point, then field-cooled

facts.label: Remanence
facts.value: ~0.35-0.45 T; roughly a third of a Nd-Fe-B magnet

children.note: Medium confidence on the remanence figures; these are typical class values.

children.name: Strontium carbonate
children.description: The only geologically interesting part: strontium is the rarest of the three alkaline-earth metals used in ferrites and ceramics, because it has no ore of its own that anyone uses. Strontium sulfate (celestine) is mined in Spain, Mexico and Iran, and almost all of it is converted to strontium carbonate. A C64 contains no strontium, so this is a dead end, but it is a real example of a mineral that exists only to make a ceramic.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: celestine, SrSO4

facts.label: Main sources
facts.value: Spain, Mexico, Iran, China

children.note: Strontium supply is a genuine constraint on hard-ferrite production; medium confidence on the source countries' relative shares in 1982.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 or BaFe12O19, sintered; remanence about 0.3-0.4 T

facts.label: C64 use
facts.value: none; the magnets are in the concentrator and in small motors

children.name: Radio-frequency and rod ferrite
children.description: A third shape family: ferrite rod and toroid for antenna and RF applications, pressed with an anisotropic die so the ferrite is oriented in the pressing direction. An isotropic pressed ferrite has half the usable permeability along the pressing axis as across it, because the pores are flattened; a ferrite maker who wants an antenna rod presses it in a die that aligns the grains. This is the ferrite in a portable radio's antenna, and it is the same powder as the transformer core, pressed in a different die.

facts.label: Anisotropy
facts.value: pressed ferrite has about half the through-thickness permeability of the in-plane value

facts.label: Use
facts.value: antenna rods, ferrite beads on cable, EMI cores

children.note: Low confidence on the anisotropy ratio; the effect is real and well known but the number varies with the pressing pressure.

children.name: The anisotropic pressing die
children.description: A ferrite pressed in an ordinary die has its pores flattened in the pressing direction, and flattened pores cut the permeability in that direction roughly in half - so a plain-pressed ferrite rod is a poor antenna core along its length. To avoid that, a rod core is pressed in a die with a fine central punch, so the powder is displaced radially and the pores and the grains align across the rod instead of along it. The same die idea is behind the toroid's oriented product and behind ferrite for read heads. It is a small piece of die engineering with a large effect, and it is why ferrite die makers were a specialist trade in the 1980s.

facts.label: Die
facts.value: a fine central punch displacing the powder radially rather than axially

children.note: Low confidence on the specific die geometry; the anisotropy effect is well established but the tool design is proprietary.

children.name: Barium titanate: the ceramic capacitor dielectric
children.description: The disk and multilayer ceramic capacitors on a 1982 C64 mainboard are barium titanate - BaTiO3 - and barium titanate is an industrial material made from barite, the same heavy white mineral that makes the drilling mud. The chain is barite to barium sulphide to barium carbonate to barium titanate, and then a 1000-1400 C calcination and a ceramic pressing. It is the most complete oxide-mineral chain in this file: a sulphate ore, a carbothermal reduction, a carbonate, a perovskite, and a dielectric constant of several thousand.

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~1000-5000 for X7R barium titanate; ~10,000 for the pure material near its Curie point

facts.label: Barite
facts.value: BaSO4, 90-98% in commercial grades; 53% Ba

facts.label: China's share
facts.value: China supplied the majority of world barite in 1982

facts.label: Also used for
facts.value: the glass frit of the ferrite coating, the ferrite body itself, and the barium ferrite magnet

children.name: Barite (BaSO4) ore, 90-98%
children.description: Barite is a very heavy, very white, chemically inert mineral - specific gravity 4.5 - which occurs as veins, as replacement bodies in limestone, and as a residual clay. It has two completely separate markets. The drilling-mud market is by far the biggest and takes barite that has simply been crushed and graded to 200 mesh, because all it needs is density and a low quartz content. The chemical-grade market, which is where the barium titanate comes from, needs the barite to be low in iron and low in silica, because those impurities end up in the ceramic. In 1982 the chemical-grade barite was a small, carefully selected part of the output, and China and Morocco were the dominant suppliers.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 90-98% BaSO4 for drilling grade; chemical grade requires Fe2O3 <0.5% and SiO2 <1-2%

facts.label: Ba content
facts.value: 58.8% by mass

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: underground or surface; sometimes a byproduct of lead-zinc and of fluorspar

children.name: Barite vein and replacement mine
children.description: Barite is mined as a primary vein mineral - a gangue mineral of many lead-zinc hydrothermal deposits - or as a replacement of limestone. The processing is simple: crush, wash off the clay, and either float or just size and sell. A barite plant of the 1980s was a jaw crusher, a log washer and a deslimer, and the quality specification was almost entirely about the Fe2O3. The chemical-grade plants did a rougher job: a flotation and an acid leach to take the iron down.

facts.label: Processing
facts.value: crush to 25 mm, log wash, deslime, size to 200 mesh for drilling grade

facts.label: Chemical grade
facts.value: flotation plus an acid leach to bring Fe2O3 below 0.5%

children.note: Medium confidence on the chemical-grade processing route; it varies a lot by deposit.

children.name: Barite vein in limestone or as a hydrothermal gangue
children.description: The leaf: white bladed or massive barite filling a fracture, or replacing a fossiliferous limestone bed. The barite has essentially no use as a rock - it is only ever interesting where it happens to be 90% or better and low in iron.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: hydrothermal vein or replacement body in carbonate rock

children.name: Barite, bentonite and lime: the drilling mud system
children.description: A drilling mud is not one material; it is a designed composite. The barite is the weight - it is the only cheap, abundant mineral dense enough to hold back formation pressure at a density of 1.5-2.0. The bentonite is the viscosity and the filtration control, and it works because its sodium montmorillonite swells in water to several times its dry volume. The lime and the lime-soil inhibitors control the calcium contamination that comes up with the cement and that would flocculate the bentonite. So the barite branch of this tree converges with the bentonite branch of the steel branch, and both converge on the drilling of the oil and gas wells that produce the crude oil the plastics agent starts from.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: barite takes the mud to 1.5-2.0 specific gravity

facts.label: Viscosity
facts.value: bentonite, swollen to several times its dry volume

facts.label: Calcium control
facts.value: lime and inhibitors, because calcium flocculates the clay

children.note: Medium confidence; the mud chemistry is standard drilling engineering.

children.name: Drilling grade barite and its mud
children.description: The larger half of the barite market, and the reason a chemical-grade barite supplier has to be selective. Drilling mud needs a barite that is dense, grindable to a very fine size, low in soluble salts and above all low in cadmium and other toxic heavy metals, because the drill cuttings go into a mud pit and the barite is not recovered. In 1982 the drilling grade specification was a gravity of at least 4.2 and a particle distribution such that 90% passed 45 um. A 1982 rig's mud for a deep well used 100-300 tonnes of barite per kilometre.

facts.label: Specification
facts.value: specific gravity above 4.2, 90% below 45 um, low soluble salts

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 100-300 t of barite per km of hole in a deep well

children.note: Medium confidence; the mud consumption figure is representative rather than a specific well.

children.name: Barite to barium sulphide, then barium carbonate
children.description: The chemical reduction of barite. Barite plus coke at 900-1100 C in a rotary kiln gives barium sulphide: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO. That reaction needs about 1100 C to proceed at a useful rate, and the kiln is a long steel tube, 2-3 m diameter and 30-50 m long, rotating at 0.5-1 rpm, heated by a gas or oil burner at one end. The barium sulphide is leached out of the cooled cake with water, giving a solution of BaS, and that solution is carbonated with carbon dioxide - from a coke oven, from the sinter plant, from anywhere - and barium carbonate precipitates: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S. So the barium carbonate is made from a sulphate ore, a coke-oven gas and a stream of hydrogen sulphide, and the H2S is either burned to sulphur or sent to a Claus plant.

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO at 900-1100 C

facts.label: Kiln
facts.value: rotary, 2-3 m diameter, 30-50 m long, 0.5-1 rpm

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: the cake is leached with water, hot, and the BaS solution is clarified

facts.label: Carbonation
facts.value: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S, at room temperature

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~90% on the reduction, 95%+ on the carbonation

facts.label: Barium carbonate purity
facts.value: 99.0-99.5% for ceramic grade; iron is the impurity to watch

children.name: Ceramic-grade barium carbonate
children.description: A fine white powder, 99%+ BaCO3, and the actual commodity that the barium titanate maker buys. Its iron and sulphur contents are the specification that matters, and both come back from the reduction step. It is also used directly - in the glass frit of the ferrite coat, in the barium ferrite magnet, in the dielectric of the lower-value ceramic capacitor grades, and in the ferrite itself.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.0-99.5% BaCO3 for ceramic grade

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: BaTiO3, glass frit, ferrite, barium ferrite magnets

children.name: Calcine the carbonate to a reactive powder
children.description: The barium carbonate that comes out of the carbonation tank is 99.0-99.5% pure but coarse and dense, and barium titanate needs a reactive powder. So the carbonate is calcined at 1000-1200 C to break it down to the oxide and then re-carbonated lightly, or it is ground extremely fine. Either way it is a chemical-material step rather than a smelting one, and it is where a lot of the ceramic-grade versus technical-grade distinction is made.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: to raise the reactivity of the carbonate for the solid-state reaction with TiO2

children.note: Medium confidence; the calcination step is standard but the specific practice varies.

children.name: Iron and sulphur in the ceramic grade
children.description: The ceramic-grade barium carbonate specification is essentially a statement about two impurities. Iron, carried through from the barite and from the flue of the reduction kiln, if it survives into barium titanate, acts as an acceptor and shifts the Curie point and the dielectric constant and hurts the loss - so iron has to be below a few hundred ppm. Sulphur, carried from the reduction and not removed by the carbonation, sits at the grain boundary of the fired ceramic and hurts the breakdown voltage. Both of them are the same answer as in the ferrite branch: wash, precipitate, and calcine in a controlled atmosphere. It is a recurring theme in ceramics that the last hundred ppm is the whole specification.

facts.label: Iron
facts.value: below a few hundred ppm; an acceptor dopant that degrades the dielectric

facts.label: Sulphur
facts.value: must be removed by the carbonation and the calcine; it degrades the breakdown voltage

children.note: Medium confidence; the impurity mechanisms in barium titanate ceramics are standard in the ceramics literature.

children.name: Hydrogen sulphide from the carbonation
children.description: The barium carbonate process makes hydrogen sulphide as a by-product, roughly 0.2 t of H2S per tonne of barium carbonate, and H2S is an acutely toxic gas that a 1982 barium plant either burned in a flare or sent to a Claus plant for elemental sulphur. It is also, if you are unlucky, a gas that kills by olfactory paralysis: at high concentration you cannot smell it, which is why a barium works had an H2S alarm on the roof and why the workers carried a supplied-air respirator. It is the least well-known hazard in this tree and a real one.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: roughly 0.15-0.3 t of H2S per tonne of BaCO3

facts.label: Control
facts.value: flared or sent to a Claus plant, with continuous monitoring

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: H2S paralyzes the sense of smell at high concentration

children.note: Medium confidence on the H2S yield; the hazard mechanism is textbook.

metal.rosin.activator.name: The halide activator in the flux core
metal.rosin.activator.description: Plain rosin is a weak flux. The electronics industry improved it by adding a small amount of acid activator - in 1982 almost always zinc chloride, or in the more aggressive grades a zinc chloride-ammonium chloride mixture - so the flux can remove oxides that rosin alone would leave. The trade is real: more activator means a better joint and a corrosive residue that, if it is not washed off, eats the copper. This is why the flux grade is a specification on the wire, and why the electronics-grade rosin wire of 1982 was normally a mildly activated (MA) or activated (A) flux rather than pure RMA.

facts.label: Activator
facts.value: zinc chloride at 0.1-2%, or zinc-ammonium chloride

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: RA (rosin-ammonia), RMA (rosin mildly activated), MA, A

facts.label: The trade
facts.value: more activator means better oxide removal and worse corrosion of copper if residues remain

metal.rosin.activator.note: Flux grade nomenclature and the activator levels are standard; medium confidence on which grade Commodore specified in 1982.

metal.pine-resin.name: Pine resin from a plantation or a pulp mill
metal.pine-resin.description: The leaf: resin bled from the trunks of Pinus species in managed plantations in the American Southeast, Brazil, India, Malaysia, Portugal and China. In the 1980s most rosin came not from tapping but from distilling pine stumps and pulping residues left over from the paper industry - a pulp-mill residue. So the flux in a C64 solder joint is, quite literally, a by-product of making pulp, which makes it a convergence point with the paper and pulp side of the organics chain.
places: Kraft pulp mill, southeastern United States

facts.label: Rosin yield
facts.value: roughly 1-3% of softwood pulp-mill residue

metal.pine-resin.note: By the 1980s the pulp-mill (wood rosin) route supplied the majority of industrial rosin; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split between gum and wood rosin.

children.name: Turpentine from the same stump
children.description: When pine stumps are distilled for rosin, the first thing off is turpentine - alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene - and it is the solvent the flux paste is made with. So the same 5 kg of pine stump that ends up as the flux in a C64's solder joint first gives up its turpentine, and the two are the two halves of one stump-distillation plant. The turpentine went into the paint and printing-ink industry, which means the soldering branch of this tree converges with the coatings branch through a barrel of distilled turpentine.

facts.label: Product
facts.value: alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene, by steam distillation of the stumps

facts.label: First fraction
facts.value: turpentine, then rosin as the residue

children.note: Medium confidence on the order-of-processing; the distillation sequence is standard.

metal.quartzite.name: High-grade quartzite (97-99% SiO2)
metal.quartzite.description: A metamorphosed, recrystallised quartz sandstone that is quarried rather than deep-mined. The chemical silicon industry does not use beach sand at all - it uses very low iron, very low aluminium quartzite, because Al and Fe are the impurities that survive the entire chain into the crystal. Two regions have essentially all of it. Note this is a DIFFERENT rock from the industrial silica sand used for glass, foundry moulds and copper-smelter flux, which is a much more common material.

facts.label: Main sources
facts.value: Norway (The Quartz Corp, JOlster and Tana), Brazil, and the Spruce Pine district of North Carolina

facts.label: Why not ordinary sand
facts.value: iron and aluminium in silica sand carry straight through to the crystal

children.name: Quartzite quarry, ~100,000 t/year
children.description: The Norwegian quartzite quarry is a bench mine in metamorphosed sandstone: drilling, blasting, a primary jaw crusher, and a sorting step where workers - and, later, optical sorters - remove the visibly iron-stained lumps by hand. The rock is then crushed, washed on a sluice or in a scrubber, dried and size-graded, because a single grain of iron left in the batch makes a bad day of the whole furnace.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open-pit bench quarry, drill and blast, ~15-25 m benches

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 100,000 t/year for the largest suppliers

children.note: Site-specific tonnages vary; this is a representative figure for a world-scale supplier rather than a cited figure for one named quarry.

children.name: Quartz sandstone protolith (metaquartzite)
children.description: The rock as a geologist would name it: a quartz-rich sandstone or siltstone, now a hard white metaquartzite of interlocking quartz grains with the bedding picked out by iron oxides. Some of the Norwegian material is a hydrothermal replacement body in a metasedimentary sequence. Either way the leaf of the silicon chain is a sedimentary or metamorphic rock exposed at the surface and dug out of a hillside.

facts.label: Rock type
facts.value: metaquartzite / quartzite; SiO2 >95% by definition

metal.silica.mgsi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
metal.silica.mgsi.description: The commodity-grade output of a submerged arc furnace: a grey-black brittle lump material about the density of bone. In 1982 a Japanese or Taiwanese silicon plant bought it as if it were ore. The specification that matters is not the silicon but the boron - anything above roughly 20 ppm boron cannot reach electronics grade, which is why the silicon furnace takes a low-ash petroleum coke and not the 10-12% ash coke the steel industry uses.

facts.label: Why not steel coke
facts.value: coke ash carries boron and phosphorus above the electronics budget

children.name: Submerged-arc furnace reduction at 1800-2000 C
children.description: A three-phase submerged arc furnace drops quartz, coal and woodchips down between graphite electrodes into a molten carbide bath at 1800-2000 C, and carbothermic reduction strips the oxygen off silica. Chemical silicon came to dominate this furnace by the late 1970s because the copper-clad electrode could then be pushed to a much higher current density. The off-gas, silicon monoxide at 400-1000 C, carries the energy away and is what lets the furnace run near-thermoneutral on the electrode side.

facts.label: Reaction
