facts.value: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO

facts.label: Furnace size
facts.value: 25-75 MVA, 3-6 electrodes, 150-400 t/day of silicon

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: graphite or UHP carbon, consumed at ~1-1.5 t per t of silicon

facts.label: Off-gas
facts.value: SiO-rich gas leaving at 400-1000 C, cleaned in cyclones and baghouses

facts.label: Power
facts.value: order 11,000-13,000 kWh per tonne of silicon from the arc furnace alone

children.note: The off-gas silicon monoxide chemistry was well understood by the 1980s and was the basis of several recovery processes that were still being commercialised then.

children.name: Carbothermal reductant: coke and woodchips
children.description: The silicon furnace burns roughly one tonne of high-ash-reduction carbon per three tonnes of silicon, and the recipe is a tight compromise: too much ash and you get slag, too much volatile and the furnace fumes. Producers blend low-ash petroleum coke or anthracite with a proportion of woodchips, because the wood brings in hydrogen and potassium that volatilise out and are quietly useful, and because the porosity of the burnt wood helps the charge breathe. The same class of carbon, at different purity, is the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, ferrosilicon, ferromanganese and ferrochrome branches of this file.

facts.label: Ash target
facts.value: <1% for the reducer, versus the 10-12% typical of foundry coke

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.9-1.1 t of carbon per t of silicon

children.note: The consumption ratio varies with furnace design and recovery; treat as order of magnitude.

children.name: Calcined petroleum coke for silicon
children.description: Delayed-coker green coke calcined in a rotary or shaft kiln to 2200-2800 C and quenched. The silicon grade is chosen for low ash, low vanadium and low sulphur, which is a narrow slice of the coke market - needle coke and sponge coke are the mainstream products and both carry more vanadium than the silicon furnace wants.

metal.silica.polysilicon.name: Polysilicon ingot and rod, 9N
metal.silica.polysilicon.description: Shiny grey metalloid deposited as a polycrystalline boule on electrically heated silicon seed rods and then sawn into chunks. The chunks are the cathode-grade feedstock that the crystal puller charges. In 1982 the world outside Japan consumed polysilicon as an expensive specialty chemical, not as a commodity. The 6510 is an NMOS part, so its 1982 die uses aluminium gate metal and thermally grown oxide rather than a polysilicon gate; this branch is the industry feedstock route behind that, and it is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

facts.label: Typical purity
facts.value: 9N (99.9999999%); 6N-7N was typical of the 1982 era

facts.label: Form
facts.value: sawn rod segments, 5-30 kg per chunk in 1980s practice

facts.label: Energy for the whole route
facts.value: 100-200 kWh per kg of polysilicon

children.name: Siemens deposition on UHF-heated rods
children.description: Trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow over silicon rods held just below their melting point by radio-frequency induction, and silicon atoms drop out as polycrystalline growth. Rod temperature is the whole ballgame: too cold and you get powder, too hot and you get liquid droplets that fall into the bed. Two temperature measurement methods were in use - an optical pyrometer sighted on a blackened patch of rod, and a movable thermocouple in the gas stream - and calibrating that pyrometer was a plant secret worth millions.

facts.label: Induction frequency
facts.value: 200-500 kHz historically, multi-MHz later

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 100-200 kWh per kg of polysilicon across the whole chlorosilane route

facts.label: Deposition rate
facts.value: single-digit micrometres per hour per rod in 1980s reactors

children.name: Doped vs undoped polysilicon
children.description: Two grades were produced side by side in the same plant. UNdoped polysilicon went to the crystal puller for Czochralski ingots. Heavily doped material - p-type with boron or phosphorus, n-type with phosphorus or arsenic - went to subcollector plugs, to doped polysilicon films in later processes, and, most importantly, to the heavily doped epi and subcollector wafers that the NMOS logic was built on. In 1982 the dopant was dosed into the trichlorosilane stream as phosphine or the corresponding trichloride.

facts.label: Target resistivity
facts.value: 0.005-0.02 ohm-cm for a doped polysilicon film; subcollector 0.1 ohm-cm

facts.label: Dopant sources
facts.value: PH3 for both polarities in older practice; AsH3 for n-type

children.note: I could not confirm which dopant gas a given 1982 Taiwanese polysilicon plant used; the specific pairing is medium confidence.

children.name: Crushing, flaking and acid etching of the rod
children.description: The deposited rod is sawn with a slurry-impregnated circular saw, then the pieces are fractured and leached in hot hydrochloric-nitric acid to strip near-surface contamination from the seed end. What the puller wants is small pieces with clean fracture faces, because every surface is a chance to recontaminate. Rod ends were also ground back and reused as seed.
children.note: The etch chemistry varied plant to plant and was rarely published; described here from general practice.

facts.label: Chunk size
facts.value: 5-30 kg per sawn rod segment in 1980s practice

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: a hot HCl/HF polish removes the saw damage and the surface boron before the chunk is charged to the puller

children.name: Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N
children.description: Colourless fuming liquid, the money molecule of the whole silicon industry. Made by chlorinating impure silicon with hydrogen chloride in a fluidised bed, then purified to 11 nines purely by fractional distillation, because every one of the metal impurities that matter happens to be a chloride with a different boiling point from HSiCl3.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 11N (99.999999999%) after distillation

children.name: Fractional distillation of HSiCl3
children.description: Tall, stainless, pressure-rated columns that separate trichlorosilane from its neighbours purely on volatility. The separation is the entire purification strategy: nothing clever happens chemically, the same material is simply re-fractionated until the boron is gone.
children.note: The boron cuts are the hard part: BCl3 boils close to trichlorosilane and boron has a low distribution coefficient, so 1980s plants used tall columns and many theoretical plates.

children.name: Fluid-bed chlorination of silicon at ~300 C
children.description: Metallurgical silicon is fluidised with nitrogen and metered HCl gas at 290-320 C. Silicon converts to trichlorosilane with hydrogen off; a large fraction of the feed instead goes to silicon tetrachloride, because the oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals push the stoichiometry. The bed is a tall stainless vessel with a distributor plate, and the reaction is exothermic enough that cooling coils matter.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Si + 3HCl -> HSiCl3 + H2, with Si + 4HCl -> SiCl4 + 2H2 as the side reaction

facts.label: Feed requirement
facts.value: ~99% Si with boron below ~20 ppm

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: historically copper or copper chloride; most modern plants run catalyst-free

children.name: Silicon tetrachloride by-product and recycling
children.description: Roughly half to two thirds of the silicon fed to a fluidised-bed chlorinator leaves as SiCl4 instead of HSiCl3, because oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals conspire. SiCl4 boils at 57.6 C and separates easily; it was largely dumped in the 1970s and later re-admitted as a chlorinating agent. The stoichiometric route that lets a plant recycle SiCl4 back into HSiCl3 by adding hydrogen and more silicon is the reason modern plants get the yields they do.

facts.label: 1980s practice
facts.value: a large fraction of by-product SiCl4 was sold as a solvent or to fumed-silica makers; full recycle came later

children.note: The fraction and its fate vary strongly between plants and years; high confidence in the chemistry, medium on the 1982 commercial split.

metal.caustic-soda.name: Caustic soda (NaOH), 50% solution
metal.caustic-soda.description: Two entirely different consumers in this tree. The Bayer process digestion liquor, where a caustic grade tanker holds roughly 300-400 t of 50% solution and a refinery's caustic and steam costs dominate its operating cost. And the chlor-alkali industry, where the same product comes out of the same cell as the chlorine and hydrogen that make the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Cost accounting in aluminium is dominated by caustic and steam; every tonne of caustic lost to red mud is recovered by lime in the causticisation circuit or bought.

facts.label: Bayer consumption
facts.value: order 100-200 kg of Na2O-equivalent per tonne of alumina, plus process losses

facts.label: Concentration sold
facts.value: 50% w/w membrane-grade solution

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, done with lime

children.name: Chlor-alkali electrolytic cell
children.description: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2. In 1982 almost all of it was a diaphragm cell or a mercury cell. The diaphragm cell - an asbestos-cloth cathode separator - gave low-purity caustic loaded with salt and was steadily displaced through the late 1970s and 1980s by the membrane cell, which delivers 50% NaOH essentially free of salt. Mercury cell caustic went to a short finishing step, causticisation with sodium carbonate, to strip the last mercury; the Hooker Chemical conversion of its Niagara Falls works to membrane in 1984 is the emblematic date.

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 3.0-4.5 V diaphragm, 4-5 V membrane, 4.5-5 V mercury

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: ~2300-2700 kWh per tonne of chlorine

facts.label: 1982 technology split
facts.value: diaphragm dominant, membrane a fast-growing minority, mercury still common

facts.label: Chlorine purity
facts.value: ~98-99% dry, enough for HCl synthesis

children.name: The diaphragm cell and the asbestos problem
children.description: The 1980s chlor-alkali cell was a rectangular steel box, 2-3 m long, with an anode compartment of brine and a cathode compartment of water separated by an asbestos cloth diaphragm deposited on a wire gauze. The diaphragm was cheap, durable and effective, and it was the reason the world's chlor-alkali industry had a mesothelioma problem. The cell voltage was low, 3.0-3.5 V, and the caustic carried 10-15 g/L of salt because the diaphragm let chloride through. The Hooker Chemical conversion at Niagara Falls in 1984 to a membrane cell was the moment the asbestos diaphragm began to disappear from the industry.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: 2-3 m long rectangular steel box, brine anode compartment, water cathode compartment

facts.label: Diaphragm
facts.value: asbestos cloth on a steel gauze

facts.label: Caustic impurity
facts.value: 10-15 g/L of NaCl carried through

facts.label: Transition date
facts.value: Hooker Chemical converted its Niagara Falls works to membrane in 1984

children.note: The Hooker conversion year is a well-documented landmark in the chlor-alkali industry.

children.name: Dechlorination and the brine circuit
children.description: The brine leaving a cell still has hypochlorite in it, because chlorine dissolves in the caustic. It is treated with sodium sulphite and then acidified, the brine is re-saturated with salt and re-purified on a soda ash and barium carbonate cycle, and it goes back to the cell. So a chlor-alkali plant also consumes sodium carbonate and barium carbonate - the latter being, note, the barium carbonate from the barium branch of this file. The barium carbonate is there to remove the sulphate from the brine as barium sulphate, which is filtered off and, until the 1980s, dumped.

facts.label: Dechlorination
facts.value: sodium sulphite, then hydrochloric acid to pH 2-3

facts.label: Sulphate removal
facts.value: barium carbonate -> barium sulphate sludge, filtered and discarded

facts.label: Brine consumption
facts.value: order 0.3-0.6 t of salt per tonne of chlorine

children.note: Medium confidence on the consumption figures; the barium carbonate sulphate removal is standard practice.

metal.chlorine.name: Chlorine gas (Cl2)
metal.chlorine.description: A pale yellow-green gas denser than air, made in the chlor-alkali plant and piped or tanker-shipped to the hydrochloric acid synthesis unit. Around 1982 much of it went to solvent makers and to water treatment as chlorinated organics; only a fraction ever reached a silicon plant, and silicon-grade chlorine must be bone dry, because water plus trichlorosilane gives hydrochloric acid and hexasiloxane gel that plugs the fluidised bed.

facts.label: Water content spec
facts.value: <40 ppm H2O for electronic-grade silicon plants

facts.label: Liquefaction
facts.value: shipped as liquid at about -34 C, or as dry gas in tube trailers

metal.chlorine.note: The water specification varies by plant; stated as a typical order.

metal.hydrogen.name: Electrolysis hydrogen from the chlor-alkali cathode
metal.hydrogen.description: The wet hydrogen off the cathode goes to acid synthesis, and in a silicon plant it also goes to the Siemens reactor as the carrier that carries trichlorosilane to the rod and strips the chlorine off. The purification train is a caustic scrubber, then a drying tower, and the carbon monoxide has to be taken below a few ppm or the polysilicon comes out with carbon in it. The same hydrogen, purified a stage further, is what a stainless bright-annealing line uses.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: chlor-alkali cathode gas

facts.label: Purishment
facts.value: caustic scrub, molecular-sieve dry, CO below 5-10 ppm

metal.hydrogen.note: The CO limit is my recollection of silicon-grade hydrogen specifications; medium confidence.

metal.hydrochloric-acid.name: Hydrochloric acid (32-37%)
metal.hydrochloric-acid.description: The hydrochloric acid that chlorinates metallurgical silicon. Industrial acid is made by burning hydrogen in chlorine, both products of the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the silicon plant's feedstock chain runs back through a 1970s chlor-alkali plant and, behind that, a salt mine or a solar salt pan. The same acid is used for galvanising pickling, for the stainless pickling line, for the tinplate line, and for regenerating ferric chloride etchant at the board fab.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl

facts.label: Commercial strength
facts.value: ~32-37% w/w, the azeotrope

facts.label: Typical silicon-plant demand
facts.value: order 10-30 t of acid per tonne of polysilicon plant output

children.name: HCl synthesis and absorption
children.description: Chlorine and hydrogen are fed to a steel burner with a plug of graphite or a water film that quenches the flame - a free gas-phase hydrogen-chlorine reaction is not something you leave unattended. The hot HCl gas is then absorbed in a water scrubber to make the azeotrope, and the acid is pumped out to wherever it is going: the fluidised bed, the pickle line, the tankhouse.

facts.label: Flame temperature
facts.value: >2000 C, quenched below 400 C within milliseconds

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: water scrubber, adiabatic, controlled by a weak-acid bleed

metal.salt-brine.name: Rock salt and solar salt brine
metal.salt-brine.description: Two very different-looking things that are the same feedstock. Rock salt is a bed of halite pushed up by evaporation of a restricted sea and then mined; solar salt is the same chemistry done in the sun, in shallow evaporation ponds that turn a square mile of bay into a crystalliser. The chlor-alkali cell does not care which it gets: what matters is a saturated brine with the calcium and magnesium removed, because both precipitate as scale in the diaphragm cell and would otherwise carry oxygen into the chlorine.

children.name: Halite bed: Wieliczka, Michigan, the saltbelt
children.description: Salt deposited in an evaporating sea and buried later; mined by room-and-pillar, with the salt crushed and screened for the brine saturator. The Wieliczka mine in Poland is the oldest deep salt mine still working, and Polish rock salt was the classic feed for the eastern European chlor-alkali industry.

facts.label: Typical assay
facts.value: NaCl 95-99%, with calcium and magnesium salts as the impurity

facts.label: Method
facts.value: room-and-pillar underground mining

children.name: Halite evaporite: the rock
children.description: The leaf of the sodium branch: a bedded evaporite sequence of halite with interbedded gypsum and clay, laid down when a restricted sea evaporated. Nothing chemical about it - just a dried-up ocean.

facts.label: Lithology
facts.value: massive to bedded halite with gypsum, anhydrite and clay partings

children.name: Evaporate brine in a solar salt pond
children.description: A series of shallow ponds, from 2 m down to 30 cm, through which seawater is stepped down in salinity, precipitating gypsum first and then halite. A hectare of pond evaporates tens of thousands of tonnes of salt a year. The leaf is a solar pond on a coastal lagoon.

facts.label: Depth steps
facts.value: 2-5 m intake, 0.3 m evaporator, 0.2 m crystalliser

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 100-200 kg per m2 of pond per year

children.note: Yields are strongly climate-dependent; medium confidence on the per-hectare figure.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: rock salt (halite) mined at Wieliczka, Michigan and along the saltbelt; solar salt evaporated in the San Francisco Bay and the Great Salt Lake

facts.label: Purity to the chlor-alkali cell
facts.value: brine made up to saturated, about 310 g/L NaCl before it enters the cell

facts.label: Per tonne of chlorine
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.1 t of NaCl, plus about 1 t of electrical energy

metal.limestone.name: Limestone (CaCO3) quarry
metal.limestone.description: High-calcium limestone for the Solvay towers, the blast furnaces, the Bayer plant, the lead sinter and the lime kilns. Quarried by bench mining with a face shovel or a chain dragline, crushed, and graded; a blast furnace wants roughly a third of a tonne of limestone per tonne of hot metal. The same rock is the flux in the copper flash furnace, the causticisation reagent in alumina refining, and the neutraliser at the board fab.

facts.label: Use rate
facts.value: order 0.2-0.35 t per tonne of hot metal in the blast furnace

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: surface quarry, 5-15 m benches, crushed to 10-50 mm

children.name: Carbonate platform limestone
children.description: The leaf: a fossiliferous carbonate rock, mostly calcite, laid down on a shallow warm sea floor and now quarried a few metres at a time out of a 10-40 m face.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: fossiliferous limestone, commonly a carbonate platform deposit

children.name: Limestone quarry and crushing plant
children.description: A 5-15 m bench taken out of a 10-40 m face with a face shovel or a chain dragline, drilled and blasted where the rock is competent, then a primary jaw or gyratory crusher to 50-150 mm and a crushing and screening plant that produces three fractions: 0.5-5 cm for the sinter plant, 5-40 mm for the blast furnace and the kilns, and a fines fraction that goes back. A limestone quarry is one of the least complicated mines there is, which is why lime is cheap everywhere and why the Bayer process's caustic and lime costs are the alumina industry's real cost base.

facts.label: Product sizes
facts.value: 0.5-5 cm sinter feed, 5-40 mm furnace and kiln feed, plus fines

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 0.2-5 Mt/year for a chemical-grade supplier

metal.quartz.name: Natural vein quartz
metal.quartz.description: Vein and pegmatite quartz, of which Brazil's Minas Gerais was the world source for the resonator industry. In 1982 it had two jobs: the seed for hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz, and, in small volume, high-stability resonators for frequency standards where natural material genuinely beat synthetic on Q. A computer clock did not need that. The industrial silica sand and the silicon-grade quartzite elsewhere in this file are processed rocks; this is crystal-grade rock.

facts.label: Occurrence
facts.value: vein quartz in a granitic pegmatite or a hydrothermal vein

facts.label: Use
facts.value: resonator-grade seed and, for high-Q parts, natural crystal

metal.graphite.electrode.name: Graphite and carbon electrodes
metal.graphite.electrode.description: The EAF electrodes, the submerged arc furnace electrodes of the ferrosilicon, ferrochrome and ferromanganese industries, the aluminium pot anodes, the silicon furnace electrodes and the large carbon blocks of a blast furnace hearth all consume the same two feedstocks: calcined petroleum or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as the binder. A 'graphite' electrode is green-milled from petroleum coke, extruded, and baked above 2500 C; a 'carbon' electrode stops at 800-1200 C. Pitch coke dominates for the graphite grades because it gives the higher density and the lower ash.

facts.label: Graphite grade
facts.value: baked at 2500-3000 C, ash <1%, density ~2.2 g/cm3

facts.label: Carbon grade
facts.value: baked at 800-1200 C, ash 2-5%, density ~1.6-1.8 g/cm3

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 20-30% coal-tar pitch

facts.label: Diameters in 1982
facts.value: 75-350 mm for electrodes; 400-1000 mm for pot anodes and hearth blocks

metal.graphite.electrode.note: Pitch coke is the highest-grade carbon feedstock and is itself a coke-oven by-product; see metal.coke in this file for the oven that makes the tar.

metal.carbon.anode.name: Carbon anode for the Hall-Heroult cell
metal.carbon.anode.description: Calcined petroleum coke at 90-95% carbon, ground to 1-20 mm, mixed with 25-30% of crushed and baked coke returns and 25-30% coal-tar pitch as the binder, extruded through a die with a threaded stud on the end, and roasted at 1000-1100 C for 20-30 hours. The point of roasting rather than baking is to drive the volatiles out before the anode goes into the cell, because an anode that gases in the pot poisons the metal. Consumption is 0.45-0.55 t of anode per tonne of aluminium, and the anode is consumed continuously - which is what makes aluminium smelting a carbon business as much as an electrochemical one.

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 90-95% C, 1-20 mm, from petroleum coke

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 25-30% by mass of the green anode

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: 1000-1100 C for 20-30 h in a ring or tunnel kiln

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 0.45-0.55 t of anode per tonne of aluminium

facts.label: Anode effect
facts.value: the carbon dioxide from the anode that is not captured at the plant, plus the periodic anode effect, is the smelter's main CO2 and fluoride emission

metal.carbon.anode.note: The anode effect was not well understood until the 1980s-90s and was the subject of active investigation precisely in this period.

metal.cryolite.name: Cryolite (Na3AlF6), the electrolyte solvent
metal.cryolite.description: The white, insoluble, water-repellent mineral that makes aluminium electrolysis possible at all. Pure alumina melts at 2072 C; a bath of cryolite with excess aluminium fluoride and some calcium fluoride is liquid at 950-970 C, and the alumina dissolves in it at 6-10%. The other crucial property is that cryolite is not consumed stoichiometrically - it is a solvent - and only the fluorine lost as HF and in the fume has to be replaced. Correcting the brief: consumption was roughly 0.5-1.0 t of cryolite per tonne of aluminium in 1980s practice (theoretical about 0.5 t, higher in practice because of fluoride loss), not 'four tonnes of aluminium per tonne of cryolite'.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: Na3AlF6; natural cryolite is 3NaF.AlF3

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 1012 C pure; the bath runs at 950-970 C because of the excess AlF3 and CaF2

facts.label: Alumina solubility
facts.value: 6-10 wt% in the cryolite melt

facts.label: Bath composition
facts.value: cryolite 75-80%, excess AlF3 6-13%, CaF2 3-5%

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.5-1.0 t per tonne of aluminium

facts.label: Natural source
facts.value: Ivittuut, Greenland - the only commercial natural cryolite deposit - was still being mined in 1982 and closed in 1987; every other tonne was synthetic

metal.cryolite.note: Explicit correction of the 4 t Al per t cryolite figure in the brief: cryolite is a solvent, not a stoichiometric reactant, so consumption is roughly a tonne per tonne of metal, not a quarter of that. High confidence on the mechanism; medium on the exact consumption range, which varies with the fluorine recovery practice.

children.name: Synthetic cryolite from hydrofluoric acid
children.description: Because natural cryolite was one mine in Greenland, the industry made its own. Sodium carbonate or caustic soda reacts with hydrofluoric acid and aluminium hydroxide at 60-90 C: 6HF + 3Na2CO3 + Al(OH)3 -> 2Na3AlF6 + 3CO2 + 3H2O. So the electrolyte solvent of the aluminium pot is manufactured from fluorspar, caustic soda and alumina - three of this file's other endpoints in one reaction.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 6HF + 3Na2CO3 + Al(OH)3 -> 2Na3AlF6 + 3CO2 + 3H2O

facts.label: Also used for
facts.value: the sodium cryolite is a constituent of the EPA-registered rodenticide and insecticide 'cryolite' - a genuinely different market

children.name: Aluminium fluoride and the bath
children.description: The excess AlF3 in the bath is not a deliberate additive so much as the consequence of the water and the fluorides in the alumina; smelters add it back to hold the bath at the composition that gives the best current efficiency, which is somewhere between 8 and 14% excess AlF3. Too little and the bath's freezing point rises and the pot freezes; too much and the current efficiency falls and the crust gets hard. Getting this balance right is the potline operator's entire job, and it is checked by sampling the frozen bath and analysing it in a laboratory.

facts.label: Excess AlF3
facts.value: 8-14% maintained in the bath

facts.label: Source
facts.value: made by reacting alumina and hydrofluoric acid

facts.label: Test method
facts.value: freezing-point depression of a sample of frozen bath

children.note: The 8-14% excess AlF3 window is well documented in the aluminium literature; medium confidence because smelter practice varied.

metal.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) ore
metal.fluorspar.description: Calcium fluoride rock, the only commercial source of fluorine. A 1982 hydrofluoric acid plant buys 97-98% acid made by treating acid-grade fluorspar (97%+ CaF2) with sulphuric acid in a kiln, and the acid then goes into the aluminium fluoride and cryolite that the Hall-Heroult bath needs and into the fluoride digestion that turns coltan into soluble tantalum fluoride. The ore is mined in open pits and underground, in hydrothermal veins in limestone and as replacement bodies in dolomite.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 60-95% CaF2 after flotation

facts.label: End use
facts.value: ~90% to aluminium smelting for cryolite and bath flux; the rest to HF and to steelmaking

children.name: Fluorite open-pit and underground mine
children.description: Fluorite fills the cavities and fracture zones of limestone, so it is mined either as a replacement body in a working limestone quarry or as a vein. Mexican fluorite was underground at Naica - where it grows the famous 12 m transparent crystals in a cave - and in open pits in Chihuahua. The South African deposits are in the carbonate sequences of the Transvaal Group, and the Chinese and Mongolian ones, which became dominant in the late 1980s, are in greisen and vein systems related to granite.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: epigenetic fill in limestone cavities, and veins in greisen

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit and underground, with flotation to 60-95% CaF2

children.name: Fluorite vein in limestone
children.description: The leaf: a purple, green or white vein of CaF2 a few centimetres to a few metres thick in a fractured carbonate host, in a limestone hill.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: limestone with fluorite veining

children.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
children.description: The corrosive reagent. Fluorspar plus sulfuric acid gives hydrogen fluoride in a kiln at 200-300 C; fluorspar plus concentrated sulfuric acid in a rotary kiln gives anhydrous HF directly, and the anhydrous route is what makes water-free fluorinations possible. HF is the reagent for silicon to trichlorosilane, tantalum to K2TaF7, glass etching, uranium hexafluoride, and the fluorochemical industry generally.

facts.label: Wet route
facts.value: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2HF at 200-300 C

facts.label: Anhydrous HF
facts.value: fluorspar + concentrated H2SO4 in a rotary kiln at 200-250 C

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: HF causes deep burns and systemic hypocalcaemia; anhydrous HF handling required nickel or Monel equipment

metal.sulphuric-acid.name: Sulphuric acid, 93-99%, from smelter SO2
metal.sulphuric-acid.description: The most-produced inorganic chemical in the world, and about half to three fifths of it was made not from burning sulphur but from the offgas of the copper, zinc and lead smelters in this file. The plants are the same: gas cleaning, drying, 10-14% SO2, 400-450 C over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst, absorption in 98-99% acid in the first absorber, and then a second absorber with fresher acid - the double contact, double absorption process that was the industry standard by 1982. This node is the deliberate convergence point: the copper flash furnace, the zinc sinter plant, the lead sinter plant, the copper tankhouse and the zinc leach all feed or draw from the same acid plant.

facts.label: Inlet SO2
facts.value: 8-14% from a flash furnace, roaster or sinter plant

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: V2O5 on silica, 400-450 C

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: double contact / double absorption, the 1980s standard

facts.label: Acid per tonne
facts.value: roughly 3-6 t of 100% acid per tonne of copper

children.name: Where the smelter acid goes
children.description: Roughly half of world sulfuric acid production is made from smelter offgas. In 1982 the biggest single use was fertiliser: phosphoric acid from Florida apatite, then superphosphate. The second was metal refining - the copper tankhouse electrolyte, the zinc plant leach circuit and the iron and steel pickling line, all of which are in this tree. The third was hydrofluoric acid. So a great deal of the world's phosphate rock was fertilised with acid made from the sulphur in somebody else's copper ore.

facts.label: Global split
facts.value: ~50-60% of sulfuric acid capacity was smelter-based in the early 1980s

facts.label: End uses
facts.value: phosphoric acid and fertiliser, metal pickling, hydrofluoric acid, oil refining

metal.phosphate-ore.name: Apatite ore for phosphoric acid
metal.phosphate-ore.description: The Florida pebble phosphate - a marine sedimentary phosphorite of fossil bones and excreta - is the classic source, and it is the end consumer of most of the sulfuric acid made in the copper and zinc branches of this file. It is mined by dragline or bucket-wheel stripping of 5-15 m of overburden over a 3-6 m ore layer, then crushed and slurry-piped to a beneficiation plant. Almost no phosphate rock in 1982 came from a chemical process: the whole fertiliser industry downstream of the copper and zinc smelters is a sedimentary rock mined out of a swampy coastal plain.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 28-32% P2O5, often dolomitic in Florida

facts.label: Method
facts.value: strip mining with a dragline or bucket-wheel, 3-6 m of ore under 5-15 m of overburden

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: crushing to 2-3 cm, washing in a sluice, and gravity or flotation upgrading

children.name: Marine phosphorite bed
children.description: The leaf: a 1-10 m bed of unconsolidated, often glauconitic phosphatic sand and clay in a marine or coastal plain sequence, sitting directly on limestone. It is dug, washed in a slurry pipeline, and floated or gravity-separated.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: marine shelf and coastal plain phosphorite, commonly over limestone

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: carbonate-fluorapatite with clays and quartz sand

metal.red-mud.name: Red mud (bauxite residue)
metal.red-mud.description: A caustic, red, kaolin-rich sludge, typically 2.5-6 mol/L free NaOH, containing essentially all the iron, titanium and silica from the ore. A large refinery produces 100-150 tonnes of it per tonne of alumina. In 1982 the industry standard for handling it was to build a dam and pump it in; the search for a use was real academic work with no commercial outcome. Successful commercial red-mud use at scale did not arrive until the 2000s and later, so nothing in a 1982 C64 contains it.

facts.label: Free NaOH
facts.value: 2.5-6 mol/L

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 100-150 t per tonne of Al2O3

facts.label: 1980s handling
facts.value: thickened to a dry-stack dam; clay-dry-lining of the dam floor became common in the 1990s-2000s

metal.alumina.name: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5% Al2O3
metal.alumina.description: A white, sandy, hygroscopic powder delivered to the smelter in railcars or 1-2 t bags. The contract is brutal: 99.5% Al2O3 minimum, loss on ignition below about 1%, total iron below 0.02%, because every gram of iron that reaches the cell ends up in the metal and the ingot stops being 99.7%. In 1982 this was a global commodity with about a dozen producers - Alcoa, Alcan, Kaiser, Norsk Hydro, Sumitomo, and the Australian and Jamaican national producers. This is the deliberate convergence point for the bauxite and the pot branch: both hang off it.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: free-flowing sandy powder, 0.05-0.5 mm, bulk density ~1 t/m3

facts.label: Physical
facts.value: hygroscopic - shipped and stored sealed, and preheated to avoid steam spalling in the pot feed

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~1.5-2 t bauxite -> 1 t alumina -> 0.50-0.52 t aluminium

children.name: Bauxite (hydrated alumina ore)
children.description: A soft, red-brown, pisolitic or clayey laterite, 45-60% Al2O3, still essentially the ore it was before anybody wanted it. Ore below about 180 C of gibbsite digest easily at low temperature and is called low-temperature bauxite; ore with diaspore and boehmite needs 240-280 C and is called high-temperature bauxite, which costs much more in steam. The three great districts in 1982 were Boke and Kindia in Guinea, the Weipa and Gove platforms in northern Australia, and the Clarendon and Saint Ann parishes in Jamaica.

facts.label: Mineralogy split
facts.value: low-temperature gibbsitic (<180 C) versus high-temperature diasporic (>180 C)

facts.label: Silica penalty
facts.value: each 1% reactive silica costs roughly 3-6 kg Na2O and diverts alumina into red mud

children.name: Open-cast bauxite mine with dragline
children.description: Strip mining on a 10-20 m bench height, with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline stripping 10-50 m of overburden and then a bench of bauxite perhaps only 3-6 m thick. The dragline is the point: it digs the bauxite, swings and dumps it onto a ramp, and strips the next strip of cover, all in one machine. Loading is by conveyor, almost never by truck. The Weipa and Gove operations were built this way.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open cast, drill and blast where hard, dragline stripping, conveyor loading

facts.label: Bench height
facts.value: 10-20 m of overburden, 3-6 m of ore

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 1-10 Mt/year for the largest operations

facts.label: Sizing
facts.value: primary jaw or gyratory crusher to about 25-50 mm, then direct to the digestor

children.name: Lateritic bauxite profile
children.description: The leaf: a 3-12 m pisolitic blanket of iron-stained bauxite nodules sitting on a Cretaceous or Tertiary lateritic surface above a kaolinitic clay. Guinea's deposits are the classic tropical pisolite; the Australian Weipa and Gove ores are flat-lying terrace deposits on Cretaceous sediments. Either way the rock outcrops at the surface and is dug, not tunnelled.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 3-12 m of economic bauxite over kaolinite

children.name: The kaolinite and gibbsite beneath the bauxite
children.description: The leaf of the aluminium branch, and the reason the alumina process exists in the form it does. The economic bauxite is a 3-12 m blanket of iron-stained nodules sitting directly on kaolinite clay, and the kaolinite is the reactive silica that has to be neutralised by lime or washed out. Below that is the saprolite, the partly-weathered parent rock. So the aluminium in a C64 case began as an oxide that precipitated in a tropical weathering profile above a clay, on top of Cretaceous or Tertiary sediment, and the silica problem is a mineralogical fact about the same profile rather than an impurity someone failed to remove.

facts.label: Profile
facts.value: bauxite blanket over kaolinite over saprolite over parent rock

facts.label: Clay mineral
facts.value: kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4, is the reactive silica

facts.label: Gibbsite
facts.value: Al(OH)3, the low-temperature alumina mineral that digests at 150 C

children.name: Wash the bauxite in a creek sluice
children.description: The last leaf of the aluminium branch. In the Weipa and Gove deposits on the Cretaceous laterite surface, bauxite is dug in the wet season and the clay is washed out of it in a creek: a 200 m long, 30 m wide sluice excavated along the edge of the terrace, into which the bauxite is tipped and a stream of water is run, and the light clay washes away over a long distance while the pisolitic bauxite nodules, 5-50 mm and iron-stained, stay behind and are recovered by hand or by a mechanical rake. It is a 1980s technology on a Cretaceous rock surface in tropical Queensland, and it is the reason those deposits look the way they do.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: a sluice or creek 200-300 m long, washing the clay out of the nodules

facts.label: Nodule size
facts.value: 5-50 mm pisolite, iron-stained

facts.label: Season
facts.value: worked in the wet season, when there is water to run the sluice

children.note: Medium confidence; the Weipa creek-washing practice is well described in Queensland mining history.

children.name: The Cretaceous laterite surface
children.description: The leaf, geologically: a flat, deeply weathered surface on Cretaceous sandstone where a tropical lateritic profile has developed over tens of millions of years, with a bauxite horizon at the top, kaolinite below it, and the saprolite and fresh rock beneath. The flatness is the point - it is why the pits are cheap and the ore is shallow - and it is a direct consequence of the rock type and of the extraordinarily long, warm, wet chemical weathering that made it.

facts.label: Profile
facts.value: bauxite, kaolinite, saprolite, fresh Cretaceous sandstone

facts.label: Relief
facts.value: a few metres over tens of kilometres, which is what makes surface mining cheap

children.name: Bauxite crushing, washing and drying
children.description: The Bayer plant does not want a 300 mm boulder and it certainly does not want the clay. The run-of-mine ore is crushed in a gyratory or a jaw crusher to 25-50 mm, and then - in the wet-grinding route that became standard for high-temperature bauxite - it is ground in a ball mill in a rod or a wet scrubber to a slurry, and that slurry is screened and washed to remove the clay, which is called 'desilication by attrition washing'. The under-0.5 mm clay is discarded as tailings, and it is often 15-30% of the mass. What goes into the digestor is a 40-50% solids slurry of 25-50 mm lumps with the reactive silica taken out, and the moisture matters because every kilo of water into the autoclave is a kilo of steam wasted.

facts.label: Crushing
facts.value: to 25-50 mm in a gyratory or jaw crusher

facts.label: Desilication by washing
facts.value: the -0.5 mm clay fraction is removed, often 15-30% of the mass

facts.label: Feed to the digestor
facts.value: a 40-50% solids slurry

facts.label: Direct-feed route
facts.value: the older route, in which crushed ore went to the digestor unwashed, is still used on low-silica ore

children.note: Medium confidence on the mass fractions removed by washing; they are strongly ore-dependent.

children.name: Bayer process
children.description: A 110-year-old caustic-leach purification that every tonne of aluminium still goes through. Five steps: crush and wash, digest in caustic at pressure, clarify and throw away the red mud, cool and precipitate pure aluminium hydroxide, calcine to alumina. It works because the alumina in bauxite is amphoteric - it dissolves in hot caustic as sodium aluminate - while the iron and titanium oxides are not, and silica is neutralised by lime into a harmless calcium silicate.

facts.label: Steps
facts.value: preparation, digestion, dilution and red-mud separation, precipitation, calcination

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 150-200 C for low-temperature gibbsitic ore; 240-280 C for high-temperature diasporic

facts.label: Lime
facts.value: added during digestion as a desilication reagent

children.name: Caustic digestion in autoclaves
children.description: Bauxite slurry and 150-300 g/L free caustic (as Na2O) are charged into stirred autoclaves and held at temperature for 30-90 minutes. The alumina dissolves as NaAl(OH)4; the iron oxide stays as a red slurry. Older low-temperature plants used a bank of horizontal autoclaves with indirect steam heating; high-temperature plants used vertical autoclaves. The pressure was only 5-15 bar because the vessel was not a modern high-pressure autoclave but a horizontal drum with a vapour space.

facts.label: Free caustic
facts.value: ~150-300 g/L as Na2O

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 140-150 C gibbsitic; 240-280 C diasporic

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: order 5-15 bar gauge, set by the boiling point of the liquor

facts.label: Al2O3 extraction
facts.value: >95% of the available alumina

children.note: The pressure figure follows from the temperature; 1980s Bayer autoclaves were not pressure vessels in the modern sense.

children.name: Reactive silica and the lime reaction
children.description: The killer impurity in bauxite is reactive silica - kaolinite clay and opal - which dissolves in the caustic and then reacts with aluminate to form a non-redissolving kaolinite-nepheline hydrate that permanently traps alumina. Two defences. In low-temperature digestion the clay is left undissolved by keeping the caustic concentration high. In high-temperature digestion the reactive silica dissolves, so lime is added and the silica is converted to hydrogrossite; the liquor is then given a short holding period during which the silica precipitates harmlessly. Every tonne of bauxite eats some caustic and some tens of kilos of lime that never come back.

facts.label: Reactive silica penalty
facts.value: order 3-6 kg Na2O and 1-2 kg Al2O3 lost per 1% reactive silica

facts.label: Pre-desilication step
facts.value: removing clay by attrition washing before digestion, standard for high-silica ore

children.note: The penalty range depends strongly on how the silica is mineralogically bound; medium confidence.

children.name: Clarify the liquor and dam the red mud
children.description: The digested slurry is diluted with process water, cooled, and settled in a bank of gravity settlers with mechanical rakes; the red mud bottoms out and is pumped to the mud dam. A large plant produces 100-150 tonnes of red mud per tonne of alumina, which is why every alumina refinery has a mud dam engineered like a tailings facility.

facts.label: Red mud ratio
facts.value: 100-150 t per t of Al2O3 produced

facts.label: Settling time
facts.value: 1-4 hours in a deep cone settler

facts.label: Sodium loss
facts.value: order 5-15 kg Na2O per tonne of alumina goes out with the mud

children.name: Precipitate aluminium hydroxide from the cooled liquor
children.description: The clear caustic aluminate solution is cooled from 100-110 C to 60-80 C and seeded with a few grams per litre of finely ground aluminium hydroxide already in the plant. The seed grows into the supersaturated solution as a hexagonal-plate alumina trihydrate over 24-48 hours, and the mud is filtered and washed. Washing matters twice over: to remove the caustic that would otherwise attack the kiln, and to recover the soda. The mother liquor goes back to digestion, and this recycle loop is what makes the caustic consumption manageable at all.

facts.label: Cooling
facts.value: from about 105 C to 60-80 C

facts.label: Seed
facts.value: 0.5-5 g/L of fine Al(OH)3

facts.label: Product
facts.value: alumina trihydrate, 2-8% soda before washing

children.name: Rotary vacuum filtration and counter-current washing
children.description: The hydrate is filtered on a rotating vacuum drum with cloth- or paper-covered segments, then washed on a multi-stage counter-current filter. By the time the wash water reaches the pregnant liquor the caustic is essentially recovered, so the caustic circuit closes to better than 95%. This single piece of equipment is why alumina refining has the caustic efficiency it does.

facts.label: Filtration rate
facts.value: order 0.3-1.5 kg of hydrate per m2 of filter area per minute

children.note: Filtration rates vary with product particle size; medium confidence on the range.

children.name: Calcine the trihydrate to smelter-grade alumina
children.description: The hydrate goes into a rotary kiln or, more often by 1982, a fluidised-bed calciner, and at 1000-1100 C it gives off its water of crystallisation and recrystallises from gamma through theta to alpha alumina. Alpha alumina is the hard, insoluble, spark-resistant form that will dissolve in cryolite. The rotary kiln burns 400-600 kg of fuel oil or gas equivalent per tonne of alumina and emits a lot of carbon dioxide; the fluidised bed is more efficient and was being adopted through the 1980s.

facts.label: Product form
facts.value: alpha-Al2O3, 99.5%+, with under 1% loss on ignition

facts.label: Water removed
facts.value: 3 H2O per Al2O3, i.e. 34% of the hydrate's mass

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: ~300-600 kg of oil equivalent per tonne of alumina

facts.label: Steam recovery
facts.value: the kiln flue gas is used to generate process steam, standard since the 1970s

children.name: Fluidised-bed calciner
children.description: Hot gas from a multi-flash evaporator is blown through a bed of alumina hydrate on a distributor of alloy nozzles, holding the bed fluid at 1000-1100 C by balancing gas throughput against feed rate. The bed fluidises like a boiling liquid and every grain sees the same temperature, which is exactly why the alpha alumina comes out with a tight particle-size distribution. The 1980s smelter-grade alumina market effectively standardised on this machine.

facts.label: Particle size out
facts.value: roughly 20-100 um, closed-loop ground

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: uniform residence time, so alpha conversion completes in one pass

metal.aluminum.ingot.name: Primary aluminium ingot, 99.7%
metal.aluminum.ingot.description: The metal itself, and the deliberate convergence point of the electrolysis branch and the rolling branch. Tapped from the pot every 24-48 hours, brought up to about 720 C, filtered to remove the entrained alumina and metal droplets, alloyed if the customer wants it, and cast. In 1982 the standard product was the 20-25 kg P1020 ingot, or the 500 kg or 1.5 t minimum-content ingot that newer smelters preferred, 99.70% minimum aluminium with iron and silicon the main impurities. Rolling ingots for the foil mills were a different shape entirely - see the foil branch.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.70% Al minimum (P1020 / grade A7)

facts.label: Impurities
facts.value: Fe 0.1-0.25%, Si 0.05-0.2%, plus Ga, Ti and Zn traces

facts.label: Ingot forms
facts.value: 20-25 kg stackable ingot, 500 kg minimum-content ingot, or 1.5 t

facts.label: Pour temperature
facts.value: about 710-730 C

children.name: Hall-Heroult electrolysis of alumina in cryolite
children.description: The cell is a steel shell the size of a bathtub lined with carbon, containing 300-500 t of molten cryolite at 950-970 C. Alumina dissolves in the melt and is reduced at a carbon cathode; current passes through the anodes, where the oxygen from the alumina burns the carbon away and makes carbon dioxide. The metal pools on the floor and is tapped every day or two. A pot takes 3-6 V at 100-200 kA, which is why a 200,000 t/year smelter is also a 2-3 GW power station.

facts.label: Bath temperature
facts.value: 950-970 C; cryolite alone melts at 1012 C

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 3.5-4.5 V against a theoretical minimum of about 2.1 V

facts.label: Current
facts.value: 100-200 kA per pot; one pot makes 1-3 t of aluminium a day

facts.label: Current efficiency
facts.value: 80-90% in 1980s plants

facts.label: Power
facts.value: 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne of aluminium; 1982-era plants were commonly 15,000-17,000

facts.label: Net reaction
facts.value: 2 Al2O3 + 3 C -> 4 Al + 3 CO2

facts.label: 1980s technology
facts.value: the point feeder and prebaked anode design of 1980, which raised current density to 0.7-0.8 A/cm2, is still the state of the art; no fundamental change since

children.note: The ~2.1 V theoretical minimum cell voltage and the ~90% ceiling on current efficiency are why the energy number has barely moved since 1950.

children.name: Carbon pot lining and the cathodic block
children.description: The steel shell is lined first with refractory brick, then with a monolithic carbon lining about 400-600 mm thick made of calcined coke, graphite and hot pitch, rammed in place. A block lining of graphitised carbon blocks is better and was common in newer cells. The lining is deliberately cathodic: the aluminium that seeps into the pores becomes a cathode of itself, and when the cell is finally relined after 3-8 years the spent lining is leached for the metal it swallowed.

facts.label: Lining thickness
facts.value: 400-600 mm monolithic, plus 200-300 mm of brick

facts.label: Lining life
facts.value: 3-8 years

facts.label: Pitch coke after bake-out
facts.value: about 2000-3000 C

facts.label: Metal locked up in a spent lining
facts.value: order 5-15 t of aluminium per pot

children.name: Alumina dredges and the alumina crust
children.description: Alumina fed into the pot floats and solidifies into a chilled crust on the bath surface, which is far more stable than loose powder. Machines called dredges or skimmers break holes in this crust and feed alumina down them at a controlled rate; the classic 1980 design was the dual-feed with pneumatic runners. The holes are also where carbon dust from the anode is skimmed off. A floating crust is good for the pot but insulates the bath, so the balance between a thick stable crust and a cool cell is the operator's whole job.

facts.label: Feed rate
facts.value: order 1-1.5 kg of alumina per kA-hour

children.note: The feed rate is a rule of thumb that varies with cell design; medium confidence.

children.name: Aluminium dross and the skimmings
children.description: Two or three tonnes of dross and sludge per pot per year: oxide, carbon, and aluminium that never reached the cathode. Because aluminium dross burns spectacularly it must be handled under cover, and the smelter had a dross furnace to burn out the aluminium and get it back. The recovered metal is dirty and low grade, and in 1982 it went straight back into the pot - a small but real recycling loop, since remelted aluminium needs only about 5% of the energy of primary metal.

facts.label: Yield loss
facts.value: roughly 2-4% of metal production leaves as dross

facts.label: Remelt saving
facts.value: ~5% of the primary electrolysis energy

children.note: The roughly 5% remelt saving is the widely quoted fraction of primary energy; medium confidence on precision.

metal.aluminum.foil.name: Aluminium foil, 6-25 um, for capacitors
metal.aluminum.foil.description: The C64's power supply is full of electrolytic capacitors, and every one of them is an aluminium foil sandwich: a thin cathode foil wound with a thicker anode foil and a paper separator soaked in electrolyte. Making 6 um foil is a genuinely hard rolling problem - at that gauge the metal is thinner than the oxide skin that forms on it, so the rolls and the housekeeping are the whole technology. This is a deliberate convergence node: the foil branch, the anode-foil etch branch and the rolling-mill branch all hang off it.

facts.label: Gauges
facts.value: 6-9 um cathode foil, 8-16 um anode foil

facts.label: Roll gauge count
facts.value: of the order of 20-30 um rolled per pass to reach foil

children.name: DC casting to a rolling ingot
children.description: Molten aluminium at 700-750 C is poured into a steel mould that is being withdrawn by a hydraulic jack at a controlled few millimetres per second, so the metal freezes progressively behind a solidification front instead of all at once. The front is water-cooled and the emerging surface is squirted with a water mist to control its shape. This produces a big flat rectangular billet - typically 500-1000 mm wide, 600 mm thick, 5-25 t - with a fine equiaxed chill zone at the surface. Because it is a continuous process, a 1980s smelter and a modern one produce ingots of essentially identical shape.

facts.label: Ingot mass
facts.value: 5-30 t, most often 10-25 t

facts.label: Section
facts.value: 0.5-1.0 m wide by 0.5-0.8 m thick, 1-6 m long

facts.label: Ingot temperature
facts.value: 720-750 C at the mould

facts.label: Chill zone
facts.value: 10-25 mm of fine equiaxed surface grains, which helps the ingot survive rolling without cracking

facts.label: Homogenisation
facts.value: a follow-up soak of 6-24 h at 450-600 C to dissolve Al-Zn-Mg clusters

children.name: Homogenising soak
children.description: A long hold in a gas- or electrically-heated pit furnace, typically 12-24 h at 450-600 C, whose only job is to let the alloying elements diffuse evenly. Without it a slab rolled on one edge behaves differently from the same slab rolled on the other and the foil tears. It also rounds the dendritic structure into equiaxed grains, which is what makes the achievable surface quality possible.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 6-24 h depending on section

children.note: Typical range; specific alloy timetables vary by producer.

children.name: Hot rolling to 2-6 mm
children.description: The ingot is preheated to 300-400 C for wide slab or 450-550 C for narrower, thicker slab, and a reversing hot mill takes it down to 2-6 mm in one or two passes. Aluminium's rolling window is famously narrow - too cold and it tears at the edges, too hot and the ingot surface oxidises and scales - so a 1980s reversing hot mill had two or three stands and quite tight control. Scale is removed with hot descaling rolls, which presses a rolled-in oxide pattern into the surface that later helps the lubricant out of the pores.

facts.label: Reheat temperature
facts.value: 300-400 C for wide slab, up to 450-550 C

facts.label: Exit thickness
facts.value: 2-6 mm

facts.label: Reduction per pass
facts.value: order 3-8 mm per pass, about a 30% reduction limit

facts.label: Descaling
facts.value: hot descaler rolls force water under the oxide scale and knock it off

children.name: Mill scale (iron-bearing aluminium oxide)
children.description: Hot rolling oxidises the surface and the scale is knocked off by the descaling rolls. The chips that fall are a mix of alumina and iron oxides pulled in from the ingot surface, and they are the same material the ferroalloy and cement industries fought over - and, ground and magnetically separated, the raw iron oxide for soft ferrites. In 1982 most was dumped.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Al2O3 with 5-30% Fe2O3

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 30-60 kg of scale per tonne of hot-rolled strip

children.note: Iron content varies with ingot surface condition; medium confidence on the range.

children.name: Cold rolling on a Sendimir high-roll mill
children.description: The 2-6 mm hot strip goes to a multi-high cold mill - a Sendimir 20-high or 24-high arrangement where a small work roll is backed by many intermediate rolls, giving the enormous rolling force needed at a small gap without a mill body the size of a building. The work rolls are hardened tool steel, 100-300 mm diameter, with a chasing finish that the operator keeps polished with emery and a lint-free cloth while the mill runs; at 6 um a single fingerprint is a visible defect. Between passes the strip is annealed at 200-400 C in a gas-fired or electric furnace, because the roll gap cannot take the whole reduction in one pass and because that anneal is what resets the rolling texture. The finished 1-2 t coil, 400-1300 mm wide, is then slit into customer widths with tungsten-carbide or ceramic-coated knives and re-spooled, which is the least forgiving part of the whole operation: at 6 um the foil has almost no stiffness and simply tears on a blunt knife. From 1980 onwards the Sendimir Z-High mill, which adds separate work-roll bending and flattening control, was the state of the art for aluminium foil width.

facts.label: Mill configuration
facts.value: 20-high or 24-high Sendimir; the Sendimir Z-High from 1980

facts.label: Work roll diameter
facts.value: 100-300 mm, tool steel, changed frequently

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: about 40-70% per pass, 15-30 um per pass to foil

facts.label: Gauge control
facts.value: hydraulic or electromechanical gap and bending control to about 1-2% thickness tolerance

facts.label: Interstage anneal
facts.value: 200-400 C, batch or inline; also where the rolling-direction texture is set

facts.label: Slitting
facts.value: a 1-2 t coil of 400-1300 mm slit to 100-600 mm on carbide or ceramic-coated knives

children.name: Etched aluminium anode foil
children.description: The trick that made a decent electrolytic fit into an 8 mm diameter can. Plain anode foil etched in a hot acid bath grows an aluminium oxide/hydroxide layer over essentially the whole surface - up to about a hundred times the geometric area, and therefore a hundred times the capacitance per unit of volume. The 1980s etching chemistry was a chloride bath or, in the Japanese-dominated high-end market, a chlorate bath with acetic acid; the etch pits are then hardened with a phosphate or chromate formation treatment and the surface is impregnated with the electrolyte. The chloride ion eats its way into the foil along the grain boundaries and leaves a field of round tunnels 0.1-2 um across; oxidation inside those tunnels is what multiplies the area. A formation step then grows oxide in a controlled taper so the weakest point - the mouth of each pit - is the first to fail if the etch is wrong, which is why a 1982 capacitor that failed early failed as a short circuit and a vent rather than as a slow leak.

facts.label: Surface area gain
facts.value: ~50-100x the geometric area after etching and formation

facts.label: Oxide layer
facts.value: order 0.1-1 um of Al2O3, grown by a DC formation voltage

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: chloride, or chlorate plus acetic acid, at about 60-80 C

facts.label: Formation voltage
facts.value: raised in steps to the working voltage of the finished capacitor, typically 6-25 V for a computer supply rail

facts.label: Etch pit
facts.value: 0.1-2 um tunnels along grain boundaries; oxide breakdown at the pit mouth is the failure mode

children.note: The 1980s high-capacitance anode foil industry was concentrated in Japan and the exact etch chemistry was proprietary, split between the chloride and the chlorate camps. Medium confidence on the bath detail. Some formation treatments used chromate for stability, and hexavalent chromium was already being restricted in the workplace by 1982.

metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.name: Aluminium rolling oil and the degreaser
metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.description: Cold rolling of aluminium would tear without a lubricant: a water-in-oil emulsion or a neat mineral oil with fatty-acid esters, applied by nozzles at order 0.1-1 g/m2. The oil is what lets the gauge get down without the surface tearing, and it has to be removed afterwards - a few grams of oil left on capacitor foil ruin the capacitor, because the electrolyte chemistry and the oxide interface are that sensitive. Foil mills ran a dedicated degreasing line with naphtha or trichloroethane and a 200-300 C bake.

facts.label: Oil application
facts.value: order 0.1-1.0 g per m2 of strip

facts.label: Residual after degrease
facts.value: below about 50 mg/m2, lower for capacitor foil

facts.label: Degrease solvent
facts.value: naphtha, perchloroethylene or trichloroethane, plus a 200-300 C bake

metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.note: Solvent choice varied with local regulation; perchloroethylene was being phased out in Europe and North America through the 1980s. Medium confidence.

children.name: Fatty-acid esters from tallow and palm fat
children.description: The ester lubricants are made from animal or vegetable fats - tallow, palm, rapeseed - hydrolysed to fatty acids and re-esterified, on a paraffinic mineral base or a synthetic ester. This is the one place in the aluminium chain where biomass chemistry is genuinely load-bearing: an aluminium rolling lubricant is a soap-and-fatty-acid chemistry, not a petrochemical one. In 1982 tallow was still the dominant base; vegetable ester formulations grew through the 1990s.

facts.label: Feedstocks
facts.value: rendered animal fat, pressed palm oil, rapeseed oil

facts.label: Note
facts.value: crude petroleum was still a common base in the cheaper grades

children.note: Medium confidence on the 1982 split between tallow, vegetable and petroleum-based grades.

metal.aluminum.sheet.name: Aluminium sheet: the case and the shields
metal.aluminum.sheet.description: Two uses in a C64: the heat-sink and shield material, and the case itself. The Commodore breadbin case is an aluminium extrusion with a stove-enamel finish, and the internal shields and the modulator compartment are plain sheet. Cold-rolled 1050A or 3003 sheet at 0.3-1.5 mm goes into drawing and stamping; the anodising or powder coating is the plastics-and-paint agent's business, but the substrate starts here. Also the convergence point for the die-casting branch: a 1982 C64 has several kilograms of aluminium foundry alloy in its key plungers and the joystick and case-bracket castings.

facts.label: Alloys
facts.value: 1050A (pure, for foil and case), 3003 (Al-Mn, general sheet), 6063 (extrusion), A13 (Al-Si casting alloy, for die castings)

facts.label: Typical gauge
facts.value: 0.3-1.5 mm for a case or shield

children.name: Alloying to 3003, 6063 or A13
children.description: The rolling mill is not a refinery. It melts primary ingot, remelted can scrap and dross recovery in a reverberatory or an induction furnace, adds the alloying elements as lumps of master alloy, degasses with a rotating argon lance to strip hydrogen, and skims the dross. Manganese for 3003, magnesium and silicon for 6063, silicon for the A13 casting alloy. So the C64's case metal is partly recycled metal, and its chemistry is set in a small furnace rather than a pot.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: oil- or gas-fired reverberatory melting furnace of 100-300 t, or an induction furnace

facts.label: Degassing
facts.value: rotating argon or nitrogen lance, or a chlorine-salt flux
~1.0-1.2% Mn, balance aluminium

facts.label: A13 (casting)
facts.value: ~11-13% Si, the standard 1980s die-casting alloy

children.note: The specific alloy used for the Commodore case is not something I can confirm; 6063 and 1050 are the plausible candidates. Medium confidence.

metal.aluminum.extrusion.name: Aluminium extrusion: the case and the heat sinks
metal.aluminum.extrusion.description: A hot billet is forced through a steel die by a ram at 420-500 C, at 20-100 MN of pressure, at several metres a second, and the profile that comes out is straight and, if the die is good, dimensionally within a fraction of a millimetre. The Commodore case is a complicated extrusion: the cooling fins, the rail and the case walls are all one profile, and the visible finish is a consequence of the die geometry. The rectifier and regulator heat sinks are separate small extrusions or machined blocks.

facts.label: Extrusion pressure
facts.value: 20-100 MN, of order 500-1500 t of force

facts.label: Extrusion speed
facts.value: up to about 100 m/min for a light 6063 section

facts.label: Die material
facts.value: hot-work tool steel; 600-1000 roughing holes and 1000-1500 h of die life in order

facts.label: Case profile
facts.value: 6063 with a 0.2-0.4 mm wall and integral cooling fins

children.name: Hydraulic extrusion press, 500-2500 t
children.description: The industry standard was the 2300-2500 t class press with a 200-500 mm container, driven by a hydraulic intensifier that gave a hard step change in speed at the start of the stroke. A heated soak furnace beside the press holds the billets, a shear cuts them to length, and the runout bench stretches the profile while it is still hot. A C64 case would have been pressed at a Taiwanese or Hong Kong extrusion shop on a machine of exactly this size.

facts.label: Press size
facts.value: 2300-2500 t in the largest class, 500-1500 t for smaller sections

facts.label: Straightening
facts.value: in-line stretcher on the runout bench

children.name: The soak furnace and the billet's temperature history
children.description: Billet quality is set before the press ever sees it. The billets are heated in a gas- or oil-fired pit furnace to 420-500 C and held for 3-24 hours so that the temperature is uniform through the section, because a billet with a hot core and a cold skin extrudes with a surface tear and a soft interior. The furnace is a 3-5 m long box with a hot zone and a transition zone, and the entire extrusion industry's reputation for inconsistent profiles is mostly the reputation of its furnaces. A C64's case extrusion depended on the profile being within a fraction of a millimetre, because it had to fit a plastic moulding and a painted finish.

facts.label: Why so long
facts.value: a 25 t billet needs hours for the core to reach temperature

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: gas or oil fired pit furnace with hot and transition zones

children.note: Medium confidence; the soak practice is standard but the times depend entirely on the section size.

children.name: Steel extrusion die and its forging
children.description: The die is a disc of hot-work tool steel with a cavity machined into it, and it has to be made before it can be used: drilled, rough-machined, heat-treated, then finish-machined and nitrided. A case profile takes a lot of steel and a lot of hours, which is why the extrusion industry is full of small specialist shops rather than a few giants. The same die steel family, SKD61 and H13, is the tooling steel of the plastics agent's injection-moulding branch.

facts.label: Die life
facts.value: order 1000-1500 h, then repair

facts.label: Steel per die
facts.value: 100-600 t, machined over days

children.note: Die lives vary enormously with profile complexity and alloy; medium confidence.

metal.copper.cathode.name: Electrolytic copper cathode, 99.99%
metal.copper.cathode.description: The end product of the mine-to-metal chain and the shape in which essentially all world copper trades. A flat plate grown on a stainless steel or copper starter sheet, with a characteristic slightly rough surface because too many nucleation sites make a soft, dull deposit. Cathode mass is 45-125 kg depending on the refinery. Weighed, sampled, stamped and shipped. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tankhouse branch, the foil branch and the wire branch.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99%, LME Grade A at 99.9935% minimum

facts.label: Typical impurities
facts.value: Fe 3-8 ppm, S 1-10 ppm, Pb 1-10 ppm, O 10-50 ppm

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 45-125 kg per plate

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: 40-60 g/L free Cu2+, 180-230 g/L free H2SO4, 10-25 ppm Fe/As/Bi

children.name: Copper ingot and rod casting
children.description: The cathode is melted in an induction furnace or a reverberatory with a controlled sulphur addition, then cast - either continuously into wire rod by the Properzi upcast method or into 250-450 kg ingots for further processing. The 1980s standard route to rod was continuous casting; the alternative, longer route was a DC casting machine feeding a wire rod mill. Melting loses almost nothing because copper does not oxidise appreciably; the real problem is gas absorption.

facts.label: Melting
facts.value: 1150-1250 C, induction or gas-fired reverberatory, under a cover

facts.label: Rod diameters
facts.value: 6.0-8.0 mm for drawing, cast as wire rod

facts.label: Deoxidation
facts.value: phosphorus added as a copper-phosphorus master alloy, 0.01-0.05% residual

children.name: Upcast wire rod line
children.description: In the Properzi upcaster the melt runs out of a horizontal holding furnace into a vertical casting trough behind a steel die that is being drawn upward by a rotating carousel; the trough is water-cooled and the copper solidifies against the moving die face, giving a controlled solidification structure. It makes 6-9 mm rod very cheaply and was standard in the 1980s, though the resulting cast structure needs patenting before drawing.

facts.label: Cast speed
facts.value: order 0.1-0.5 m/s

facts.label: Output
facts.value: single upcaster order 2-6 t/h

children.note: Upcasting was still widely used in the 1980s but continuous casting replaced it from the 1990s; medium confidence on the 1982 split.

children.name: Anode casting and the anode scrap stream
children.description: About 10-20% of the anode never makes it into a cell - it is broken in handling, or the bars are too thin, or the busbar is corroded away - and it goes back to be remelted and recast. Every tankhouse therefore has a stub and an anode scrap yard and a melt, and the plant's anode book is a mass balance between the smelter's output and the tankhouse's demand. At the end of its life an anode is a thin, perforated, gold-bearing skeleton of iron and lead oxide that goes back to the smelter, so the gold in the anode is in a closed loop with the refinery and the melt is where the loop is closed.

facts.label: Anode stub and scrap
facts.value: 10-20% of the anode mass returns to remelting

facts.label: Busbar
facts.value: a cast copper bar, and the contact point where the anode is electrically connected

children.note: Medium confidence on the stub and scrap rate; it varies by tankhouse practice.

metal.copper.wire.name: Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings
metal.copper.wire.description: The switch-mode transformer in a C64's power supply - and any small mains-frequency transformer - is a coil of enamelled copper wire. The wire starts as 6-8 mm rod, is patented (heated to 200-350 C so the work-hardening from drawing anneals out), then drawn through a series of diamond dies to 0.15-0.5 mm, then enamelled and baked. 1982's magnet wire was overwhelmingly polyurethane enamel, sometimes with a nylon or polyester overcoat; polyurethane is the classic because it strips cleanly from the copper and does not need a flame to remove. This is a deliberate convergence node: the transformer winding, the ferrite core and the soldered joint all come off it.

facts.label: Gauge
facts.value: AWG 24-34 (0.5 down to 0.2 mm) for a small transformer; AWG 38-42 for fine coils

facts.label: Enamel
facts.value: polyurethane, thermal class 130-155, sometimes with a polyester or nylon overcoat

facts.label: Film build
facts.value: 15-40 um total for a class 155 wire

children.name: Patenting: annealing the rod before drawing
children.description: Copper work-hardens fast: a few percent of reduction raises the tensile strength enormously and the wire simply snaps in the die. So the rod is heated - in steam, in air, or in a fluidised bed - to about 200-350 C, which recrystallises the elongated drawing structure back to equiaxed grains, and then quenched. The black oxide that air patenting leaves is actually helpful, because it stops the wire rusting in the draw bin. Patenting is the cheapest trick in the whole wire business.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 200-350 C in steam, or a fluidised bed at up to about 400 C

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: recrystallisation: copper goes from about 60-70 kg/mm2 work-hardened to 35-45 kg/mm2 annealed

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: steam or air - air leaves a useful black oxide; inert gas only for fine wire

children.name: Drawing lubricant: copper sulfonate or oil emulsion
children.description: The die must be lubricated or the copper galls and the die wears out. In the 1980s the standard was a water-based emulsion or a copper-sulfonate-and-fatty-acid concentrate, applied in a die box or as a once-through bath. Lubricant chemistry is also the friction and galling story in the die, which is why the drawing lubricant industry is a small speciality chemical business rather than an oil business.

facts.label: Lubricant
facts.value: copper sulfonate or ammonium sulfonate in a fatty-acid base, or an oil-in-water emulsion

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: order 0.5-5% in the emulsion

children.note: Formulations are proprietary; medium confidence on the general chemistry.

children.name: Multiwire drawing through diamond dies
children.description: Since the 1960s the industry stopped drawing one wire at a time and started drawing 7-19 wires simultaneously through a cone of dies, so the die size needed for a 0.2 mm wire is much larger and lasts much longer. The dies are natural diamond - or, as synthetic diamond tooling matured through the 1980s, polycrystalline diamond compact - set in a steel holder with a hardened steel casing. Drawing to 0.15 mm means the copper has been elongated by a factor of order 1600, which is why magnet wire is made only from low-oxygen, low-sulphur electrolytic cathode and never from cast copper.

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: 7-19 wires per pass through coned dies

facts.label: Die material
facts.value: natural diamond or synthetic PCD in a steel holder

facts.label: Total reduction to 0.2 mm
facts.value: from 8 mm, a total elongation of order 1.6 x 10^3

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: needed above about 1-2 mm drawn diameter

children.name: Enamelling and cure of magnet wire
children.description: The drawn wire is passed through a die and coated with liquid polyurethane enamel in a continuous length of 10-20 coats, each flash-dried, then cured in a vertical oven at 150-220 C for up to an hour. The result is a wire whose insulation survives a 155 C winding temperature and whose dielectric strength is 5-10 kV between turns. Enamelling is a chemical coating line rather than a metallurgy process, but the wire underneath it is this branch's problem.

facts.label: Coats
facts.value: 10-20 flash-dried coats for a 15-40 um build

facts.label: Cure temperature
facts.value: 150-220 C, up to about 1 h

facts.label: Dielectric strength
facts.value: 5-10 kV across the enamel

children.name: Polyurethane enamel from a di-isocyanate
children.description: The wire enamel is a thermosetting urethane, made from a diol and a di-isocyanate such as toluene di-isocyanate, with a blocked-isocyanate cure so the coating is stable in the coating bath and only reacts in the cure oven. Its advantage over phenolic (vinyl formal, the pre-war standard) and polyester is that it strips cleanly and bonds without a heat gun. So a C64 transformer's insulation is a chemical product of the polyurethane industry, not a distillation product.

facts.label: Former standard
facts.value: vinyl formal (phenolic) enamel, still used for thermal class 180

facts.label: 1982 class
facts.value: polyurethane dominated thermal class 130-155

children.note: The chemistry of commercial wire enamels is proprietary; medium confidence on the general description.

children.name: The enamelling line and the cure oven
children.description: A magnet-wire enamelling line is a 20-40 m long machine: a pay-off, a bunch of dies applying 10-20 coats with flash-off between them, a vertical cure oven 8-15 m tall, a capstan, a take-up. The cure oven is gas or electric at 150-220 C with the wire passing through it in a helix, and it is the cure schedule and not the coating that decides the wire's class. A class 155 wire needs a full hour at temperature; a class 130 wire can get away with less. In 1982 the whole world's magnet wire was made on lines of exactly this design, whether the wire came from Japan, France or the United States.

facts.label: Coats
facts.value: 10-20, each flash-dried

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 150-220 C, up to about 1 h

facts.label: Speed
facts.value: 60-300 m/min depending on the wire gauge

children.note: Medium confidence on the speed range; it is strongly gauge-dependent.

metal.copper.foil.name: Copper foil: 35 um PCB and 6-18 um capacitor foil
metal.copper.foil.description: Two completely different foils with the same name, and this is a deliberate convergence node. The PCB foil is 35 um copper (70 um on very old boards) electrolytically deposited or rolled; the C64's board is single-sided, so it is one sheet of foil laminated to 1.6 mm FR-4. The capacitor foil is electro-deposited drum foil, deposited 6-18 um onto a rotating stainless or titanium drum from a copper sulphate bath, stripped and wound, then roughened again for etching just like aluminium foil.

facts.label: PCB foil
facts.value: 35 um (2 oz/sq ft) standard, 70 um on very early boards

facts.label: Capacitor foil
facts.value: 6-18 um electro-deposited, with base copper under the etched layer

facts.label: Thickness tolerance
facts.value: +/-10% on 35 um foil

children.name: Electro-deposited drum foil
children.description: A rotating drum cathode, 1-2 m diameter and 1-1.5 m wide, dips into an acid copper sulphate bath and turns; copper plates onto it at 20-100 A/dm2. A scraper peels the foil off at the top of the drum as a continuous 6-18 um web, which is then slit and wound. The deposit is not bulk metal: it is a columnar, sometimes dendritic growth, which is exactly why it etches into foil capacitors so well and why, for PCBs, it needs a bonding treatment before the laminate resin will stick to it.

facts.label: Drum
facts.value: 1-2 m diameter, rotating cathode, 100-500 A/dm2

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: CuSO4/H2SO4 with a brightener and a suppressant; the additive package is proprietary

facts.label: Grain
facts.value: columnar and favourably oriented, unlike rolled foil's rolled structure

children.name: Nodular treatment for PCB foil adhesion
children.description: Bare copper foil will not bond to epoxy; it delaminates. So the foil is treated in a warm sulfuric acid bath with a silicofluoride or a silane - historically sodium silicofluoride, later silanes - which grows a forest of microscopic oxide nodules on the surface. The resin flows into the forest and locks in, and the peel strength goes from a few N/cm to about 20 N/cm.
