This etching of the foil surface is the single most important step in making a copper-clad laminate, and the silicofluoride comes from the same fluorochemical industry as the hydrofluoric acid in the aluminium and tantalum branches.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: 0.5-2.5% silicofluoride in 15-30% sulfuric acid at 40-70 C

facts.label: Peel strength
facts.value: order 20 N/cm after treatment, versus a few N/cm untreated

facts.label: 1982 practice
facts.value: sodium silicofluoride in sulfuric acid; the chromic-acid treatment was being phased out

children.note: The exact chemistry shifted through the 1980s and the chromate-era process was being abandoned for toxicological reasons; medium confidence.

children.name: Rolled annealed copper foil
children.description: The traditional foil: heavy copper strip rolled on a Sendimir mill to 35-105 um and slit. It has a rolled, fibrous grain that is anisotropic, so it is easy to form and easy to drill, and it was the foil of record for anything that needs to be bent rather than etched. By 1982 electronic-grade rolled foil had been mostly displaced by electro-deposited foil for PCBs because deposition was cheaper and the bonding treatment was more reliable, but rolled foil remained the foil of choice for fine pitch and for capacitor cathodes.

facts.label: Grain
facts.value: rolled and elongated along the rolling direction

facts.label: 1982 position
facts.value: electro-deposited foil had taken most of the PCB market; rolled foil kept the high end and the cathode business

children.note: Copper foil mills are Sendimir-type 20-high machines, the same family as the aluminium foil mill; medium confidence on which mill type made which foil in 1982.

metal.anode-slime.name: Anode slime: the real reason to smelt copper
metal.anode-slime.description: The sludge on the tankhouse cell floor, 5-20 kg per tonne of copper refined, containing gold, silver, platinum, palladium, selenium and tellurium. It is dried and shipped to precious-metals refineries, where the gold is separated by cupellation, the selenium by roasting to SeO2 and volatilising, and the platinum group metals by solvent extraction and precipitation. By 1982 the anode slime was typically worth more per tonne than the copper in the anode, and a copper mine with good gold credits could be a gold mine that happened to have copper in it. This is a deliberate convergence node: the copper, gold and silver branches all meet in it.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 5-20 kg of dry slime per tonne of copper

facts.label: Value in 1982
facts.value: typically 30-100% of the value of the contained copper

children.name: Platinum-group metals from the anode slime
children.description: The anode slime also carries platinum, palladium, ruthenium, iridium, rhodium and osmium, at grams per tonne of copper rather than kilograms, so the volumes are tiny and the values are astronomical. In 1982 most of the world's refined palladium came from the nickel-copper ores of the Sudbury and Norilsk basins and from the Bushveld's platinum mines rather than from the copper anode slimes, but the slimes were a real secondary source for platinum and rhodium. The refining route is a solvent extraction and precipitation circuit followed by a final electrolytic or thermal refining, and by 1982 the platinum-group market was dominated by South Africa and the Soviet Union, whose platinum was the ore of choice for autocatalyst converters in the 1970s - which is a genuine and slightly absurd piece of industrial history, since the autocatalyst is a device for cleaning up the exhaust of a car and the platinum came out of the same layered intrusion as the chrome in the ignition plugs.

facts.label: PGM in anode slime
facts.value: grams per tonne of copper; order 0.5-5 g/t of each metal

facts.label: Primary sources 1982
facts.value: the Bushveld Complex in South Africa and the Norilsk nickel-copper ores in the USSR

facts.label: 1970s driver
facts.value: autocatalyst demand set the platinum-group market

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: solvent extraction and precipitation, then electrolytic or thermal refining

children.note: Medium confidence on the slime assays; the primary sources and the autocatalyst history are well documented.

children.name: Cupellation of the gold-silver dross
children.description: The slime is smelted with lead and flux into a litharge, then the litharge is blown with air in a cupellation furnace. The lead and everything else oxidises and is absorbed by a bone-ash or magnesite cupel, and what is left on the cupel is gold and silver together. This is the oldest refinery process in the book and it was still standard in 1982, because it is simple and it works.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 1100-1200 C in the cupellation furnace

facts.label: Cupel material
facts.value: bone ash (calcium phosphate) or magnesia

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 6-24 h per charge depending on the mass

children.name: Bone ash cupel from animal bone
children.description: Traditional cupels are made of calcined bone - tricalcium phosphate - ground and pressed into a shallow cup with a porous, low-density surface that absorbs the molten litharge. Bone ash is the reason cupellation is called what it is, and by the 1982 industry the major refineries had largely moved to magnesia and alumina cupels for the big furnaces, though bone ash was still in use. So a refinery furnace foot was, historically, a rendering-house product.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: calcined bone ash Ca3(PO4)2, or magnesia or alumina for larger units

children.note: By 1982 the major refineries were largely on magnesia or alumina cupels; medium confidence that bone ash remained in use anywhere significant.

children.name: Selenium and tellurium from the anode slime
children.description: Two of the minor metals that pay for a copper smelter. The slime is roasted in a fluidised bed and the selenium volatilises as SeO2, caught in a hot cyclone or an electrostatic precipitator; the tellurium comes out of the roasted residue by leaching and electrowinning. Both are a few per cent of the slime's mass and both sell at a price per kilogram above the copper, so by 1982 a smelter could not afford to throw them away.

facts.label: Assay in the slime
facts.value: Se 1-5%, Te 0.5-3% of the dry slime

facts.label: Selenium route
facts.value: fluidised-bed roast to SeO2, volatilised and caught; the residue returns to the copper circuit

facts.label: Tellurium route
facts.value: leached from the roasted residue and electrowon

facts.label: End use
facts.value: selenium in glass, pigments and rectifiers; tellurium in thermoelectric and free-machining alloys

metal.tin.ingot.name: Refined tin ingot or tin powder, 99.9-99.97%
metal.tin.ingot.description: Shipped as a 25-50 kg or 250 kg ingot at 99.9-99.97%, or - for the electronics industry - atomised into a fine powder. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tin smelting branch and the solder branch: the solder manufacturer needs the ingot, and the solder-paste manufacturer needs the powder. Iron is the impurity that matters, because iron is a solder poison that wets badly and raises the liquidus.

facts.label: Powder
facts.value: atomised, 10-25 um, for solder paste and for making solder alloy powder

facts.label: 1982 context
facts.value: most electronics soldering was still a hand or wave-solder pot of solid-core wire; paste was a minority

children.name: Air atomisation of tin to powder
children.description: Molten tin at about 1150 C is poured into a launder and a high-pressure air jet at the bottom of a vertical stack sprays it into a fog of droplets that solidify on the way down. It is cheap, it works for metals that do not oxidise much, and it gives a bimodal powder. Under nitrogen it gives the fine, oxide-free powder that solder paste needs. Every particle in the can came out of a slot in a nozzle.

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: 10-25 um for solder-grade powder

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: air, or nitrogen for the low-oxide grade

children.note: The 1980s powder market was real but small relative to solid wire; medium confidence on relative volumes.

metal.tin.plating.name: Tin plating of steel and of copper alloys
metal.tin.plating.description: Tinplate - a 1.1-11.2 g/m2 tin coating on 0.15-0.3 mm of steel - is made by electrolytic tinning of a continuous steel strip on a horizontal passivating line: the strip is degreased, pickled in acid, tinned in a sulphate or fluoroborate bath, rinsed, and then either passivated in chromic acid (food can) or - through the 1980s - given an electrolytic chromate or tin-oxide passivation to stop the tin growing dendrites during storage. Food can was the dominant market by mass. A C64 uses tinplate only incidentally, in a switch body or a shield; tin plating of copper-alloy contacts uses a different chemistry altogether and is the node that matters for the machine.

facts.label: Coating mass
facts.value: 1.1-11.2 g/m2 (2.8-28.2 g per 100 cm2); 5-6 g/m2 typical for electronics sheet

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: chromic acid for food can, or an electrolytic chromate or oxide passivation in the 1980s

facts.label: Tinplate market
facts.value: food can was about 90% of production

children.name: Tin plating of copper-alloy contacts
children.description: Not tinplate on steel, but tin on brass or phosphor bronze - the plating on the contacts of a C64 switch or a keyboard connector. The 1980s chemistry was an acid stannate or an alkaline stannate bath: SnSO4 with sulfuric acid, or sodium stannate with caustic soda and a puller such as sodium gluconate. Tin is on a connector contact because it forms a soft, low-resistance, non-tarnishing intermetallic with the copper. The reason it fails is the tin whisker - a single-crystal filament of tin that grows out of the plating under compressive stress in humid storage and can bridge a 0.1 mm gap. Tin whiskers were the reliability nemesis of exactly this kind of contact.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: acid sulphate (SnSO4/H2SO4) or alkaline stannate (Na2SnO3/NaOH)

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: 2-5 um of tin on a Cu-Sn alloy or brass

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: tin whisker growth, and on tin-plated copper under high stress, copper-tin intermetallic embrittlement

children.note: The specific plating system used on Commodore's connectors is not something I can confirm; both chemistries were in use in 1982. Medium confidence.

metal.lead.ingot.name: Refined lead ingot, 99.99%
metal.lead.ingot.description: Cast into 25 kg pigs or into 500 kg slabs. About two thirds of all the lead refined in the world was never made into a product in the refinery - it went straight into an alloy, most of it lead-acid battery plate and cable sheath. The solder industry took a small fraction, on the order of five to ten percent, and in 1982 that fraction was the entire basis of the electronics solder business. This is a deliberate convergence node: the blast furnace branch, the Parkes desilverisation branch and the solder branch all meet here.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) standard; 99.999% 'five nines' was available for special applications

facts.label: End use split
facts.value: batteries about 60%, cable sheath about 15%, solder about 5-10%

children.name: Cupellation of the silver dross to silver and gold
children.description: The dross from the Parkes process is mixed with lead and flux and cast into a 30-50 kg charge, which is placed in a cupellation furnace at 1000-1150 C and blown with air. The lead oxidises to litharge, PbO, which melts at 888 C and is absorbed by the porous cupel, while the silver and gold do not oxidise and stay on the surface. When all the lead is gone the silver is 96-99% pure and the gold is 30-50% of it; the gold is then cupelled again, or electrorefined, to 99.9%. So every lead bullion makes a small pile of very pure silver - a deliberate convergence of the lead and silver branches.

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 30-50 kg of dross with litharge and flux

facts.label: Products
facts.value: silver at 96-99%, gold dore at 30-50% Au

children.note: Points to metal.silver.ingot and metal.gold.ingot in the same tree.

metal.solder.wire.name: 63/37 solder wire with a rosin core
metal.solder.wire.description: The wire that went through a C64 assembly line: a solid 63/37 core inside a flux core inside a tin-lead sheath, made by the cored-wire method and drawn on the same kind of multiwire machine the copper industry uses, in a smaller and more delicate setup. This is a deliberate convergence node: the solder alloy branch, the rosin branch and the wave-solder branch all meet here, and it is the single most identifiable material in the whole tree - it is why the C64 is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

facts.label: Gauge
facts.value: 0.5-0.8 mm for through-hole boards; 0.3 mm for fine work

facts.label: Flux core
facts.value: 10-25% of the diameter by volume

facts.label: Spool
facts.value: 100 g to 2 kg retail, 5-10 kg industrial spools for wave solder

facts.label: Consumption in a C64
facts.value: roughly 3500 through-hole joints at about 30 mg each, so order 100 g per machine

metal.zinc.ingot.name: Special high grade zinc ingot, 99.995%
metal.zinc.ingot.description: Twenty-five kilogram ingots, or the 500 kg minimum-content ingot that the bigger plants preferred by 1982. Special high grade at 99.995% was the grade specified by the galvanising industry and by die-casters, because both are very sensitive to lead, cadmium and iron. Two thirds of world zinc goes into galvanising and roughly a sixth into die casting. The four markets below are the whole of the demand: galvanising, die casting, electroplating with a chromate passivate, and brass. An ingot that misses any of the four impurity limits is unsellable, which is why the smelter spends its margin on the assay rather than on the metal.

facts.label: End use
facts.value: ~65% galvanising, ~15-20% die casting, ~10% brass, rest chemicals

children.name: Hot-dip galvanising of steel strip
children.description: Steel sheet, strip or fabric is pickled in hydrochloric acid, fluxed in an ammonium chloride-zinc chloride bath, and dipped in a kettle of molten zinc at 450-470 C. The zinc wets the steel, forms an iron-zinc intermetallic, and the kettle surface is skimmed of dross by a wiper roll. Every galvanising line in the world consumed thousands of tonnes of zinc a year this way, and a big continuous strip line used 50-300 t a day. The C64 itself is not galvanised, but its chassis and any sheet-metal bracket, and much of the world around it, was.

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: 45-85 g/m2 for sheet; 300-600 g/m2 for fabric

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: a continuous strip line uses 50-300 t of zinc a day, of which the dross is a real loss

facts.label: Coating form
facts.value: pure zinc for general use; Zn-Al alloy for high-drip lines; Zn-Ni for automotive sheet

children.note: Zinc-aluminium and zinc-nickel coated sheet for automotive was a 1980s development, not a 1982 consumer-electronics one.

children.name: Recover the zinc from the galvanising dross
children.description: The iron-rich dross and the bottom ash skinned off a galvanising kettle are picked out, and the metal is recovered in a specialised horizontal crucible furnace, where the dross is heated with a flux and the iron drops out as Fe-Zn hard zinc. The remaining zinc is pumped out. A galvanising line therefore recovers most of its zinc, and in 1982 the galvanising industry was also the main secondary source of zinc, second only to galvanised scrap.

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 70-90% of the dross metal is recovered

children.note: Recovery efficiency varies with dross age; medium confidence.

children.name: Zamak die-cast alloy and the pressure die-caster
children.description: Zinc's most interesting product for this tree. A zinc alloy with 4% aluminium and a little copper - Zamak 3 is Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5, Zamak 5 with 5% aluminium for better die-castability - is injected into a steel die at 380-430 C under 20-150 MPa by a cold-chamber machine with 200-800 tonnes of clamping force. It fills the thinnest sections any metal can fill - 0.8 mm walls, and details you could not machine - and it holds a fine surface as cast. The 1982 pressure die-caster was a 350-800 tonne machine, and the seconds per shot multiplied by the shots an hour is the number that set the cost of a key plunger or a case bracket.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: Zamak 3: Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5; Zamak 5: Zn 95 / Al 5 / Cu 0.5

facts.label: Clamp force
facts.value: 200-800 t on a 1982 machine

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 1-5 s per shot; 400-700 shots per hour on a small machine

facts.label: Minimum wall
facts.value: 0.8-1.0 mm, tighter than aluminium

children.note: Zinc die casting lost share to aluminium and to engineering polymers during the 1980s-90s, and the alloy names (Zamak, ZA, ZA-8) are supplier-dependent. High confidence on the chemistry and the process, medium on the specific alloy for any Commodore part.

children.name: Zinc alloy melting furnace
children.description: The die-caster does not melt its own alloy from primary metal; it buys 10-25 kg alloy ingots of a certified composition and melts them in a thermostatically controlled holding furnace - typically a 100-500 kg crucible furnace with an immersed resistance heater and a lead bath to keep the alloy away from air. A crucible furnace full of molten zinc is the classic source of metal-fume fever among die-casters, because zinc oxide fume is generated wherever the surface is disturbed.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: 100-500 kg crucible, resistance or oil-heated, 380-430 C, held under a cover flux

facts.label: Occupational hazard
facts.value: zinc oxide fume from disturbed surfaces; metal-fume fever

children.note: Furnace design varies widely; medium confidence on capacities.

children.name: Electrolytic zinc plating of steel
children.description: For small plated parts - chassis fasteners, brackets, EMI shields - zinc is electroplated rather than dipped. An alkaline cyanide bath, a non-cyanide acid chloride bath, or in the barrel a simple sulphate. The deposit is sacrificial: even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially and protects the steel underneath. A chromate passivation on top gives the characteristic yellow or olive colour and much better corrosion resistance, and by 1982 chromate was already being restricted because of hexavalent chromium.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: alkaline cyanide zincate, or acid chloride, or sulphate

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: 5-25 um for passivated decorative and EMI shielding work

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: yellow or olive chromate conversion coating

children.note: Trivalent chromium passivation arrived in the 1990s-2000s; hexavalent chromate was the 1982 norm.

children.name: Brass (Cu-Zn)
children.description: Zinc's largest engineering use is as the alloying element in brass and bronze. Brass is 60-95% copper with zinc, and the connector bodies, bus bars, shield cans and some switch frames in a C64 are brass, often brass plated with tin or nickel. Brass is melted and cast from cathode copper and zinc ingots in a small reverberatory or induction furnace, then extruded or rolled and machined. It is included because roughly a third of the world's refined zinc goes into brass, and because it is a genuine convergence of the copper and zinc branches.

facts.label: Common grades
facts.value: C26000 cartridge brass (70/30), C36000 free-machining brass (62/38 with 0.5% Pb)

facts.label: Zinc share
facts.value: brass takes roughly a third of refined zinc

facts.label: Famous problem
facts.value: dezincification of alpha brasses in seawater; the cartridge brass avoids it

children.name: Zinc oxide varistor: the mains spike clamp
children.description: The C64's power supply faces the mains directly. A zinc oxide varistor disc - ZnO powder pressed and sintered between two fired electrodes - sits across the input, and its resistance is astronomically high until the mains edge is exceeded, at which point it conducts and clamps the surge. ZnO is essentially a doped semiconductor ceramic: zinc oxide powder mixed with a few mol percent of the oxides of bismuth, cobalt, nickel, manganese and antimony, calcined, granulated with a binder, dry-pressed at 100-200 MPa, fired at 1100-1300 C, and cooled under a reducing atmosphere so the grain boundaries become the non-stoichiometry that gives the voltage knee. So the surge protection on the input filter is a zinc metallurgy product - and, incidentally, the same powder metallurgy as the ferrites.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: ZnO with 0.5-2 mol% each of Bi2O3, CoO, MnO and other dopants

facts.label: Clamp voltage
facts.value: ~240 V for a mains disc, ~700 V for a DC-side disc

facts.label: Energy handling
facts.value: 10 J to over 1 kJ per disc, set by diameter

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1100-1300 C, then a controlled-atmosphere cool

children.name: Zinc oxide powder
children.description: Zinc oxide for ceramics was, in 1982, made by burning high-purity zinc in air, by calcining high-purity zinc carbonate, or - for the highest grades - by the vapour-phase oxidation of high-purity zinc metal, which gives spherical sub-micron particles with a very tight size distribution. A varistor powder needs high-purity ZnO because any foreign phase at the grain boundary changes the voltage knee. So the varistor in the C64's power supply starts with 99.99% zinc.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: combustion or calcination; vapour-phase oxidation for the best powder

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: sub-micron for the vapour route

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 2Zn + O2 -> 2ZnO at 400-600 C

children.note: The exact powder route for a given varistor is proprietary; medium confidence. The atmospheric oxidation of zinc metal is the bottom of this branch and is a certainty.

metal.zinc.electrowinning.name: Electrowinning of zinc on aluminium cathodes
metal.zinc.electrowinning.description: Zinc is one of the few metals won by electrolysis out of an aqueous solution at industrial scale. The reason is that zinc is more negative than hydrogen and would just deposit hydrogen from water if it were not for the high hydrogen overvoltage on aluminium; each cathode is an aluminium plate of 1-2 m2 and 10-25 mm thick, and the scraper at the top of the cycle knocks off a 5-25 kg slab. The slabs are melted in a small induction furnace and cast into 25 kg ingots at 99.995%. The energy is 3,000-3,500 kWh per tonne of zinc - high, but the purity and the by-product recovery make the route worth it for ores that cannot be smelted. This is the convergence point of the roast, leach, purification and ingot branches.

facts.label: Current density
facts.value: 500-1200 A/m2 of cathode

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: 1-2 m2 of aluminium plate, 10-25 mm thick

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 24-72 h, then strip; plates weigh 5-25 kg of zinc each

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 3000-3500 kWh per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.992-99.995% zinc, cast into 25 kg ingots

metal.zinc.electrowinning.note: The zinc-iron plant was the dominant new-build technology through the 1980s; the Imperial Smelting zinc-iron process and the roast-leach-electrowin are the same family.

children.name: Lead-silver anode in the tankhouse
children.description: The insoluble anode is a lead alloy - 99% Pb with 0.5-1% Ag, cast as 10-40 mm thick plates - which works because when it does corrode slowly, the lead dioxide layer that forms is a perfectly good anode surface. Silver is added because it slows the corrosion. So the zinc tankhouse is structurally a lead operation: it consumes lead anodes at a rate of a few kilograms per tonne of zinc, which is one of the more elegant hidden cross-links between the lead and zinc branches in this file.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 2-5 kg of lead alloy anode per tonne of zinc

children.name: The single-deck electrolysis cell
children.description: The 1980s zinc tankhouse cell was a plain open-top concrete or rubber-lined steel box, 3-6 m long, 1.5-2.5 m wide, 2-3 m deep, with an aluminium cathode every 15-25 mm and a lead anode between them. The electrolyte is fed in at one end and pulled out at the other; the plates go in, run for 24-72 hours, come out, get scraped, and go to the melting furnace. A modern plant with 300,000-400,000 m2 of cathode area is a building the size of a football pitch. This is one of the least mechanised and most manually-intensive electrolysis plants in the industry, because the plate handling has never lent itself to automation.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: 3-6 m long, 1.5-2.5 m wide, 2-3 m deep, 2-5 V

facts.label: Electrode pitch
facts.value: 15-25 mm between an anode and a cathode

children.note: Medium confidence; the cell layout is standard but varies between plants.

children.name: Strip the cathodes and melt the SHG ingot
children.description: At the end of the cycle each cathode is lifted out, tipped against a steel plate that shears the zinc slab off, and the slabs are charged to a 100-500 kg induction furnace. The furnace has to be held at 450-470 C and under a cover flux because zinc oxidises readily and every gram of oxide is a loss. Two refinements came in during the 1980s: induction furnaces with better stirring and better control, and the move to a single large furnace rather than a fleet of small ones, which cut the oxide loss and the labour.

facts.label: Melting
facts.value: 450-470 C in an induction furnace under a cover flux

facts.label: Slab
facts.value: 5-25 kg per cathode

facts.label: Loss
facts.value: 1-3% of the metal is lost as oxide and dross

children.note: The oxide loss figure is a rule of thumb; medium confidence.

metal.chromate-passivation.name: Chromate conversion coating
metal.chromate-passivation.description: A nitric acid or chromic acid bath - most often a sodium dichromate bath in 1982 - converts a zinc, tin or cadmium surface to a chromium oxide-hydroxide film a few hundred nanometres thick. Yellow is dichromate, olive is chromic acid, and the black 'iridium' used on some zinc die castings is a different chromate chemistry altogether. This is where the electronics industry met hexavalent chromium: not only in the plating baths but on every chromate-passivated steel part, on every tin-plated part that went through a passivation tank, and in the anode foil formation treatment. It is the reason the OSHA hexavalent chromium standard, published in 1971, was one of the first such rules in the United States, and it is a deliberate convergence point of the zinc, tin, aluminium-foil and chromium branches.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: sodium dichromate plus nitric acid, 5-30 s at room temperature

facts.label: Film
facts.value: ~0.1-0.5 um of mixed chromium oxide-hydroxide

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) in the film, which is why the dried chromate coating itself is not toxic

facts.label: Applicable to
facts.value: zinc electroplate, tinplate, cadmium, and aluminium anode foil formation treatments

metal.chromate-passivation.note: This node is the third of chromium's three markets - ferrochrome into stainless steel, electrolytic metal into the plating bath, and chromate conversion on the plated surface - so it is deliberately given two parents, the chromium branch and metal.zinc.electroplate.

metal.hex-chrome-plating.name: Hexavalent chromium electroplating bath
metal.hex-chrome-plating.description: The classic chromiumic acid bath: CrO3 at 50-250 g/L in dilute sulfuric acid at 100-250 g/L, run at 45-60 C, 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2, with a lead-lead dioxide anode. A special steel anode is used and the bath is extremely hard to waste-treat: the chromium has to get from Cr(VI) down to Cr(III) before it can be precipitated. Cr(VI) is acutely and cumulatively toxic with a demonstrated carcinogenicity, and the 1971 OSHA standard for airborne hexavalent chromium was one of the first such rules in the United States. A C64's hard chrome on the switch contacts, the case hinges and the shield-contact points would have been plated in a plant subject to it.

facts.label: Voltage and current
facts.value: 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2 for hard chrome

facts.label: Anode
facts.value: lead-lead dioxide; 5-15% Sn-Pb alloy

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: an automatic catalyst based on sulphate, in the 1980s

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: OSHA standard on airborne hexavalent chromium, 1971

metal.hex-chrome-plating.note: Hexavalent chromium plating is essentially unchanged since the 1980s except for the trivalent and hex-free alternatives developed after 2000; high confidence on the chemistry.

metal.nickel.ingot.name: Electrolytic or cathode nickel, 99.9%
metal.nickel.ingot.description: Nickel metal arrives at the user as a cathode or a briquette: 99.8% for ferronickel-grade stainless, 99.9% for stainless and for plating. For a plating line the metal arrives as matte or as a soluble anode, but in 1982 the majority of nickel plating anodes were still the insoluble carbon steel anode, with the nickel actually coming from the electrolyte as nickel sulphate made from nickel oxide. This is a deliberate convergence node: the laterite branch, the Mond branch, the plating branch and the stainless branch all meet here.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.8% cathode, 99.9% for plating and stainless

facts.label: 1982 supply route
facts.value: mostly ferronickel-derived; electrolytic and carbonyl nickel were the premium products

children.name: Nickel electroplating and the gold underplate
children.description: The single most important metallurgical fact about nickel in a 1982 C64: gold plating does not sit on copper. It sits on a nickel underplate of 1-3 um, and the reason is electrochemistry - gold will not plate directly onto copper because the copper dissolves faster than the gold deposits, and a gold-copper diffusion couple makes a brittle, corrosion-prone joint. So the connector fingers and the IC leads get nickel and then a thin gold flash, or electroless nickel - a nickel-phosphorus deposit from a hypophosphite bath - followed by gold. The electroless route was standard in the semiconductor industry of the era and was how the die-attached gold on a hybrid IC was built.

facts.label: Watts bath
facts.value: nickel sulphate plus nickel chloride plus boric acid, 50-60 C, pH 4.0-4.5

facts.label: Voltage and current
facts.value: 3-8 V, 2-8 A/dm2; 15-60 s for a flash

facts.label: Underplate
facts.value: 1-3 um of nickel under 0.05-0.25 um of gold

facts.label: Electroless nickel
facts.value: Ni-P from nickel sulphate and sodium hypophosphite, 3-8% phosphorus, at 85-95 C

children.note: The Watts bath composition is textbook; the specific underplate thicknesses on Commodore's connectors in 1982 are not something I can confirm. Medium confidence on the specific figures, high on the mechanism.

metal.stainless.304.name: AISI 304 and 430 stainless steel
metal.stainless.304.description: The iron-chromium-nickel family, and a deliberate convergence point of three branches in this file. 304 is 18% chromium, 8% nickel, the balance iron - austenitic, non-magnetic, non-hardenable. 430 is 16-18% chromium with no nickel - ferritic, magnetic, and cheap. Both are made the way any steel is made: blast furnace for the iron, then a stainless steelmaking step that decarburises in an argon-oxygen decarburisation vessel, and the key is that the melt must not pick up more than about 0.05% carbon or the chromium goes into carbide and the metal loses its corrosion resistance. Stainless is the audio jack shell, the shield cans, some of the chassis and any fastener. Its cost is driven almost entirely by the chromium and the nickel, which is why the nickel price crash of 1982-83 directly cheapened stainless.

facts.value: 18% Cr, 8% Ni, C below 0.08%, austenitic
16-18% Cr, C below 0.12%, ferritic, magnetic

facts.label: Decarburisation
facts.value: AOD or VOD down to 0.02-0.05% C

facts.label: Nickel share of cost
facts.value: 8% of 304 by mass but roughly half the alloy cost

facts.label: 1982 supply note
facts.value: a lot of consumer-electronics 'stainless' was actually nickel-chromium plated or tin-plated mild steel

metal.stainless.304.note: The point about plated versus solid stainless is a genuine and important ambiguity for a consumer case: both were used in 1982 consumer goods and I cannot tell which is in a specific C64 without the part.

children.name: Cold rolling, bright annealing and finishing of stainless
children.description: Stainless is rolled and formed by the same equipment as mild steel - a Sendimir mill, a continuous annealing line, a Timesaver - but the tooling is different, because austenitic stainless work-hardens violently and needs much more force, and because a bright anneal must be carried out in hydrogen or in a vacuum to avoid discolouration and to avoid needing a thick pickling. A 1982 bright annealing line used hydrogen at 1000-1100 C with dewpoint control, which is a very refined piece of metallurgy for a machine that cost $395.

facts.label: Bright anneal
facts.value: 1000-1100 C in dry hydrogen, or in vacuum

facts.label: Pickling
facts.value: mixed nitric and hydrofluoric acid, or a nitric-sulphuric alternate

facts.label: Work hardening
facts.value: 304 work-hardens to about 1.3 GPa tensile before it must be annealed

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: 20-30% nitric acid, 30 min, at room temperature or 50 C

children.note: The nitric-hydrofluoric pickle is the classic stainless pickling line; by 1982 lower-HF alternatives were being developed for environmental reasons. Medium confidence on the transition timing.

children.name: Where a 1982 C64's stainless actually is
children.description: Not much: the outer shell of the composite or RCA connector, the shield cans over the analogue sections, some of the tuner and modulator housings, the hinge hardware, and any stainless fastener. In practice much of what looks like stainless in 1982 consumer electronics was nickel-chrome electroplated or tin-plated mild steel, because solid 304 in a thin stamping cost several times what a plating operation cost. The distinction matters and cannot be settled without the part.

facts.label: Mass in a C64
facts.value: order 50-200 g of solid stainless at most

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: nickel-chrome or tin-plated mild steel sheet, which looks identical from outside

children.note: Low confidence on which specific Commodore parts are solid stainless versus plated; this needs the actual hardware or the parts drawings.

metal.ferrochrome.name: High-carbon ferrochrome, 60-70% Cr
metal.ferrochrome.description: Chromite ore and coke are charged into a submerged arc furnace at 1400-1600 C with a chromite self-fluxing slag, and the result is an alloy of 60-70% chromium, 1-3% silicon and 5-8% carbon. It consumes about 500-700 kWh per tonne of ferrochrome - a fifth of aluminium's energy per tonne but on a much smaller tonnage. In the 1980s the industry was the classic vertically integrated single-industry town: the chromite mine, the power station with its 400 MW supply contract, and the smelter were all owned by the same company in the same town. The 1982-85 US and European voluntary export restraints on ferrochrome were aimed squarely at the market power of one country, and it is why ferrochrome is one of the very few metals where the 1982 price environment is a real story.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-105 MVA, three electrodes, 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 60-70% Cr, 1-3% Si, 5-8% C, balance iron

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 500-700 kWh per tonne of ferrochrome

facts.label: 1982-85 trade measure
facts.value: the United States and the European Community imposed voluntary export restraints on ferrochrome

metal.ferrochrome.note: Explicit correction of the brief's framing of chromium: the chromite-to-ferrochrome branch is dominated by South Africa, not by any American or European mine, and the 1982-85 export restraint is the period's defining event in it.

children.name: The self-fluxing chromite slag
children.description: A ferrochrome furnace is self-fluxing, which means the ore's own silica is balanced by the ore's own magnesia and there is nothing to add - the chromite is 16% MgO and 20% SiO2 and the ratio of the two is already about right for a liquid slag at 1500 C. That is why the smelter does not need lime, and it is also why the ore is smelted as it is rather than being beneficiated: a ferrochrome plant is a furnace and a power station, and the beneficiation happens in the ore dressing only if the ore is too fine to charge.

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: MgO/SiO2 about 0.8-1.0, so no lime is needed

children.note: Medium confidence on the exact oxide balance; the self-fluxing character of chromite is well established.

metal.ferromanganese.name: High-carbon ferromanganese, Mn 65-80%, C 6-8%
metal.ferromanganese.description: Made in a submerged arc furnace, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, at 1400-1600 C with the electrode tips submerged in the slag. The charge is sintered manganese ore, coke, limestone and often a good deal of iron ore, because the aim is an alloy of about 70% manganese at 6-8% carbon, and manganese is expensive enough that the industry buys more ore than stoichiometry requires in order to reach the assay. The manganese comes out as a carbide, Mn7C3, not as the metal, which is why the alloy has a carbon content at all. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: high-carbon ferromanganese is 6-8% C, not 13-15%; medium-carbon is 1-4% and low-carbon is under 0.5%, so 13-15% is not a real grade.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Medium and low carbon
facts.value: C 1-4% and C below 0.5%

facts.label: Phase
facts.value: manganese is present as carbide, mostly Mn7C3

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.5 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel made

metal.ferromanganese.note: Correction to the brief: 6-8% C for high-carbon ferromanganese, not 13-15%. Confidence high on the grades; the furnace size range is a class figure.

children.name: Sintering the manganese ore
children.description: Manganese ore is very fine and very friable, so it cannot be blown into a submerged arc furnace as a powder; it is sintered first, on a travelling grate exactly like the lead sinter, to make a 30-50 mm porous cake. The sinter belt at a manganese works is a zinc-works sinter plant or a lead-works sinter plant wearing different clothes, which makes it a nice example of a single machine serving three of the branches in this file.

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: travelling-grate sinter strand, 1100-1300 C in the burn zone

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 30-50 mm cake

children.note: Medium confidence on the sinter temperature range; the process itself is standard.

children.name: Deoxidation and desulphurisation in the steel ladle
children.description: Where the alloy is actually used. During tapping, ferromanganese is added to the steel. Manganese has a higher oxygen affinity than iron, so it combines with the dissolved oxygen to form MnO inclusions - which is the point: the oxygen is now safely tied up in an oxide the steelmaker can float out instead of being trapped as a gas bubble or an oxide stringer. Manganese also lowers the sulphur by forming MnS. The cost is that every kilo of manganese added becomes an inclusion unless the steel is properly deoxidised and the slag properly cleaned, which is why the amount is carefully calculated and why clean, low-inclusion steel is a specific technical achievement.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Mn + [O] -> MnO, and Mn + [S] -> MnS

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.5 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: during tapping or in the ladle, before the degasser

children.name: Aluminium and silicon deoxidation
children.description: The last step in the ladle is the one that actually decides the steel's quality. Manganese ties up the bulk of the dissolved oxygen as MnO inclusions, and then a calculated addition of aluminium - 0.5-2 kg per tonne - ties up the rest as Al2O3. Those inclusions have to go, and in a well-run plant they are floated out in the ladle or removed later by degassing and filtering. Manganese is what makes the aluminium deoxidation work: without manganese in solution, aluminium would oxidise preferentially as Al2O3 straight out of the bath and never reach the steel.

facts.label: Sequence
facts.value: Si, then Mn, then Al - the order matters

facts.label: Aluminium
facts.value: 0.5-2 kg per tonne, for a final soluble oxygen of 2-5 ppm

facts.label: Result
facts.value: fine Al2O3 inclusions dispersed in a MnS-bearing matrix

children.note: Medium confidence; the sequence is standard practice in aluminium-killed steel.

children.name: Removing the inclusions: degassing and filtration
children.description: A modern low-sulphur steel has few MnS inclusions but a lot of fine Al2O3, and that is a different problem: fine alumina does not float out, so it has to be filtered. A 1980s plate mill that wanted clean, formable sheet for deep drawing or for tinplating ran a ladle through a vacuum degasser to flush hydrogen and nitrogen and then through a ceramic foam filter in the ladle, or poured through a tundish filter. This is the technology that made the C64's chassis panel and the tinplate base material reproducible rather than lucky.

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: <10 mbar, 10-25 min, with argon stirring

facts.label: Filter
facts.value: ceramic foam, 0.4-1.0 mm pore, in the ladle or the tundish

facts.label: Target
facts.value: total oxygen below 20 ppm and sulphur below 0.005% for ultra-clean steel

children.note: The filtration step is a genuine 1980s development; medium confidence on the specific purity targets.

children.name: The submerged arc furnace and its refractory
children.description: A ferromanganese furnace is 25-100 MVA with three electrodes 1.5-2.0 m in diameter, and the difference from a silicon furnace is the slag: the ferromanganese process makes a large volume of a liquid, low-basicity slag, so the furnace is a slag vessel with an electrode in it. The shell is steel with a refractory lining of magnesite or magnesite-carbon, and the lining is eroded by the slag at 1500 C faster than in a silicon furnace. Carbon pastes, electrode paste made of the same coke-and-pitch as the aluminium anode, are rammed into holes in the roof around each electrode. So a ferromanganese plant is a coke-and-pitch shop as much as a manganese shop, which is the same convergence as the ferrochrome and ferrosilicon branches.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: 25-100 MVA, three electrodes 1.5-2.0 m diameter, 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Lining
facts.value: magnesite or magnesite-carbon, eroded by the low-basicity slag

facts.label: Electrode paste
facts.value: rammed into roof holes, made of coke and pitch

children.note: Medium confidence; the ferromanganese furnace design is well described in ferroalloy practice.

children.name: Why a ferroalloy smelter is built beside its power station
children.description: A 100 MVA submerged arc furnace draws about 80-90 MW continuously and cannot be stopped without destroying the furnace. So it needs a long-term supply contract and, in most cases, its own generating plant or a dedicated hydro or coal share. In the 1980s several ferroalloy industries - Norway's ferrochrome and ferrosilicon, South Africa's ferrochrome, Norway and Quebec's ferrosilicon - were built around cheap hydropower, and the industry's geography is essentially a map of where the cheap electricity was. It is the same fact as the aluminium smelter's, and the reason the same two or three countries dominated both.

facts.label: Furnace load
facts.value: 80-90 MW continuous for a 100 MVA unit

facts.label: Energy per tonne
facts.value: 3,000-6,000 kWh for ferromanganese; 8,000-11,000 for ferrosilicon; 500-700 for ferrochrome

children.note: The energy figures are consistent across the ferroalloy literature; medium confidence on the exact values by product.

metal.manganese.ore.name: Pyrolusite and manganiferous ore, 25-50% Mn
metal.manganese.ore.description: Manganese ore is almost never a clean manganese mineral. The Groote Eylandt and South African supergene ores are a hard, black, sooty mass of MnO2 cryptocrystalline material - wad and psilomelane - interbedded with iron formation. Grade is 25-50% Mn, and low-grade ore needs beneficiation: the South African ores were washed and jigged to reject the iron, and Groote Eylandt is washed in a scrubber and on a sluice. Silica and phosphorus are the two impurities that destroy value. This is a convergence node: the ferromanganese furnace, the ferrite branch's manganese carbonate and the steel deoxidiser all hang off it.

facts.label: Forms
facts.value: hard lumps (metallurgical), fines, sinter feed, and nodule fines

facts.label: Supply 1982
facts.value: South Africa and Australia were the dominant sources; the Groote Eylandt mine had been shipping since 1969

children.name: Supergene manganese mining in the Kalahari
children.description: The Transvaal and the northern Cape were the world's largest producers in 1982 by a wide margin, and the operation was surface mining on a 5-20 m ore layer over a 100 m thick band of black manganese-bearing sandstone. Drag hoists, belt conveyors, and a scrubber-and-jig beneficiation plant, then a sinter belt. The ore is a black, hard, siliceous rock and it is dug out of a 30 m face.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit, shovel and dragline, 5-20 m ore benches

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: scrub and jig to reject iron; 30-40% Mn product

children.note: The Kalahari field was opened in the 1970s and by 1982 was the dominant world source of metallurgical manganese ore; medium confidence on bench details.

children.name: Scrubber, sluice and jig beneficiation
children.description: Groote Eylandt and the South African operations do not smelt the raw lump: they wash it. The ore is dumped on a heap, a high-pressure water monitor scrubs off the fines and the clay, and the coarse goes over a sluice and a jig where the density difference between the manganese minerals (4.5-5.1) and the iron formation (5.0-5.3 but with a very different mineralogy) and the waste gangue separates the product. That is why a 30% Mn ore can make a 40% Mn product at low cost: the operation is a placer operation with a shovel in it.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: scrubbing with water monitors, sluice boxes and jigs

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 30-40% Mn, and the fines go to the sinter belt

children.note: The scrubbing and jigging flowsheet is well documented for Groote Eylandt; medium confidence on the exact recoveries.

children.name: The oxide and carbonate phases of the ore
children.description: The leaf of the manganese branch's rock: the manganese in a supergene ore is not one mineral but four. Pyrolusite MnO2 is the black, soft, fibrous one; psilomelane is a barium-bearing cryptocrystalline mixture; braunite Mn2O3 is the hard brown one; and rhodochrosite MnCO3 is the pink carbonate in the primary zone. The refractory braunite is the one the smelter hates, because it takes three times the reductant and gives a high slag. Which phase a shipment is made of determines whether it goes to a ferromanganese furnace or to a chemical plant, and the assay is a chemical analysis, not a visual test.

facts.label: Pyrolusite
facts.value: MnO2, black and soft, easily reduced

facts.label: Braunite
facts.value: Mn2O3, hard and refractory, expensive to reduce

facts.label: Rhodochrosite
facts.value: MnCO3, pink, in the primary carbonate zone

children.name: Abyssal manganese nodule dredge
children.description: The other, entirely different source: polymetallic nodules lying in thousands of square kilometres of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone and the Peru Basin at 4,000-6,000 m depth, containing 30% Mn, 2% Ni, 1% Cu and 25% Fe. Collecting them means a 10,000-tonne ship dragging a pipe across the seabed for 20,000 hours a year. It was never commercial in 1982 - technology trials were running but no mine was producing - and the incentive that eventually made it real was nickel, not manganese. This node is here because the 1980s seabed mining industry was built by exactly the people looking at the ore as a nickel resource, and by 1982 the C64's nickel supply chain and this geological curiosity were the same corporate conversation.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: hydraulic collector on a dragline with a riser to a ship, or a riserless system

facts.label: 1982 status
facts.value: technology demonstration only; no commercial production until decades later

children.name: Manganese oxide concretions on pelagic clay
children.description: The leaf: millimetre-to-centimetre potato-shaped concretions of Mn-Fe oxide lying unattached in a soft abyssal red clay. The metal has precipitated out of seawater around a nucleus, slowly, over millions of years. It is the most extraordinary leaf in this tree: the manganese in a C64's steel is, in principle, available from the floor of an ocean.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: pelagic abyssal red clay, thousands of metres down

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: 1-10 mm per million years

children.name: The abyssal red clay beneath the nodules
children.description: The true bottom of the manganese branch: a soft, red, pelagic clay that covers the abyssal plains at 4,000-6,000 m and that took the better part of 100 million years to accumulate, one centimetre at a time. The nodules sit on top of it. So the deepest leaf in this tree is a handful of dark potatoes on a carpet of red mud at the bottom of the Pacific, and the entire industrial-manganese question of whether to mine it is a question about that carpet.

facts.label: Sedimentation rate
facts.value: order 0.1-1 cm per million years

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: abyssal pelagic clay, far from any land-derived sediment

children.note: Medium confidence on the sedimentation rate range.

children.name: Why the 1970s nodule trials were abandoned
children.description: By 1982 seabed nodule mining was a real programme with real money behind it, and the money is the interesting part. The incentive was not manganese - the grades were assumed recoverable but nobody had proved it at scale. The incentive was nickel and cobalt, because the strategic metal studies of the 1970s and early 1980s concluded that the West had too little nickel and too little cobalt and that the seabed was the answer. The trials - the French Nodule, the American DOMES and NOAA work, the Japanese and the German programmes - put a collector on the bottom and brought up tonnages. Nothing commercial resulted before the 2000s, largely on legal grounds, but the 1982 assessment was optimistic, and that is a genuine piece of the 1982 story rather than hindsight.

facts.label: Programmes
facts.value: Nodule (France), DOMES and NOAA (United States), and Japanese and German programmes

facts.label: Incentive
facts.value: strategic-mine concern about nickel and cobalt supply, not about manganese

facts.label: 1982 outcome
facts.value: no commercial production; trials demonstrated recovery at the collector only

children.note: Low confidence on the specific programme details and outcomes; I am summarising a period I know well at the level of the strategic argument and poorly at the level of individual trials.

children.name: The hydraulic collector head
children.description: The machine the whole idea rests on: a manifold of suction nozzles, 10-30 m across, towed along the seabed at 1-3 knots, that lifts the nodules into a riser pipe and up to a ship 4,000-6,000 m above. The 1970s trials worked at the point where the ocean is deepest to learn whether nodules survive being lifted - the attrition of the nodules on the way up turned out to be a genuine engineering problem - and the riserless concepts that would have solved it were still on paper. It is a beautiful illustration of how much of deep-sea mining is really a fluid mechanics problem.

facts.label: Collector
facts.value: 10-30 m manifold of suction nozzles, towed at 1-3 knots

facts.label: Riser
facts.value: several thousand metres of pipe to a surface ship

children.note: Low confidence on the specific dimensions; the general design is standard and the detail is prototype-specific.

metal.chromite.name: Chromite ore (FeCr2O4), 38-46% Cr2O3
metal.chromite.description: A hard, black, opaque spinel - FeO plus chromium oxide in a cubic lattice - that occurs not as veins but as layer after layer in the lower part of the Bushveld Complex and the Transvaal Group. It is unusually resistant to both chemical attack and heat, which is why chromite is also found in beach placer sands in Oregon and California, and it is effectively the only chromium ore of commercial scale. The Bushveld chromite pits run 200 m deep on a 1-6 m seam, which is one of the more extreme geometries in mining. This is a convergence node for the ferrochrome furnace, the AOD vessel and the chromium metal plant.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 38-46% Cr2O3 for smelter-grade chromite

facts.label: Occurrence
facts.value: layered in the Lower Zone of the Bushveld Complex and the Transvaal Group

facts.label: Other sources
facts.value: Kemi in Finland, the Appalachian and Oregon beach sands, Kazakhstan and Zimbabwe

children.name: Layer-seam chromite open pit, 200 m deep
children.description: The Bushveld chromite mines are among the deepest and most geometrically awkward open pits in the world. A 1-6 m chromitite layer is covered by 100-200 m of layered norite, and the pit must be advanced strip by strip along the seam, so the benches are narrow and the truck travels a long way for every tonne. The waste is platinum-group ore, so the chromite mines and the platinum mines are the same mines, and their combined revenue is what made the region what it is. The ore is crushed to about 100 mm and shipped to a smelter, sometimes 400 km away.

facts.label: Seam thickness
facts.value: 0.5-6 m chromitite layer

facts.label: Cover
facts.value: 100-200 m of layered norite and pyroxenite

facts.label: Co-product
facts.value: the waste rock is platinum-group ore

children.name: Layered norite of the Bushveld Complex
children.description: The leaf: a 2 km thick layered mafic intrusion with a spectacularly regular magmatic stratification - a metre-scale layering of plagioclase and pyroxene laid down by a magma chamber over about a million years - with the chromite concentrating into a single thin seam at one horizon. It is the single most chromium-rich geological structure on Earth.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: layered norite, pyroxenite and anorthosite with a chromitite seam

facts.label: Age
facts.value: about 2.05 billion years

children.name: The Merensky Reef: the same layer as the chrome
children.description: Just below the chromitite seams of the Bushveld Complex lies a 0.4-1 m layer of pyroxenite carrying 3-8 g/t of platinum-group metals - the Merensky Reef - and it is the reason the chromite is mined as it is. The waste from a chromite pit is a platinum ore, so the two industries are financially intertwined, and the chromite pits were dug by companies that made their real money on platinum. So a chrome-bearing steel for the key plungers of a computer came out of a pit whose main product was a catalyst for a chemical that is not in this tree at all.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 3-8 g/t of platinum-group metals

facts.label: Relationship
facts.value: lies directly beneath the chromitite seams

children.name: Following a seam: the narrow-bench problem
children.description: A normal open pit advances in benches 15 m high and 100-200 m wide, with haul roads on every bench. A chromite seam is 1-6 m thick, so the pit has to advance along the seam instead, and the benches are 100-200 m high with a 5-10 m working width and a haul road cut into the wall. The consequence is a bench width of a few tens of metres where a truck needs twenty, so the ore is either hauled a long way or handled by a shovel that strips the ore off the face and tips it down to a loading point on the bench floor. That is why the Bushveld pits look nothing like an iron ore pit even though they move similar tonnages, and it is a nice demonstration that mining cost is a function of geometry before it is a function of the rock.

facts.label: Bench
facts.value: 100-200 m high with a 5-10 m working width

facts.label: Advance
facts.value: along the seam, not across it

facts.label: Truck requirement
facts.value: order 20 m of road width, more than the seam provides

children.note: Medium confidence; the geometry argument is sound and the specific figures are representative of the Bushveld pits.

metal.chromium.aod.name: Argon-oxygen decarburisation and the stainless vessel
metal.chromium.aod.description: The step that makes stainless steel possible. A 300-450 tonne ladle is fitted with a lance that injects a mixture of argon and oxygen under the steel surface. The argon stirs the melt and dilutes the carbon, the oxygen burns carbon to carbon monoxide, and because the gas is argon rather than air the melt does not pick up nitrogen - and nitrogen is exactly what stops 304 from being fully austenitic. At the end the gas is switched to pure oxygen and then back to argon to dilute the carbon without oxidising the chromium. The whole cycle takes 40-90 minutes and takes carbon from about 0.6% down to 0.03%, and it is why a stainless melt shop looks like nothing else in the steel industry. A deliberate convergence point of the chromium, nickel, ferrochrome and steel branches.

facts.label: Ladle
facts.value: 300-450 t, with a submerged lance

facts.label: Gas
facts.value: ~78% Ar / 22% O2 initially, rising to pure O2, then back to Ar

facts.label: Chromium loss
facts.value: some chromia goes to the bath, recovered from ferrochrome dust

children.name: Where the chromium ends up in a 1982 C64
children.description: AISI 304 in the audio jack shell, the shield cans and any stainless fastener or bracket; 430 where a magnetic ferritic grade was wanted. Chromium at 18% is above the roughly 11% needed for the surface to passivate, which is the whole trick: chromium forms a self-healing chromium oxide film about 2 nm thick, and that film is why stainless does not corrode. The passivation step in nitric acid is what removes the free iron that welding and machining leave on the surface, and without it the stainless rusts.

facts.label: Cr in 304
facts.value: 18%, well above the ~11% passivation threshold

facts.label: Passive film
facts.value: ~1-5 nm of chromium(III) oxide

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: 20-30% nitric acid, room temperature or 50 C, 30 min

children.note: The passivation chemistry is standard; whether Commodore's specific parts were passivated in manufacture is medium confidence.

children.name: The AOD lance and its tuyere block
children.description: The lance is a 10-25 cm carbon-molybdenum or refractory tube lowered into the metal on a mast, and it carries both the argon and the oxygen. Around it sits a refractory tuyere block in the ladle lining with a single small hole through which the gas is injected into the melt, so the gas is introduced a few hundred millimetres below the surface and the stirring is far more effective than a surface lance. The lance itself is a consumable: the oxygen attacks the tip, and a lance lasts one heat or a few hours, so there is a pile of spent lances outside every AOD vessel.

facts.label: Lance
facts.value: 10-25 cm diameter, carbon-molybdenum, a consumable

facts.label: Injection depth
facts.value: 200-500 mm below the metal surface

facts.label: Argon flow
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 Nm3 per minute per tonne of steel

children.note: Medium confidence; the lance geometry and injection depth are standard practice.

children.name: The refractory ladle lining
children.description: The AOD vessel is lined with magnesia or with magnesia-carbon, and the slag at pH 5 or higher eats a basic lining - which is why a stainless ladle lining is more expensive and more carefully maintained than a mild steel one. The lining is a consumable of its own, replaced every few hundred heats. So the chromium branch reaches the bottom not only in an ore body but in a sea of magnesia sand, and the magnesia is from seawater or from a magnesite mine.

facts.label: Lining
facts.value: magnesia or magnesia-carbon brick, 200-300 mm

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: dead-burnt magnesite (MgCO3) or seawater magnesia (Mg(OH)2)

children.note: Medium confidence; the magnesia supply chain is well documented but is not part of this subsystem's requested scope.

metal.chromium.metal.name: Electrolytic chromium metal from chrome alum
metal.chromium.metal.description: Pure chromium metal - for the chromium plating chemistry and for chromium sputtering targets - is made the opposite way to ferrochrome: hydrometallurgically. Chromite is roasted with soda ash to a water-soluble sodium chromate, the chromate is leached, the hexavalent chromium is reduced to trivalent in an acid solution, and the metal is electrowon onto a lead cathode to 99.9%. It is a short, small industry - a few thousand tonnes a year of a metal worth a great deal. The chrome alum the world consumed came largely from chemical processing plants, and the sulphur dioxide from the roast was a nuisance that pre-1950 plants simply released. The same hydrometallurgical route also produced the sodium chromate that went into the chromate conversion coatings of the zinc and tin plating branches.

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 500-700 C with soda ash, to water-soluble sodium chromate

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: sodium metabisulphite to Cr(III) as chrome alum

facts.label: Electrowinning
facts.value: lead cathode, low voltage, to 99.9% Cr

metal.chromium.metal.note: The hydrometallurgical chromium route is well documented; I have medium confidence on the exact 1982 process parameters.

children.name: Chromium electrowinning cell and the diaphragm
children.description: Chromium is electrowon from a trivalent chromium sulphate solution at 5-8 V with a lead or lead-alloy cathode, in cells separated by a diaphragm - traditionally asbestos cloth, later a synthetic fibre - because the anodic chlorine would otherwise oxidise the trivalent chromium back and the two would meet and precipitate. The product is 99.9% chromium at 80-90% current efficiency. The cell room is the most noxious part of the whole chromium industry: hexavalent chromium in the feed, acidic mist, and an operator who must be in a respirator.

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: lead or lead alloy

facts.label: Diaphragm
facts.value: asbestos cloth, later synthetic fibre

children.note: Low confidence on the cellroom details; this part of the industry is poorly documented outside the chrome plating literature, where the figures for chromium metal electrowinning are not commonly given.

children.name: The diaphragm and the asbestos inheritance
children.description: The cell needs the anodic chlorine kept away from the trivalent chromium in the catholyte, and the membrane that does that was, until the 1980s, asbestos cloth - the same asbestos as the chlor-alkali diaphragm cells. So the chromium and chlor-alkali industries of the early twentieth century share a materials problem that was only being dealt with in the 1980s, in both cases by a conversion programme driven by worker exposure rather than by metallurgy. The 1982 answer was a synthetic fibre diaphragm, which worked and cost more.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: asbestos cloth, replaced by synthetic fibre and PTFE-lined designs through the 1980s

children.note: Low confidence on the specific 1982 chromium cell diaphragm practice; the asbestos overlap with chlor-alkali is real but I am inferring the chromium side of it.

metal.cassiterite.name: Cassiterite concentrate (SnO2)
metal.cassiterite.description: Cassiterite is a very heavy, very hard, brown-to-black mineral - the specific gravity of 7 makes gravity separation unusually effective on it, which is why tin mining has always had a placer tradition. The concentrates bought by an smelter in 1982 came from four very different operations: alluvial and offshore dredging in Malaysia and Indonesia, hard-rock lodes in the Bolivian and Brazilian Precambrian shields, hard-rock in Cornwall and the Pan, and shallow residual deposits in Thailand and Nigeria. Concentrates assayed 40-80% Sn with arsenic, iron, tungsten and fluorine as the problem impurities - fluorine in particular is the reason the Bolivian smelter needed a roast.

facts.label: Smelting route
facts.value: 70% of world tin was smelted in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Bolivia; China emerged in the 1990s

facts.label: Problem impurities
facts.value: As, Fe, W, and F (fluorine in Bolivian concentrates)

children.name: Alluvial cassiterite gravel: dredging and panning
children.description: Tin gravel is a beach or stream deposit: pebbles and clay with a few grams of cassiterite per tonne. The classical recovery is the sluice and the jig, where a stream of water over an inclined riffled box stratifies by density and the heavy mineral stays behind. The Kinta Valley in Perak, Malaysia, was dredged on an enormous scale from the 1900s through the 1980s by suction dredges working a 100 m wide alluvial fan at 30-100 m depth, pumping gravel through a 3-6 inch suction pipe to a floating washing plant and a jig. Off Thailand and Indonesia it was offshore and shallow-sea dredging. Gravel is essentially quarried from a sea floor.

facts.label: Dredge
facts.value: cutter-suction dredge, 100-300 mm gravel, 200-500 L/s

facts.label: Recovery route
facts.value: sluice box, jig, then a shaking table and a magnetic separator

facts.label: 1982s shift
facts.value: the Kinta dredging era was ending and hard-rock and residual mining was taking over as the Malaysian industry

children.name: Stanniferous alluvium and laterite
children.description: The leaf: unconsolidated stony clay and gravel of a valley floor or a coastal plain, with cassiterite grains scattered through it and concentrated at the base of gravel layers where the wave or the stream action is right. In Malaysia it is a young alluvial fan over limestone; in Bolivia it is not alluvial at all but a hard-rock lode in Ordovician slates and granites, which is why Bolivia's process chain is longer.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: alluvial gravel over limestone (Perak) or residual laterite over a lode (Bolivia, Cornwall)

children.name: Cassiterite lode in the Bolivian and Cornwall tin belt
children.description: For contrast: the tin lodes of the Cordillera Real in Bolivia and of the Cambrian granite cupolas in Cornwall are hydrothermal cassiterite in quartz veins and greisens, and they have to be blasted and milled. Bolivia's Oruro and La Paz districts still supply a fraction of world tin from ore averaging 0.3-1% Sn, with the famous manioc mill and the hydraulic concentrator. Cornwall's industry was by 1982 essentially finished - the last deep mine closed in 1984 - a hundred years after the smelter industry had been moved to the East.

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% Sn in lodes and pipes

facts.label: Cornwall's end
facts.value: Grezmerry closed in 1984, ending Cornish tin mining after 2,500 years

children.name: Greisen and quartz vein
children.description: The leaf for the hard-rock route: a pneumatolytic alteration halo of topaz-bearing greisen and milky quartz with cassiterite disseminated through it, around a granite cupola. It is a rock, it is in a hillside, and it is drilled.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: greisen and quartz vein in a granite cupploa

children.name: Topaz and the greisen alteration
children.description: The leaf, geologically: a pneumatolytic alteration halo around the granite cupola in which the feldspars are replaced by topaz (Al2SiO4F2) and quartz, and in the interstices sit the crystals of cassiterite, wolframite and native bismuth. The fluorine in the topaz is the whole reason the alteration happened - it is a fluorine-rich hydrothermal fluid - which is a satisfying way for the tin branch to close, because the same fluorine chemistry that greened the rocks is the fluorine chemistry that made the cryolite in the aluminium pot and the hydrofluoric acid for the silicon plant.

facts.label: Topaz
facts.value: Al2SiO4(F,OH)2, a fluoriferous alteration mineral

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: greisen around a granite cupola, with quartz and cassiterite in the interstices

children.note: Medium confidence; the greisen mineralogy is standard, the specific Cornwall detail is a generalisation.

metal.galena.name: Galena (PbS) concentrate
metal.galena.description: Galena is cubic, bright grey when fresh and dull grey when oxidised, extremely heavy at 7.6 g/cm3, and it is one of the few common ores that a prospector could identify by eye. The great mining districts in 1982 were the Tri-State district of Missouri, Oklahoma and Kansas (which supplied most of the United States' lead and is a fossil limestone-hosted deposit), the Broken Hill and Mount Isa districts of Australia, Cerro de Pasco and Huancavelica in Peru, and the Iberian and Atlas belts. Concentrates assay 40-75% Pb and are always accompanied by enough silver and zinc to make a good deal of the mine's revenue.

facts.label: Concentrate assay
facts.value: 40-75% Pb, typically 0.5-3% Ag, 2-8% Zn

facts.label: Host
facts.value: carbonate-hosted replacement bodies (Tri-State) and metamorphosed massive sulphide (Broken Hill)

children.name: Underground lead-zinc mine
children.description: The Tri-State district's galena bodies sit as veins and bedding replacements in Mississippian limestone only a few metres thick, and they were worked by room-and-pillar mining - essentially taking the limestone out and leaving the lead in place, because the ore grade at 3-6% Pb did not pay for selective mining. The mineral was hand-picked off the back of the working face and off the cars. This is a soft-rock, shallow, cheap mining operation, and its day had largely gone by 1982 as the deeper and lower-grade Missouri deposits took over.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: room-and-pillar in limestone, ore bodies 3-15 m thick

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 3-6% Pb, and a lot of hand sorting

children.name: Galenite replacement in carbonate rock
children.description: The leaf: galena crystals and veins in a fossiliferous limestone - literally the remains of a Carboniferous sea floor. The Tri-State district is one of the great fossil-mineral coincidences of industrial history: a lead-bearing limestone under a farm field.

facts.label: Host rock
facts.value: Mississippian limestone and dolomite

facts.label: Form
facts.value: replacement bodies and veins along bedding and fractures

children.name: Hand picking and gravity sorting
children.description: The Tri-State district's ore was a 3-6% lead limestone that could not be selectively mined and could not be concentrated, so the technique was brute force: the rock was shot down, the lead-bearing rock was picked out of the face by hand by a face worker, and then the cars were run over a sorting table or a picking table where a sorter took out the visibly lead-coloured lumps from the limestone. In 1930 the Tri-State had about 15,000 sorters - a third of them children - and that is what made the district the largest lead producer on Earth. It is a labour technique rather than a machine, and it is a genuine leaf of the tree.

facts.label: Recovery by sorting
facts.value: a face worker and a car sorter could double the mill feed grade

facts.label: Sorters
facts.value: order 15,000 sorters at the peak of the Tri-State, a third of them children

facts.label: Why it stopped
facts.value: the ore got deeper and thinner, and the labour became uneconomic; the district closed in the 1960s-70s

children.note: Medium confidence; the Tri-State hand-sorting era is well documented in the labour history literature.

children.name: The sorting table
children.description: A sloping table with a light on it and a raised lip, worked by two or three people, one on each side. Galena is bright and heavy and galena-bearing limestone is dark and light, so the visual contrast is real, and the sorter's job is to lift out the dark lumps at perhaps 2-4 tonnes per shift. It is the lowest-skill, lowest-pay, highest-volume job in the lead industry, and it is where a great many Missouri families started.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: order 2-4 t of rock sorted per person per shift

children.note: Medium confidence; sorting rates are anecdotal and vary enormously with the ore.

metal.sphalerite.name: Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate, 50-60% Zn
metal.sphalerite.description: Sphalerite is one of the few ores that is not visually recognisable: it is a black to honey-brown cubic crystal whose colour depends on the iron substituting in the lattice, so the industry grades it in grades of iron - a 4% iron concentrate looks black and a 12% iron concentrate looks ruby red-brown. Concentration is by flotation with an amine or xanthate collector. The great districts were the Red Dog and the Sullivan mine in British Columbia, Broken Hill, the Cerro Rico of Potosi, the Rammelsberg of Goslar, and the Appalachian and Midwestern US zinc districts such as the Bartlesville and the Tennessee mines.

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: usually underground room-and-pillar or long-hole stoping in a stratiform or replacement body

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: differential flotation or bulk float with amine collectors

children.name: Underground zinc-lead mine
children.description: The Red Dog and Sullivan type deposit: a massive sulphide body in a sedimentary basin, mined underground from a ramp or a shaft, with the ore hoisted in a friction hoist or a skip, and the mill right at the portal. Broken Hill's Broken Hill Proprietary was the other archetype, an open pit above a very large primary orebody that was mined for sixty years. Where the zinc and lead are in separate veins, gravity and flotation split them: galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 do separate well on a dense-medium separator.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: underground room-and-pillar or long-hole stoping; open pit for large primary bodies

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: dense-media / differential gravity for galena vs sphalerite, then flotation

children.name: Massive sulphide in a sedimentary basin
children.description: The leaf: a lens-shaped body of fine-grained sulphide - sphalerite, galena, pyrite, with chalcopyrite and arsenopyrite - conformable with the bedding of a marine shale or carbonate, and sitting at a specific stratigraphic horizon. The Red Dog deposit is exactly this: a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin. The ore is not in a vein you can see from the surface; it is a stratigraphic layer you have to know is there.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: sediment-hosted massive sulphide lens in fine-grained clastic sediment

children.name: Zinc concentrator: differential flotation
children.description: The ore is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground to 50-100 um in a ball or autogenous mill, and floated in stages. The classic circuit is differential: copper and lead sulphides are floated first with a stronger collector and a higher pH, and then the sphalerite is floated from the tailings with a weaker collector at a lower pH, with copper sulphate added as an activator because sphalerite does not float on its own. That gives a 50-60% Zn concentrate at 85-92% recovery. The Red Dog and Sullivan concentrators were among the largest in the world and are the reason those two mines could be mines at all.

facts.label: Circuit
facts.value: Cu-Pb bulk float first, then Zn float from the tailings

facts.label: Activator
facts.value: copper sulphate, 0.1-1 kg/t

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 85-92% to a 50-60% Zn concentrate

children.note: Medium confidence on the specific additive dosages; the circuit configuration is standard.

children.name: Dense-media separation of galena from sphalerite
children.description: Galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 are separable on a shaking table or, much faster, in a dense-medium separator using a ferrosilicon or magnetite suspension at a cut density of about 3.0-3.5. The lead concentrate and the zinc concentrate are thereby split before flotation, which lets the flotation plant be small. Dense-medium separation of a polymetallic ore is one of the great quiet successes of twentieth-century mineral processing.

facts.label: Medium
facts.value: ferrosilicon or magnetite in water at 2.5-3.5 specific gravity

facts.label: Cut density
facts.value: 3.0-3.5 separates galena from sphalerite

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: 100-500 t/h on a modern separator

children.note: The cut densities and throughputs are class values; medium confidence.

children.name: Ferrosilicon powder for dense-media separation
children.description: The liquid in a dense-medium separator is ferrosilicon - an alloy of iron and silicon made in exactly the submerged arc furnace described in the electrical-steel and metallurgical-silicon branches of this file. So a 1982 concentrator that separated galena from sphalerite by density was running a slurry of metallurgical silicon, and the silicon branch of this tree reaches a zinc concentrator as well as a power transformer. Silicon really does end up everywhere: 60-90% of all ferrosilicon production goes into the steel and aluminium branches, but the rest goes into heavy-media separation, and it is the sharpest possible illustration of why a tree like this has cross-links.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 15-30% Si, ground to under 100 um

facts.label: Source
facts.value: ferrosilicon, made in a submerged arc furnace

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.2-1 kg of ferrosilicon per tonne of ore processed

children.note: Medium confidence on the consumption rate; it varies greatly with the ore.

children.name: The host basin and its caprock
children.description: The final leaf of the zinc chain is not a rock but a structure: a sedimentary basin with a metal-bearing horizon in it. The Red Dog deposit is a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin on the Tukarakka Peninsula; Broken Hill is a metamorphosed, deformed massive sulphide in a sequence of Proterozoic metasediments. In both cases the orebody sits at a specific stratigraphic level, and the mine is a series of ramps and stopes chasing a bedding-parallel body a few metres thick. So the zinc in a C64's die-cast key plunger came out of a bed that happens to lie a kilometre beneath a river delta.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: sediment-hosted massive sulphide at a specific horizon in a basin

facts.label: Ore thickness
facts.value: 5-25 m of ore under hundreds of metres of host rock

metal.nickel.laterite.name: Nickel laterite (garnierite ore)
metal.nickel.laterite.description: A soft, earthy, red-brown clay-and-laterite ore, really a weathering product of ultramafic rock: olivine and pyroxene in a serpentinised peridotite are altered from scratch, and nickel substitutes for magnesium in the clay lattice, giving garnierite. There is no nickel mineral to concentrate; the whole ore body is the ore.
