The great deposits in 1982 were the Cuban Moa and Nicaro operations - where the ore was shipped to the United States and Japan for the nickel limit of the United States Defense Production Act of 1981 made government stockpiling a political event - the Philippines' Surigao and Bacojo operations, the New Caledonian laterite, and the Queensland laterite. Laterite is mined in the open pit in soft, wet ground with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline, and often leached in place.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 1.5-3.0% Ni, 15-40% Fe, low silica (<2%) for the best, high-silica (>20%) for the Chinese and Indonesian shales

facts.label: Ore type
facts.value: limonite (high-Fe, low-Mg), saprolite, or smectitic (high-silica) - only the limonite-rich low-silica ore is worth the pressure leach

facts.label: Depth of weathering
facts.value: 5-100 m of overburden before reaching the saprolite

children.name: Bucket-wheel excavator laterite mine
children.description: The soft, wet, deeply weathered ore is the ideal bucket-wheel material. A walking or rail-mounted bucket-wheel excavator with a 20-40 m boom cuts the overburden and the ore bench itself, dropping it onto a belt conveyor, and the ore goes to a long washing and screening plant rather than to a crusher. The Philippine and Cuban operations had bucket-wheel excavators with booms over 50 m by the early 1980s. The ore arrives at the plant as a slurry, which is why the pressure leach of the 1980s was designed for a pumped pulp and not for a dry concentrate.

facts.label: Boom length
facts.value: 20-60 m; the largest bucket-wheel excavators of the era

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 0.3-0.6 m3 per bucket at 0.6-1.5 s cycle

facts.label: Conveying
facts.value: belt conveyor from the excavator directly to the washing plant

children.note: Boom lengths and bucket volumes are machine-class figures, not specific to any named mine; medium confidence.

children.name: Serpentinised peridotite
children.description: The leaf: an ultramafic igneous rock, mostly olivine, now largely converted to serpentine, that has been chemically weathered for tens of millions of years in a warm wet climate. The nickel is in the clay and in the limonite, not in a crystal. Cuba, New Caledonia and the Philippines all have large serpentinite bodies, and that is why the island arcs of the Pacific are the nickel map.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: serpentinised peridotite / dunite, weathered to garnierite-bearing laterite

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: tropical weathering profile, tens of metres thick, on an ultramafic body

children.name: The laterite washing and screening plant
children.description: The laterite arrives from a bucket-wheel excavator as a slurry, and it goes through a log washer, a scrubber, a screen tower and a series of hydrocyclones, and the -0.5 mm fraction is rejected outright as low-grade clay. The coarse fraction is dewatered on a screen and stacked in a concrete bin. In the Cuban and Philippine operations the stacked ore was then leached in place on a pad, in the Queensland operations it was dried in a rotary dryer and shipped to a furnace. The whole plant exists because the ore is a soft, wet, variable, low-grade bulk material, and the plants are mostly about handling water.

facts.label: Rejection
facts.value: the -0.5 mm clay fraction is discarded, and it is often 20-40% of the feed

facts.label: Dewatering
facts.value: screens, cyclones, and a large thickener

facts.label: Moisture in the dried ore
facts.value: reduced to below 1-2% before any furnace

children.note: Medium confidence; the flowsheet is well documented for Cuban and Philippine operations.

children.name: Limonite and garnierite: the two nickel minerals
children.description: The leaf of the nickel branch, and it is a mineral solution rather than a mineral. There is no nickel mineral in a laterite. Nickel substitutes for magnesium in the smectite and kaolinite clays - the mineral is garnierite, which is really a mixture - and it substitutes for iron in the goethite of the limonite, so a limonite laterite's nickel is spread through amorphous iron oxide at a few percent. The two grades of laterite that matter commercially are the high-iron limonite ore and the low-silica saprolite ore, and the difference between them is the grade of the nickel-bearing lattice, which is why the pressure leach was developed for one and not the other.

facts.label: Garnierite
facts.value: (Ni,Mg)3Si2O5(OH)4, nickel substituting for magnesium in a smectite

facts.label: Limonite
facts.value: nickel substituting for iron in amorphous goethite, FeO(OH)

facts.label: Two commercial ores
facts.value: high-iron limonite ore and low-silica saprolite ore

children.name: Dry the laterite before smelting
children.description: A laterite arrives at 30-45% moisture and the submerged arc furnace cannot take it wet, because the water costs more steam than the reaction releases. So the dewatered ore is dried in a rotary dryer or - in the Cuban and Philippine operations of the 1980s - in a suspension dryer with the hot flue gas, to below 1-2% moisture, and the drier's exhaust is the source of the dust and the fuel consumption that dominated the cost. Some plants solved the problem differently: the Queensland operations calcined and reduced the ore on the pad and then shipped a nickel oxide, which moved the water problem upstream to the leach.

facts.label: Feed moisture
facts.value: 30-45% from the washing plant

facts.label: Product moisture
facts.value: below 1-2%

facts.label: Alternatives
facts.value: rotary dryer, or a suspension dryer, or on-pad reduction and shipping a nickel oxide

children.note: Medium confidence; the alternative routes are well documented for specific operations.

metal.gold.ingot.name: Refined gold anode, 99.99%, and the plated flash
metal.gold.ingot.description: The gold that reaches the electronics industry is 99.99% minimum, as a rolled sheet or an anode, and it is used in three ways. Flash plating for connector fingers and IC leads: the gold is dissolved in a cyanide gold bath - typically a gold cyanide, potassium cyanide, gold hydroxide bath at 0.5-2 g/L gold - and deposited on the nickel underplate at 0.1-1 A/dm2 for a few seconds, giving 0.05-0.25 um. Wire bonding: 15-50 um pure gold wire, drawn through diamond dies like copper, is welded from the die pad to the package lead with a thermosonic bonder. And sputtering: thin film resistors and the gold metallisation on some hybrid ICs were gold, sputtered from a cathode.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99% (4N); bonding wire is 99.999% (5N)

facts.label: Flash thickness
facts.value: 0.05-0.25 um on connector fingers and leads

facts.label: Wire gauge
facts.value: 15-50 um (0.6-2 mil) gold bonding wire

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: gold cyanide / potassium cyanide with a gold hydroxide addition, 0.5-2 g/L Au

metal.gold.ingot.note: The thickness and bath figures are textbook ranges; I cannot confirm the specific plating specification on Commodore's connectors in 1982.

children.name: Gold wire bonding of the die
children.description: Each die has to be electrically connected to the package. The 1982 method was wire bonding: a 25 um gold or aluminium wire is threaded through a ceramic or carbide capillary, the tip is melted by a discharge or by a heated work holder, and the first weld is made to the die's aluminium pad. The wire is then run out and the second weld is made to the package bond pad, and the wire is cut. A 40-pin chip has 80 of these welds per package, each under a milligram of gold, and the whole thing happens a thousand times a minute. Aluminium bonding wire was already displacing gold on most logic parts by 1982 for cost reasons, but gold remained the default for anything requiring a conductive epoxy or a eutectic die attach.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 20-50 um gold or aluminium

facts.label: Methods
facts.value: thermasonic (ultrasonic plus heat), the 1980s default for gold

facts.label: Bonds per package
facts.value: order 80 for a 40-pin DIP

facts.label: Gold per bond
facts.value: order 0.05-0.3 mg

facts.label: Intermetallic
facts.value: Au-Al intermetallics form in the bond; the purple plague is AuAl2

children.name: Gold-plated contacts: the edge connector and the switches
children.description: Two very different gold contacts in the C64. The 62-way edge connector at the rear has gold-flashed fingers - a 35 um copper-alloy finger with 0.1-0.5 um of gold and a nickel underplate, inserted in the board by a wipe in the card guides. The keyboard and the rocker switches use either gold-plated copper-alloy leaf springs or, in the better keys, solid silver or silver-alloy contacts. The gold flash on the edge connector is the only place where gold must survive thousands of insertions, and it does so because the nickel underplate stops the copper from diffusing into the gold and the gold itself never oxidises.

facts.label: Edge connector
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 um gold flash on 1-3 um nickel over a copper-alloy finger

facts.label: Insertion life
facts.value: 50,000-100,000 insertion cycles is a normal target for a gold-flashed card edge

facts.label: Why gold
facts.value: no oxide, no tarnish; noble metal does not form a resistive film

facts.label: Jewel switches
facts.value: some high-end switches used solid gold-alloy leaf springs, but 1982 consumer keyboards mostly used silver-plated or nickel-plated springs

children.note: The gold flash thickness and the contact material choice on the actual Commodore keyboard I cannot confirm; these are the standard ranges. Medium confidence on the specifics, high on the metallurgy.

metal.silver.ingot.name: Silver ingot, 99.9%, and silver contact material
metal.silver.ingot.description: A 99.9% ingot is the standard commodity grade, cast as 0.5-1 kg bars or as a 15-30 kg or 1000 troy ounce bar. For the contacts of the C64's switches and keys the relevant alloy is not pure silver but a silver-cadmium-oxide or silver-tin-oxide electrical contact material - a silver matrix with 5-15% of a refractory oxide that reduces the contact resistance rise caused by metal transfer, at the cost of a bit of conductivity. Silver-graphite is a related and very common sliding contact material: 50-95% silver in graphite, sintered and infiltrated, used where the contact has to rub.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.9% (2N) commodity; 99.99% (4N) for contacts

facts.label: Contact alloys
facts.value: Ag-CdO, Ag-SnO2, Ag-graphite; typically 80-95% Ag

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: silver's conductivity is 63 MS/m; the oxide suppresses arc erosion and metal transfer

facts.label: 1950s-1980s note
facts.value: silver contacts were being displaced in low-voltage, low-current applications by silver-plated base metals and by gold

metal.silver.ingot.note: The exact contact alloy in Commodore's keyboard switches is not something I can confirm; Ag-SnO2 and Ag-CdO were both standard contact materials in the 1980s. Medium confidence.

metal.tantalum.powder.name: Tantalum powder
metal.tantalum.powder.description: The anode of a tantalum capacitor is a pressed and sintered tantalum pellet of porous sintered tantalum powder, sintered at 1200-1400 C under vacuum, then anodised - electrolytically grown Ta2O5 - to a formation voltage of about 2-4 times the working voltage. The dielectric is the anodised oxide itself, which is why a tantalum capacitor is a bipolar electrolytic part with no liquid. The powder must be pure and must be milled and classified so the particle size is right for the pellet's porosity: a sintered pellet has to have a tortuous pore path, or it will short.

facts.label: Pellet
facts.value: pressed and vacuum-sintered at 1200-1400 C, porosity ~30-50%

facts.label: Anodisation
facts.value: Ta2O5 grown electrolytically to 2-4x the working voltage, in phosphoric or nitric acid

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: classified to about 1-8 um for the pellet

facts.label: Counter-electrode
facts.value: MnO2 from manganese nitrate, or a solid silver electrolyte (a later 1980s development)

facts.label: In 1982
facts.value: tantalum bead and molded chip packages were on the mainboard; wet slug parts were being displaced by these

metal.tantalum.powder.note: The silver-electrode variant (that is, a silver counter-electrode) only became commercial around the turn of the 1990s; in 1982 nearly all molded tantalum capacitors used a manganese dioxide or silver-paste counter-electrode, so this node is a convergence of the tantalum and manganese branches.

metal.benzene.name: Crude benzene from the coke oven
metal.benzene.description: A 1982 coke oven produced a very large fraction of the world's synthetic benzene, and benzene was the root of the styrene-polystyrene, phenol-formaldehyde and epoxy industries - so this node is where the coal branch and the plastics branch join. The benzol was drawn out of the oven gas with a wash oil, and the wash oil was then steam-stripped. It is a dense, sweet-smelling, carcinogenic liquid and it is a document about the chemical industry that produced nylon, epoxy resin, phenol formaldehyde resin, styrene, and polyurethane precursors all at once.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 8-12 kg of benzene per tonne of coke

facts.label: Route
facts.value: wash oil absorption then steam stripping of the rich oil

facts.label: In 1982
facts.value: benzene was about 85-90% coal-based rather than petroleum-based; the coal route held on until roughly the 1990s-2000s before cracking economics killed it

metal.iron.burden.name: Blast furnace burden: sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke and flux
metal.iron.burden.description: The furnace eats a precisely weighed blend, batched in 1-3 t bins and dumped in a rotating order around the bell-less throat so the burden descends evenly. Sinter is 55-65% Fe and 8-12% gangue; pellets are 62-66% Fe and are nearly always the majority of the iron-bearing burden in a modern furnace because they are uniform and permeable; lump ore is 45-60% Fe and is in retreat. The blend is sized and ground so it is permeable enough for the gas to reach the burden and rigid enough not to collapse into the raceways.

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 55-65% Fe, basicity 1.0-1.6

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 30-90 mm, with a coke rate of 0.3-0.5 t/t

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal

facts.label: Gangue
facts.value: the SiO2 and Al2O3 of the ore is the slag former, hence the silica/alkali balance

children.name: Sinter the fine ore on a travelling grate
children.description: Fine iron ore cannot be charged into a blast furnace - it would be blown away or it would pack. So it is sintered: mixed with 8-12% returning sinter fines, 5-7% coke and 10-20% lime, moistened to 6-8%, spread in a 0.7-1.0 m bed on a travelling grate, and ignited. At 1200-1400 C the bed self-fuses into a porous 100-150 mm cake. A modern sinter strand produces 3,000-6,000 t of sinter an hour and consumes about 1 GJ of fuel per tonne. It is the same machine as the lead sinter and the manganese sinter, and it emits a great deal of dust.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 1200-1400 C in the flame front

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 3,000-6,000 t/h per sinter strand

facts.label: Return fines
facts.value: 10-25% of the sinter produced is crushed and recycled

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke breeze or anthracite, ~60-90 MJ per tonne of sinter

facts.label: Gas cleaning
facts.value: cyclones and an electrostatic precipitator; the sinter plant was the biggest single dust emission at a steelworks

children.name: Coke breeze: the sinter fuel
children.description: The 3-10 mm fraction of coke, screened out at the coke plant, that would be too small for the blast furnace. A steelworks' sinter plant is therefore a consumer of its own coke plant's fines - a neat example of an internal recycling loop in the iron and carbon chain that closes from the coke oven's quench, through the sinter plant, back into the blast furnace's burn.

facts.label: Use
facts.value: 8-12% of the sinter mix as the fuel

children.name: Pelletising the concentrate on a disc or a pelletiser
children.description: Very fine concentrate - under 45 um - is mixed with 5-8% bentonite binder and 0.5-1% limestone, moistened, and fed to a rotating disc pelletiser or a drum pelletiser where 3-10 mm green pellets are rolled up by capillary action. The green pellets are then fired on a travelling grate at 1200-1350 C in an oxidising atmosphere, which sinters the surface, gives the pellet its compressive strength and, if the furnace is properly controlled, magnetises it - the hematite becomes magnetite, which means the pellet can itself be recovered magnetically, and its reduction in the blast furnace is faster. Pelletising is what made the 1970s and 1980s post-and-tensile steel possible and it is the reason Brazil and Canada have a modern steel industry at all.

facts.label: Pellet
facts.value: 9-16 mm, compressive strength 200-300 daN per pellet

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 2-3% bentonite; the pellet must survive handling from the pellet plant to the furnace

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: pellet capacity became the binding constraint on a new blast furnace's size

children.name: Bentonite binder from a clay pit
children.description: A sodium bentonite with a high swelling capacity, mined from a montmorillonite clay bed and used as the binder that makes a pellet roll up instead of shatter. In 1982 the world bentonite market was dominated by Wyoming and by Italy and the Balkan sources, and it was also the drilling mud of the oil industry, so the two applications competed for the same tonnage. The particular clay a pelletiser wants is a sodium montmorillonite, which is a specific alteration product of volcanic ash - the leaf of this little branch is a bentonite bed in a Tertiary volcanic sequence.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: sodium montmorillonite, high swelling capacity

facts.label: Dose
facts.value: 2-3% of the pellet mass

children.note: Pellet binder levels are standard; the specific source geology is medium confidence.

metal.electrical-steel.name: Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES)
metal.electrical-steel.description: The C64's power supply transformer is the one place where the metal of the machine is deliberately not stainless or mild steel. Grain-oriented electrical steel is a 3.2% silicon low-carbon steel whose grains have been given a preferred orientation - the classic route is a 700-1000 C anneal in hydrogen in a field or, in the modern continuous process, a high-temperature final anneal with a bias field - so that the flux runs along the grain and the core losses and the magnetostriction both fall. The 1982 transformer in a C64 used M4 to M6 grade GOES, somewhere around 0.3-0.5 mm thick, wound as E-E laminations. Without the silicon the core would saturate, the transformer would be too big, and the whole switching supply would not fit. Silicon steel is therefore not a speciality of this tree - it is load-bearing.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: low-carbon steel with 2.5-4.5% Si

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.27-0.50 mm for a power transformer

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: M4-M6 (or the older 21-23 grade number system)

facts.label: Core loss at 1.5 T, 50 Hz
facts.value: ~3-6 W/kg for M6; un-oriented steel is 4-6x worse

facts.label: Why silicon
facts.value: silicon raises the resistivity, cutting eddy-current loss, and lowers the magnetostriction

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: Goss texture, made by a final anneal with a bias field, or by the two-step orientation route

children.name: E-E laminations and the stamping
children.description: The 0.3 mm strip is blanked and stamped into E and I shapes - or, in a cheaper 1982 supply, into E-E pairs and then stacked and interlocked - on a 400-800 tonne mechanical or hydraulic press with a compound die that does the whole lamination stack in one stroke. The stamping is heavily lubricated and the edges are deburred and then given a magnetic insulation treatment: a thin epoxy or phenolic varnish, or an 'insulation coating' of an inorganic glassy film, applied so that the laminations do not short-circuit each other. The core of the C64's transformer is about 30-60 stamped laminations, and the number is set by the stack height and the available die.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: 400-800 t, one stroke for the whole stack in a compound die

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: epoxy or phenolic varnish, or an inorganic glassy film; a C-core varnish coat

facts.label: Stacks
facts.value: 30-60 laminations for a small switcher

children.note: The interlocked E-E stamping process was the standard for small transformers in the 1980s; confidence high.

children.name: Make the ferrosilicon and add it to the steel
children.description: How does 3% silicon get into sheet steel at all? Ferrosilicon is added to the ladle, or - in the parent process - the ore is smelted with silica and coke in a submerged arc furnace to give 45-75% Si ferroalloy, and that alloy is added to the steel in the ladle or in the EAF. So the silicon steel branch intersects the ferrosilicon furnace, which is a carbon-reduction electric furnace just like the ferromanganese and ferrochrome furnaces in this tree, and which ultimately runs on the same metallurgical silicon and quartzite chain as the semiconductors. One of the more satisfying loops in the tree.

facts.label: Ferrosilicon
facts.value: FeSi45 (45% Si) to FeSi75 (75% Si), made in a submerged arc furnace at 1600-2000 C

facts.label: Addition
facts.value: to give 2.5-4.5% Si in the steel

facts.label: Grade for GOES
facts.value: high-purity, low-C, low-Al ferrosilicon is preferred because aluminium oxides in the film kill the magnetic properties

children.note: The low-aluminium requirement on silicon steel is well documented in the GOES literature; high confidence.

children.name: Ferrosilicon in the submerged arc furnace
children.description: Ferrosilicon at 45-75% silicon is made in a submerged arc furnace very like the one that makes metallurgical silicon, but with more coke and a much higher silica ratio in the slag: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO, with the silicon going into the ferroalloy instead of condensing as dust. The largest producers make it in 60-100 MVA three-electrode furnaces, and the furnace is a genuinely different beast from the silicon one - the slag is liquid and the electrode has to tap through it. So the electrical-steel transformer in a C64 and the quartzite in a silicon plant converge at two different kinds of arc furnace.

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: FeSi45, FeSi50, FeSi65, FeSi75; high-purity low-C low-Al grades for GOES

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, 1600-2000 C

facts.label: Electricity
facts.value: 8,000-11,000 kWh per tonne of ferrosilicon

children.name: Continuous casting and the Goss texture formation
children.description: Electrical steel is continuously cast, hot rolled, and then given the two anneals that make it grain-oriented. The first, at 800-1100 C, is an ordinary recrystallisation anneal in wet hydrogen; the second, at 1100-1200 C, is the orientation anneal, in which the steel is held just below the Curie point in a magnetic field aligned with the rolling direction so the alpha-iron grains with their [110] axis along the field grow preferentially. The second anneal takes a week or more in a hydrogen atmosphere, which is why GOES costs three or four times what mild sheet costs and why a C64's transformer was one of the most expensive parts in it.

facts.label: First anneal
facts.value: 800-1100 C in wet hydrogen, 1-30 min

facts.label: Orientation anneal
facts.value: 1100-1200 C in dry hydrogen in a 5-10 T field, 10-100 h

facts.label: Grain size
facts.value: 2-10 mm, with the [110] axis parallel to the rolling direction

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: GOES sheet at 0.3-0.35 mm was several times the price of mild sheet

children.note: The orientation anneal conditions are well documented; medium confidence on the exact field strength, which varies by producer.

metal.die-steel.name: Tool steel: SKD61 / H13 / D2, the moulds and dies
metal.die-steel.description: The C64's case, the keycaps, the key plungers and the disk-drive and modulator housings were all made in injection-moulding dies, and every one of those dies and every aluminium extrusion die was cut from tool steel. SKD61 in Japan and H13 in the US and DIN X40CrMoV51 in Europe are the same alloy: 5% chromium, 5% molybdenum, 1% vanadium, 0.4% carbon, air-hardening to about 50-54 HRC. It is made in a small vacuum arc or vacuum induction furnace, forged, annealed, and then given three heat treatments - austenitising at 1000-1050 C, air cooling, and double tempering at 500-550 C - before it goes near the machine. A single C64 case die weighs 1-4 tonnes and cost tens of thousands of dollars, and it is the reason the tool steel branch is in this file at all.

facts.label: SKD61 / H13
facts.value: 5Cr-5Mo-1V-0.4C, air hardening to 50-54 HRC

facts.label: Heat treatment
facts.value: austenitise 1000-1050 C, air cool, double temper at 500-550 C

facts.label: Other tool steels in 1982
facts.value: SKD11 / D2 (1.5% C, 11% Cr) for cold-work dies, SKD5 / D2 for stamping, SKS3 / W1 for simple tooling

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: a C64 case die is 1-4 t and has a life of 100,000-500,000 shots

facts.label: Nitriding
facts.value: many dies were nitrided or PVD coated before use

children.name: Molybdenum: a tool steel alloying element
children.description: Molybdenum is in the tool steel, in the stainless and in the hydrodesulphurisation catalyst, so it belongs in this tree, but its own branch is short because in 1982 almost no molybdenum came from a molybdenum mine: about half came from the molybdenite recovered as a by-product of the porphyry copper concentrators, where it is a few hundred ppm of the concentrate and reports to a separate flotation circuit, and the other half came as molybdic oxide from roasting. The ore is molybdenite, MoS2, in the Climax and Henderson porphyry in Colorado and in the Bingham Canyon concentrate. The leaf is a porphyry or a granite vein.

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: ~half by-product of copper porphyry flotation, half from primary Mo mines

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: molybdenite concentrate at 45-60% Mo from a few hundred ppm of feed

facts.label: Conversion
facts.value: roasted to molybdic oxide, then reduced with aluminium or with hydrogen

children.note: The by-product share of molybdenum supply is well documented; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split.

children.name: Molybdenite in a porphyry
children.description: Soft, greasy, platy flakes of MoS2 in the quartz and feldspar of a granitic porphyry, associated with the copper minerals of the Climax and Henderson molybdenum operations or with the Bingham copper concentrate. The leaf is the same porphyry intrusion the copper branch ends in, which is a genuine shared endpoint.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: molybdenite MoS2, as 1-10 cm flakes in veinlets

children.name: Scheelite and wolframite: the limestone vein alternative
children.description: Almost all molybdenum came from porphyry copper, but there is a second source: the molybdenite that sits in the tungsten skarn and vein deposits - the Climax and Henderson molybdenum orebodies in Colorado were actually a Colorado Clueca-type porphyry with a molybdenum-bearing skarn. The relevant geology is that molybdenum and tungsten share the hydrothermal vein environment, and scheelite (CaWO4) and molybdenite (MoS2) are sometimes intergrown in the same greisen. So the molybdenum in a C64's injection-moulding die could in principle have come out of the same vein as a tungsten electrode - which is the point the brief made when it said no tungsten in a 1982 C64, and this is where that fact becomes interesting: the tungsten was there, in the same rock, but it went into other industries.

facts.label: Molybdenite
facts.value: MoS2 in vein and skarn greisen

facts.label: Companion
facts.value: scheelite CaWO4 and wolframite, often in the same vein

children.note: Low confidence on the specifics of the Climax-Henderson molybdenum-greisen relationship; the general geology of molybdenum-tungsten greisen association is well established but the particular orebody detail is not something I would assert.

children.name: Vanadium: a small alloying element
children.description: Included only because tool steel and the AOD of stainless steel both use it, and because the source is genuinely unusual. Most vanadium came from vanadiferous titanomagnetite - a magnetite containing 1-6% vanadium - which was a problem in the iron ore of the Panzhihua district in China and in the U.S. and Canadian Mesabi ranges until somebody worked out how to separate it. By 1982 the US route was slag processing: the titanomagnetite went into a blast furnace or an oxygen converter, and the vanadium reported to the slag, and the slag was ground and reprocessed. The other source is spent petroleum catalyst, which by the late 1980s was a genuine and growing vanadium source. Both of those are consequences of processes elsewhere in this tree.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: vanadiferous titanomagnetite slag; spent petroleum hydrodesulphurisation catalyst

facts.label: Form sold
facts.value: ferrovanadium at 40-80% V

facts.label: Use
facts.value: microalloying in HSLA steel, tool steel and stainless

children.note: Vanadium's involvement in both the iron ore branch and the petroleum branch is a real and well-documented piece of industrial cross-dependence; medium confidence on the 1982 proportions.

children.name: Vanadiferous titanomagnetite
children.description: The leaf: a magnetite with the iron partly replaced by titanium and vanadium, occurring as an iron ore in itself. At Panzhihua it is a magnetite-ilmenite ore in a vanadium-bearing magnetite gabbro; in the Mesabi it was a nuisance component of the taconite. Either way it is an iron ore, and the vanadium is a consequence of somebody mining iron.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: magnetite with Ti and V substitution; also a coexisting ilmenite

children.name: Vacuum melting and the purity of tool steel
children.description: A tool steel that contains a hundred parts per million of sulphur will embrittle, and one with two hundred ppm of oxygen will pit. So the melt for a die is made in a vacuum induction or a vacuum arc furnace rather than in an air-melted crucible, and the ingot is remelted by the VAR or the EB process - electron beam - which gives a fine equiaxed grain with no inclusions and no segregation. The vacuum arc furnace is a modified version of the vacuum-arc remelting process that the titanium industry invented, and by 1982 the extrusion die industry and the mould industry both bought them.

facts.label: Processes
facts.value: VIM, then VAR or EBCHM remelting

facts.label: Sulphur target
facts.value: below about 0.005% for a good die steel

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: a 2 t extrusion die blank in vacuum-processed SKD61 cost several times a conventionally cast one

children.note: Medium confidence; vacuum melting of tool steel is standard practice but the specific purity targets are supplier-specific.

metal.hematite.name: Hematite (Fe2O3) and the Pilbara
metal.hematite.description: Hematite is a steel-grey to red mineral that occurs as specular crystals, as kidney ore, and - the mass of the world's supply - as itabirite and hematite replacements in a banded iron formation. The Pilbara ore bodies in Western Australia are the richest hematite in the world at 62-66% Fe with almost no gangue, and the Brockman and Hamersley ranges were being mined at full rate by 1982. The ore ships from Port Hedland, where the ore handling and ship loaders are among the largest machines ever built.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: lump ore, fines, and pellet feed fine

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Banded iron formation: alternating layers of hematite and chert, 2.0-1.8 Ga

children.name: Pilbara open-pit iron mine and the ore loader
children.description: The Pilbara mines in 1982 were the mining engineering standard for the industry. A 15 m bench, 100-250 tonne haul trucks, 3-4 cubic metre shovels, and - this is the part everybody photographs - the huge travelling ore loaders that straddle the width of a haul truck and scoop up a 40-60 tonne load in one pass. The ore is crushed to 250 mm and conveyed up a 1.5 km incline to a stockyard, and then a 3-4 million tonne bulk carrier is loaded in about 20 hours at Port Hedland. One Pilbara mine shipped 40-100 Mt a year in the mid-1980s.

facts.label: Truck
facts.value: 100-150 t payload; some 250 t

facts.label: Loader
facts.value: travelling bridge-type ore loader, 60-120 t bucket, 1-1.5 km/h

facts.label: Shipping
facts.value: a 180,000-250,000 dwt bulk carrier loaded in 12-24 h

children.name: Banded iron formation: a chemical precipitate from seawater
children.description: The leaf of the whole iron and steel branch, and one of the great ones. Around 2.0-1.8 billion years ago, the oceans contained dissolved ferrous iron and oxygen appeared in the atmosphere as a result of an earlier generation of photosynthetic organisms. Wherever the oxygen-rich surface water sank and met the anoxic iron-rich deep water, the iron oxidised and precipitated, as a jelly of iron oxide that settled as a chemical mud. It compacted into alternating silica and iron bands, and it is that banding which gives the rock its name and which makes the high-grade hematite ore bodies on the Hamersley Range the size they are. So the iron in a C64 chassis began, two billion years ago, as an oxide precipitating out of an ocean.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: 2.0-1.8 Ga, the Great Oxidation Event interval

facts.label: Lithology
facts.value: alternating magnetite and chert (BIF), later metamorphosed to hematite

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: a marine chemical precipitate on a continental shelf

children.name: The silica and iron oxide banding
children.description: The leaf, described properly: a stack of alternating 1 mm to 10 m bands of chert (cryptocrystalline silica) and iron oxide, the whole thing metamorphosed, with the hematite in the oxidised upper part and magnetite in the reduced lower part and the P-rich band - the band that gives the Sudbury nickel deposit and the Phalaborwa copper - where fossil bacteria oxidised the iron. Each band is a single depositional event or a group of them, and the ore-to-waste ratio of a Banded Iron Formation is often 1:2, so the pit that produces a tonne of iron ore has to move three tonnes of rock.

facts.label: Band thickness
facts.value: 1 mm to 10 m, most of them millimetres

facts.label: Ore to waste
facts.value: often 1:2 to 1:5

facts.label: Biogenicity
facts.value: the banded iron formations are associated with the rise of photosynthetic organisms and the Great Oxidation Event

children.note: The biogenic origin of banded iron formations is now a well-established interpretation; high confidence.

children.name: Crushing, screening and the lump/fines split
children.description: The ore is crushed in a gyratory and then on a screen, and the product is split three ways: lump ore above 6.3 mm that goes straight into the blast furnace, fines below 6.3 mm that must be sintered or pelletised, and a reject stream of the banded iron formation that is too low grade to smelt. The lump/fines split is a commercial decision rather than a metallurgical one: in 1982 the steelmakers wanted as much direct-shipping lump as possible because it avoided the sintering plant's capital and its fuel.

facts.label: Lump
facts.value: above 6.3 mm, direct to the blast furnace

facts.label: Fines
facts.value: below 6.3 mm, to the sinter strand or the pellet plant

facts.label: Rejects
facts.value: the banded iron formation itself, at 30-45% Fe, often stockpiled

children.name: The ore stockyard and the ship loader
children.description: Because the ships are 180,000-250,000 dwt and the mine's output is lumpy, the ore goes into a 1-2 million tonne stockyard with a stacker and a travelling shiploader. The shiploader is a 100 m long gantry on rails with a slewing chute that trims the ship's hold as it loads, so a 250,000 dwt vessel is filled flat without a bulker or a trimming machine. The whole Pilbara export chain - mine, conveyor, stockyard, loader, ship - was built to move one commodity in enormous tonnage at very low cost, and it is the reason Australian iron ore is the cheapest iron in the world.

facts.label: Stockyard
facts.value: 1-2 Mt live capacity, stacker and a travelling tripper

facts.label: Shiploader
facts.value: travelling, slewing, with a trimming chute

facts.label: Loading rate
facts.value: 1,500-10,000 t per hour

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: 180,000-250,000 dwt capesize, loaded in 12-24 h

metal.magnetite.name: Magnetite (Fe3O4) and the taconite route
metal.magnetite.description: The other main ore. Magnetite is magnetic, so it can be separated from a low-grade run of rock by magnetic separation, and that changes the economics of the whole business. The Mesabi taconite of Minnesota at 25-32% Fe is ground to 30-45 um and concentrated to 65-70% Fe pellets on a concentrator with a 3 m diameter separator. Krivoy Rog and the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly in the Soviet Union are magnetite districts at 55-65%, worked down to 100 m depths with sublevel stoping. The magnetite is also roasted in a fluidised bed to hematite before magnetic separation, or sintered and reduced.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 25-32% Fe for taconite; 55-65% for the Krivoy Rog magnetite

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: grinding to 30-45 um and magnetic separation; roasting of the concentrate

facts.label: Product
facts.value: taconite pellets at 65-70% Fe

children.name: Magnetic separation and the taconite concentrator
children.description: The separator is a rotating drum 1-2.5 m in diameter with a 4-10 pole magnet of 400-1,200 gauss at the drum surface, or a high-gradient can of ferrite pole pieces that achieves 10,000-20,000 gauss on the tips. Slurry flows past and the magnetic grains are held to the drum and carried around until they fall off the other side. With the magnetoferrite in the drum the recovery of a 30-45 um magnetite grain is above 95%. A taconite concentrator at 20-40 Mt a year is one of the largest single streams of water and solids in the world, and the tailings are a billion-tonne deposit in their own right.

facts.label: Drum separator
facts.value: 1-2.5 m diameter, 400-1200 gauss at the surface; high-gradient types to 20,000 gauss

facts.label: Grind
facts.value: 30-45 um before separation

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 65-70% Fe, 2-4% silica

children.note: Separator field strengths and grind targets are standard class values; medium confidence.

children.name: Ferrite magnets in the separator
children.description: A short and important cross-link: the permanent magnet inside a magnetic separator is a ferrite - barium ferrite or strontium ferrite, sintered like the power ferrites but with a different composition and without the permeability requirement. So the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace contains ferrite magnets, and the ferrite branch of this file is the same powder metallurgy.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 or BaFe12O19, sintered; remanence ~0.3-0.4 T

facts.label: In 1982
facts.value: ferrite magnets had largely displaced alnico in small motors and magnetic separators; the modern Nd-Fe-B magnets did not arrive until the 1980s

children.note: Nd-Fe-B magnets were commercialised around 1982-84, so an 1982 separator would be ferrite or alnico, not Nd-Fe-B. Medium-high confidence.

children.name: Deep underground magnetite mining
children.description: The Soviet iron ore industry - Krivoy Rog, the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly, and the Khibiny - mined massive magnetite bodies at 300-1000 m with sublevel stoping, sublevel caving and room-and-pillar, on a scale with no real comparison anywhere else. The magnetite ore was magnetic enough that the mine was lit by the ore's own remanence in the early shafts. It is included to mark that the iron chain has two completely different mining geometries: a 300 m wide surface pit in Western Australia, and a 100 m thick tabular body a kilometre down in Ukraine.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sublevel stoping with delayed fill, sublevel caving, or panel caving

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: 300-1,000 m, with shafts to 1,500 m

children.name: Fluidised-bed roasting of magnetite concentrate
children.description: The Krivoy Rog and Finnish magnetite concentrates were roasted before magnetic separation and before the blast furnace, because a magnetite concentrate that has been oxidised to hematite sinter is far easier to reduce - hematite is the reducible oxide, magnetite is not. A fluidised bed of concentrate with a magnetite-gangue composition can be held at 700-800 C indefinitely without sintering, and it is the only economical way to oxidise a hundred thousand tonnes of fine concentrate. The plant is a tall rectangular refractory-lined box with a bed of nozzles on the floor and water-cooled walls, and its throughput is enormous.

facts.label: Feed size
facts.value: under 0.1 mm concentrate

facts.label: Product
facts.value: hematite sinter, with the sulphur and the alkalis driven off

children.note: Medium confidence; the fluidised-bed roast is standard Soviet and Finnish practice but the parameters are plant-specific.

children.name: Oxide pellets and the direct reduction route
children.description: A different branch of the same ore: magnetite concentrate is the only ore that can be reduced to sponge iron directly, without coke, by a hydrogen-nitrogen mixture at 1100-1200 C in a shaft furnace. That is the MIDOR and HYL processes, which by 1982 were the strategic reserve of the steel industry in the oil shock years - a few per cent of world steel but a hedge, and the reason a Soviet or Brazilian or Venezuelan integrated steelworks would spend a decade building an ore-based direct-reduction plant. It is also the only ore that can be shipped as a pellet and reduced at a distant site without smelting.

facts.label: Gas
facts.value: natural gas reformed to H2/N2 at 55-65% H2

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: magnetite or hematite pellets, 8-16 mm

facts.label: 1982 share
facts.value: a small percentage of world steel, but a strategic one after 1973

children.note: Direct reduction was a genuine 1980s strategic technology; medium confidence on the 1982 share.

metal.ferrite.mnzn.name: MnZn power ferrite
metal.ferrite.mnzn.description: The material of the C64's transformer core, the rectifier choke and the bulk filter chokes. Its job is to carry a large alternating flux at 15-65 kHz with as little loss and as little audible noise as possible, and that is a tight compromise: MnO raises the permeability and lowers the magnetostriction (which is what stops the transformer singing), ZnO raises the resistivity and pushes the Curie point up but lowers the saturation, and the two oxides partly cancel. A 1982 E-core for the C64's supply would be MnZn at roughly 0.2-0.35 W/cycle at 16 kHz and about 0.35 T saturation.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Fe2O3 48-52 wt%, MnO 20-30 wt%, ZnO 10-20 wt%, balance trace dopants

facts.label: Core loss
facts.value: roughly 0.2-0.5 W/cycle at 16 kHz, 200 mT, for an E-core

facts.label: Curie point
facts.value: >200 C, which is what lets a hot supply stay a ferrite

children.name: E/EI/EE core geometry and the transformer
children.description: The shape is dictated by the winding, and the 1982 supply for small switchers was a pair of E cores with a centre leg and a window, assembled 'E-E' or interleaved 'EI' so that the joint is staggered and the effective air gap is halved. The window has to fit the magnetising inductance and the wire; the cross-section is set by the core loss target. The same ferrite pressing produces E, EI, EE, U, toroid, drum and bobbin cores, and the shapes are made by different tools in the same press. The C64's transformer is one of the smallest: perhaps 25 mm across, 30-40 turns of 0.3 mm magnet wire on a bobbin, and a gap cut into the centre leg with a scraper to set the inductance.

facts.label: Typical core
facts.value: E or EE, about 20-30 mm across the window

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 0.2-1.0 mm cut in one leg with a carbide scraper to set the inductance

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 15-65 kHz for a C64-class switcher

children.note: The exact core size and gap in the Commodore PSU transformer need the part itself; medium confidence on the range.

children.name: Cutting the air gap in the centre leg
children.description: An ungapped ferrite E core has a very high inductance and would not regulate a switch-mode supply; the switcher's magnetising current would be wrong and the whole design fails. So the gap is made deliberately, and on a 1982 E core it was cut with a carbide-tipped scraper - literally a hand blade run along the face of the centre leg - to 0.2-1.0 mm. Cutting rather than inserting a gap material keeps the inductance high and spreads the gap's fringing over an area, and it does it with a machine a ferrite buyer can operate. The tolerance of that hand cut is what sets the inductance tolerance, and the whole thing is one of the more beautiful pieces of 1980s manufacturing: a blade and a number.

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 0.2-1.0 mm, cut with a carbide scraper

facts.label: Why cut
facts.value: spreads the fringing flux over an area and keeps the inductance high

facts.label: Control
facts.value: the gap sets the inductance, so the transformer builder measured it and often adjusted it per core

children.note: Medium confidence; the scraper-gap technique is very widely documented for small E and EE cores of that era.

children.name: Filter chokes and the common-mode choke
children.description: The bulk filter chokes in a 1982 linear-supply C64 are 470 uH to a few millihenry with a current rating of 1-3 A, wound on an EE or a bobbin core of the same MnZn material. The switch-mode version instead has a common-mode choke: two windings on a single core, arranged so the two currents are equal and opposite, so the flux cancels and the choke does not need to store any energy - its only job is to present a high impedance to the common-mode noise on the mains lead. Both are the same pressed ceramic with a different winding.

facts.label: Linear filter choke
facts.value: 0.5-10 mH, 1-3 A, MnZn EE core

facts.label: Common mode choke
facts.value: 2-20 mH, bifilar or two-hole core, high common-mode impedance at 0.1-10 MHz

children.note: The C64 power supply of 1982 is a linear supply with a big transformer and 5 V regulator; the common-mode choke and the switcher belong to the later C64 power supplies and to the monitor. Medium confidence on which is which without the specific PSU. The magnetics agent owns the topology.

children.name: Dopants: calcium, silicon, cobalt and the grain boundaries
children.description: The last half percent of the ferrite recipe does most of the work. A small calcium and silicon addition forms a grain-boundary phase that makes the grain boundaries insulating and therefore suppresses eddy-current loss. Cobalt raises the anisotropy and the permeability at low field, which matters for a filter inductor. Lithium prevents wall-jumping in a high-coercivity ferrite. These additions are 0.1-2% each and they are why a power ferrite's chemistry is a trade secret and why the same nominal composition from two suppliers will not behave the same way.

facts.label: Ca and Si
facts.value: 0.1-1% each, to form an insulating grain-boundary phase

facts.label: Co
facts.value: 0.1-3% for low-field permeability and anisotropy

facts.label: Li
facts.value: used in high-coercivity ferrite for memory and inductor cores

children.note: Medium confidence; the dopant effects are well established in the ferrite literature but the specific recipes are proprietary.

metal.ferrite.nizn.name: NiZn ferrite
metal.ferrite.nizn.description: The second family. Substituting nickel oxide for most of the manganese oxide raises the resistivity of the grain boundary by a factor of a hundred, so the eddy-current loss at high frequency collapses and NiZn is usable to about 100 MHz instead of 1 MHz. The price is a permeability of only 15-100 where MnZn gives a thousand, and a low saturation. In the C64 it is the RF modulator transformer and the video output circuitry, and off the board it is the small cylindrical bead slipped onto a wire to kill EMI. NiZn is pressed and sintered the same way; the only real differences are the raw material and the sintering atmosphere.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Fe2O3 50-55 wt%, NiO 10-30 wt%, ZnO 15-35 wt%, plus copper and cobalt dopants

facts.label: Bandwidth
facts.value: 1 MHz to about 200 MHz

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1150-1250 C in air; the copper content controls the loss

children.name: Ferrite bead: a small cylinder of NiZn or MnZn
children.description: A bead is just a pressed and fired ferrite with a hole through it, made on a bead press with a die that forms the cylinder in a few milliseconds. A 1982 board might carry a dozen: one on each supply line to the analogue section, one on the video line, one or two on the mains lead of the supply. The bead impedance is a rising curve with frequency, set entirely by the ferrite's complex permeability, and the bead's job is to convert a common-mode current into a small radiated field and a small conducted noise instead of a large one. The bead and the RF transformer are the same pressed powder.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 2-10 mm diameter, 2-6 mm long, bore 0.5-2 mm

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 50-1000 ohm at 100 MHz for a 6 mm bead

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 0.1-2 A DC, with the bead heating in free air

children.note: The exact bead count and sizes on the C64 mainboard are the magnetics/interconnect agent's call; the material route here is certain.

children.name: The RF modulator coil
children.description: The C64's TV modulator, which puts the composite video onto the RF of channel 3 or 4 so a television could display the machine, contains a small ferrite-loaded coil - a few turns of enamelled copper wire on a ferrite core or threaded through a ferrite bead. This is the one place in the machine where nickel-zinc ferrite is genuinely a radio-frequency component rather than a filter. The modulator itself and the television are the optics/television agents' business; the core is this branch's.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: channel 3 at 61.25 MHz or channel 4 at 67.25 MHz in the PAL/NTSC modulator

facts.label: Core
facts.value: a small NiZn bead or rod, 5-15 mm

children.note: Medium confidence: the modulator coil construction in the Commodore 250407 would need the actual part.

children.name: NiZn dopants: copper, cobalt and calcium
children.description: The NiZn family is doped with copper and cobalt to shape the grain-boundary physics, and with calcium to control the sintering. The NiZn product of the 1980s was deliberately split by composition into a high-permeability low-loss grade for transformers below 1 MHz and a very high-permeability grade for read heads and for antenna cores, and the difference between them was a fraction of a percent of dopant. It is a good example of a material in which the last tenth of a percent of the recipe is the difference between two products.

facts.label: Dopants
facts.value: Cu and Co to control the grain-boundary resistivity and permeability; Ca to control sintering

facts.label: Products
facts.value: high-permeability low-loss, and very high-permeability grades

children.note: Medium confidence; the effects are well established, the recipes are proprietary.

children.name: The nickel and cobalt raw materials for NiZn
children.description: The Ni-Zn family's nickel does not come as metal. It comes as nickel oxide, or as green nickel hydroxide precipitate from a laterite leach, and the cobalt comes either as cobalt metal or - much more cheaply, and this is the point - as a cobalt hydroxide carried out of the Sherritt-Gordon ammonia circuit as a precipitate, or as cobalt recovered from the spent nickel-catalyst streams. So the cobalt in a NiZn ferrite and the cobalt in a superalloy came out of the same nickel refinery, and that nickel refinery in 1982 was in the middle of a genuine cobalt supply crisis, which is a nice way for a ferrite material to be affected by a metals-market event.

facts.label: Nickel source
facts.value: nickel oxide or green nickel hydroxide precipitate, not metal

facts.label: Cobalt source
facts.value: cobalt hydroxide from the nickel circuit, or recovered metal

children.note: Low confidence on the specific ferrite raw-material supply chains; the cobalt crisis of 1982-83 is well documented but its effect on ferrite raw materials is not.

metal.barium.titanate.name: Barium titanate powder (BaTiO3)
metal.barium.titanate.description: The solid-state reaction of barium carbonate with titanium dioxide: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2. It happens in a calcination at 1100-1350 C, in a rotary kiln or a batch furnace, and the outcome is a powder of perovskite-structured grains - a cubic cell with the titanium atom at the centre of an octahedron of six oxygens and the barium in the twelve-fold site between them. It has to be de-aerated and it must be calcined in an atmosphere that keeps the titanium from being reduced to the +3 state, because a reduced titanate is a semiconductor and a lossy dielectric. This is a real problem in the ceramic industry and the reason the calciner is sealed and the oxygen partial pressure controlled. The bulk material is then ball-milled to sub-micron before the powder is pressed or cast into a film.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: perovskite, ABO3, a cubic cell with Ti in an octahedron of O6 and Ba in the 12-fold site

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ball-milled to 0.1-1 um for the dielectric; coarse powder for the low-end grades

facts.label: Reducing atmosphere
facts.value: must be avoided: Ti4+ reduced to Ti3+ turns the material semiconducting and lossy

children.name: Titanium dioxide from rutile sand
children.description: The titanium dioxide half of the equation, and it comes from a beach sand. Ilmenite, a titanium-iron oxide, is dredged from the heavy-mineral beach sands of the Cap York coast in Queensland, of Kerala in India, of the Mozambique coast and of the Richards Bay area of South Africa; it is separated from the zircon and the rutile by gravity and electrostatic separation; and it is then either chlorinated with coke and chlorine at 900-1000 C to give TiCl4, which is oxidised in a flame to give the pigment TiO2, or sulfided and digested to give synthetic rutile and then the pigment. Rutile, the TiO2 mineral itself, is also separated directly from the sand and is the higher-grade feed for ceramic-grade titanium dioxide. The pigment industry is by far the biggest user of titanium dioxide in 1982, and barium titanate is a small, very high-value user of the same commodity.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: ilmenite at 42-60% TiO2, and rutile at 90-95% TiO2, both from beach placer sands

facts.label: Chloride process
facts.value: ilmenite + coke + Cl2 at 900-1000 C -> TiCl4, then flame oxidation at 1200-1400 C -> TiO2 + Cl2

facts.label: Sulfate process
facts.value: ilmenite + concentrated H2SO4 -> titanyl sulphate, then hydrolysis and calcination

facts.label: Ceramic grade
facts.value: needs high purity and low iron; much of the pigment grade is too impure for a dielectric

children.name: Heavy mineral beach sand and the dredge
children.description: The leaf: a beach or dune sand a few metres thick carrying 1-10% heavy minerals - ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite, tourmaline - in a strip along the shoreline. A concentrator dredges a cutter suction pump from the shallow water, washes and upgrades on a shaking table and a spiral, then on gravity and electrostatic separators, recovering 200,000-300,000 t of ilmenite a year from a single operation. So the barium in a 1982 disk capacitor, having gone through a rotary kiln and a hydrogen sulphide stream, ends up in a titanium atom that came out of a Queensland beach.

facts.label: Sand grade
facts.value: 1-10% heavy minerals in a quartz sand

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: cutter-suction dredging of a beach or an offshore bar, with a gravity and electrostatic concentrator onshore

facts.label: Products
facts.value: ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite (and in Kerala, the monazite for thorium and rare earths)

children.name: The ceramic capacitor and its dielectric classes
children.description: The finished use. A 1982 C64 mainboard carries perhaps 30-60 ceramic capacitors, mostly small discs and a few multilayer blocks. The disc is a pressed or cast barium titanate body, sintered at 1250-1350 C, silver-coated on both faces and fired to make the electrodes, and dipped in an epoxy or phenolic encapsulant. The multilayer capacitor stacks hundreds of microns-thick dielectric layers with internal nickel or palladium electrodes, screen-printed and co-fired - a technology that was genuinely new in 1982 and was the reason a 10 nF 50 V part started to fit in a 1.6 mm-tall package. The dielectric classes are named by their temperature coefficient: X7R and Z5U for the general-purpose 1980s parts, Y5V for the high-capacitance low-stability ones.

facts.label: Multilayer
facts.value: 1-10 um dielectric layers, Ni or Pd internal electrodes, co-fired at 1200-1350 C in a reducing atmosphere, then re-oxidised

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: silver for discs (fired at 700-900 C); base-metal nickel for multilayer

children.note: The class nomenclature and the sintering temperatures are standard; the count of ceramic capacitors on a C64 mainboard is an estimate and belongs to the passives agent.

children.name: Grade the barium titanate powder into a dielectric class
children.description: The same powder cannot make a Y5V capacitor and an X7R one. Y5V is made from a fine, uniform, high-surface-area powder near the Curie point, where the dielectric constant is enormous and wildly temperature-dependent - a huge capacitance that changes by a factor of five over the working range. X7R is made from a coarser powder with barium zirconate or barium strontium titanate added, which flattens the temperature curve at the cost of the peak. So the capacitor 'class' is really a powder specification, and the class marking on the part is a statement about the ball mill that ground it.

facts.label: Y5V
facts.value: fine powder near the Curie point, K of several thousand, very high temperature coefficient

facts.label: X7R
facts.value: coarser powder with solid solution, K of 1000-4000, +/-15% over -55 to +125 C

facts.label: Additives
facts.value: Ba(Zr,Ti)O3, Ba(Sr,Ti)O3, and rare-earth dopants for the high-capacitance grades

children.note: Medium confidence; the class-to-chemistry mapping is standard and the recipes are proprietary.

children.name: Co-fire the internal electrodes in a low-oxygen atmosphere
children.description: A multilayer capacitor's internal electrode is nickel or palladium, printed as a paste and co-fired with the ceramic. That will not work in air - the ceramic would reduce and become a lossy semiconductor - so the whole stack is fired in a low-oxygen atmosphere at 1200-1350 C in hydrogen or in a nitrogen-hydrogen mix, and then re-oxidised afterwards so the barium titanate goes back to being an insulator. The oxygen partial pressure is controlled to a few millibars. It is the most metallurgically demanding step in the whole electronics supply chain that nobody ever sees, and it is a barium carbonate problem.

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: nickel or palladium paste, screen-printed

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: low pO2, a few millibars, in H2 or N2/H2

facts.label: Reoxidation
facts.value: a separate anneal afterwards to restore the insulator

children.note: Medium confidence; the co-firing atmosphere is standard practice but the exact pO2 is proprietary.
